The tone is terse, violent, sometimes comic and mostly realistic, though supernatural elements intrude. Cú Chulainn has superhuman fighting skills from his semi-divine ancestry, and in his battle frenzy, the ríastrad, he becomes an unrecognisable monster who knows neither friend nor foe.

Unlike most early Irish historical tradition, which presents ancient Ireland as largely united under High Kings, these tales depict a country of local and provincial kingdoms with no effective central authority. It is a pagan, pastoral society ruled by a warrior aristocracy, where wealth is counted in cattle, warfare takes the form of cattle raids and single combats at fords, and fosterage binds aristocratic families.

The events are traditionally placed around the time of Christ, a chronology that is an artificial attempt by Christian monks to synchronise native tradition with classical and biblical history. Scholars have long disagreed about the historical value of the tales. Eugene O’Curry and Kuno Meyer thought them essentially historical, T. F. O’Rahilly thought the characters euhemerised gods, and Kenneth H. Jackson saw authentic Iron Age Celtic traditions preserved. Others stress similarities with early medieval Irish society.

The cycle gave material to Irish writers of the Gaelic revival. Lady Gregory’s Cuchulain of Muirthemne (1902) retold most of the important stories, and W. B. Yeats wrote plays on them, from On Baile’s Strand (1904) onwards.
ulster-unionist-party: Modern organised unionism emerged after William Ewart Gladstone introduced the first of three Home Rule Bills in 1886. In September 1904 Arthur Balfour's Conservative government published proposals for limited devolution to Ireland, which alarmed Irish unionists, and the Ulster Unionist Council was formed on 3 March 1905 as a co-ordinating body. From the beginning it had a strong association with the Orange Order, whose delegates made up 25 per cent of the original council. Sir Edward Carson became the first leader of the Ulster Unionist Party in 1910 and in 1912 took the lead in forming the Ulster Volunteers.

After the Government of Ireland Act 1920 partitioned Ireland, the party took control of the new Government of Northern Ireland in 1921. Carson opposed partition and refused to be Prime Minister; Sir James Craig led the government until his death in November 1940, and Terence O'Neill was among his successors. In the 1960s civil rights campaigners called for changes to housing allocation and the local government franchise; O'Neill's reforms divided the party, and he resigned after the 1969 election. After Bloody Sunday the British Government threatened to remove control of security from the devolved government, and Brian Faulkner resigned with his cabinet; the Parliament of Northern Ireland was suspended and then abolished in 1972. The Sunningdale Agreement of 1973 split the party.

Until 1972 the party's MPs took the Conservative whip at Westminster, and it left the National Union of Conservative and Unionist Associations in 1985 in protest at the Anglo-Irish Agreement. Under David Trimble the party helped negotiate the Good Friday Agreement of 1998, and Trimble served as first First Minister from 1998 to 2002; he and John Hume shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 1998. The agreement split the party into pro- and anti-agreement factions. The Democratic Unionist Party overtook it as the largest unionist party in 2003, and in 2010 it was left without a seat in the House of Commons for the first time.
ulugh-beg: Ulugh Beg was born on 22 March 1394 in Sultaniyeh, during his grandfather Timur's invasion of Persia, and was named Mīrzā Muhammad Tāraghay. He was the eldest son of Shah Rukh and Gawhar Shad. Ulugh Beg, meaning roughly Great Ruler, was a title and not a personal name; it is the Turkic equivalent of Timur's title Amīr-e Kabīr.

As a child he travelled through much of the Middle East and India as Timur extended his conquests. After Timur's death Shah Rukh moved the capital to Herat, and in 1409 the sixteen-year-old Ulugh Beg became governor of Samarkand. In 1411 he was named sovereign ruler of the whole of Mavarannahr.

Ulugh Beg set out to make Samarkand an intellectual centre. Between 1417 and 1420 he built a madrasa on Registan Square and invited astronomers and mathematicians to teach there, among them Qadi Zada al-Rumi and later Jamshid al-Kashi. His best-known pupil in astronomy was Ali Qushchi. He built an observatory in Samarkand between 1424 and 1429, whose largest instrument, the Fakhri sextant, had a radius of about 36 metres. With it he compiled a star catalogue, the Zij-i-Sultani, based on new observations, which is generally considered the best between those of Ptolemy and Tycho Brahe.

He measured the length of the sidereal year and the Earth's axial tilt, and wrote trigonometric tables of sines and tangents correct to at least eight decimal places. He also kept up diplomacy with the Ming dynasty, exchanging envoys with the Yongle emperor from 1416. His military record was weaker. A campaign against Moghulistan in 1425 left its ruler Shir Muhammad in power, and in 1427 his army was defeated by Baraq, Khan of the Golden Horde, near Sighnaq. It was the last campaign he led against a neighbouring power.

On the death of Shah Rukh in 1447, Ulugh Beg marched against his nephew Ala al-Dawla, who had claimed rule at Herat, and was defeated there in 1448 by Abul-Qasim Babur Mirza. His eldest son Abdal-Latif Mirza then rebelled against him at Balkh, and Ulugh Beg surrendered to him at Samarkand.

Abdal-Latif allowed him to set out on pilgrimage to Mecca but had him assassinated in 1449. His nephew Abdallah Mirza later restored his reputation and placed his remains at Timur's feet in the Gur-e-Amir, where Soviet archaeologists found them in 1941. A crater on the Moon, named by Johann Heinrich von Mädler on his 1830 map, and the asteroid 2439 Ulugbek bear his name.
ulugh-beg-observatory: Ulugh Beg, the son of Shah Rukh and grandson of Amir Timur, became ruler of Samarkand and was skilled in mathematics and astronomy. The foundation of the observatory was laid in the first half of the 1420s, and it was completed around 1428, although the year of completion is still debated. He invited more than 60 mathematicians and astronomers, among them Jamshid al-Kashi, Salah al-Din Qadi Zada Rumi and Ali Qushji. Al-Kashi was the first director, Qadi Zada the second, and Qushji the last. The design followed the plans of the Maragha observatory, associated with Nasir al-Din al-Tusi.

The observatory declined after Ulugh Beg was assassinated by his son Abd al-Latif around 1449. The astronomers were driven away and the building was destroyed. The Russian archaeologist Vassily Vyatkin uncovered its remains in 1908.

The building stood on a hill and was cylindrical, about 46 metres across and 30 to 33 metres high, made of brick. Its main instrument was the sextant, with a radius of 40.04 metres, the largest astronomical instrument in the world at the time. To keep the building from being dangerously tall, part of the arc was set in a ditch about 2 metres wide below ground. One degree on its scale measured 70.2 centimetres. The building had three storeys, the first for the staff to live in, with observations made from the upper two.
A letter by al-Kashi to his father describes teaching largely from memory, strict adherence to Ptolemy's methods and an interest in astrology, and says that music and prosody were also studied.

The observatory's main product was the Zij-i Sultani, a Persian star catalogue and set of astronomical tables published in 1437, listing around 1,000 stars. It follows Ptolemy's planetary model, and Ulugh Beg worked on it with students and colleagues including al-Kashi and Qushji. It gave the tropical year as 365 days 5 hours 49 minutes 15 seconds, and the Earth's axial tilt as 23.5047 degrees. The Zij was used until the 19th century, and hundreds of manuscript copies survive. Today the foundations and the buried part of the quadrant are what remains of the original building. A museum opened in 1970 holds reproductions of manuscripts, astrolabes and a miniature reconstruction.
ulugh-khan: Ulugh Khan was originally named Almas Beg. His father, Shihabuddin Mas'ud, was the elder brother of Sultan Jalaluddin, founder of the Khalji dynasty, and both Almas Beg and his elder brother Alauddin married daughters of Jalaluddin. Under Jalaluddin he held the post of Akhur-beg, equivalent to master of the horse. In 1296, after Alauddin had raided Devagiri and kept the loot, Almas Beg assured the sultan of his brother's loyalty and persuaded him to visit Kara, where Alauddin killed him on 20 July 1296. The new sultan made his brother barbeg with the title Ulugh Khan, meaning Great Khan. He also held the iqta' of Bayana.

In November 1296 Alauddin sent him and Zafar Khan with an army of 30,000 to 40,000 against Multan, held by Jalaluddin's son Arkali Khan. After two months of siege the leaders of the defence went over to Delhi. Ulugh Khan promised Arkali Khan and his brother Ruknuddin Ibrahim that they would not be harmed, but imprisoned them once the city was occupied; they were later blinded or killed by Nusrat Khan on Alauddin's orders. According to the courtier Amir Khusrau, he reached the Sutlej River on 6 February 1298 and defeated the Mongols of the Chagatai Khanate there, with 20,000 Mongol dead.

On the way back from Gujarat in 1299, near Jalore, he and Nusrat Khan punished soldiers for withholding the khums, the fifth of the loot due to the treasury. Recently converted Mongol soldiers mutinied; some 2,000 to 3,000 attacked his camp and killed a nephew of Alauddin whom they took for him. Against Hammira of Ranthambore in 1301 he defeated and killed the general Bhimasimha at the Banas River, but after Nusrat Khan was killed in the siege he was forced back to Jhain, and Alauddin came in person and took the fort in July 1301.

Ordered to prepare a march on the Kakatiya capital Warangal, he assembled a large army but died a few months later. The chronicler Ziauddin Barani writes that Alauddin was greatly depressed and gave much in charity for his brother's soul. Barani's contemporary Isami claims instead that Alauddin had him poisoned, suspecting that he had been ready to take the throne when the sultan was wrongly reported dead; later chroniclers repeat this. The historian Banarsi Prasad Saksena dismisses Isami's account as false, while Kishori Saran Lal thinks it not impossible. Claims that he led the invasion of Gujarat in 1304, or governed it for 20 years, are of doubtful accuracy.
uluj-ali: Giovanni Dionigi Galeni was born to the seaman Birno Galeni and his wife Pippa de Cicco in the village of Le Castella in Calabria, in the Kingdom of Naples. His father wanted him to have a religious education, but on 29 April 1536, when he was about 17, he was captured by Ali Ahmed, a corsair captain of Barbarossa Hayreddin Pasha, and forced to serve as a galley slave. He took part in the Battle of Preveza in 1538 as an oar slave. Within a few years he converted to Islam, and by 1541 he was a corsair in the fleet of Turgut Reis. This was not unusual, since many Muslim corsairs were captured slaves who had converted.

Able and bold, he gained enough booty to buy a share in a brigantine out of Algiers and then to own a galley. He was given the administration of Samos in 1550, fought at Djerba in 1560 and was promoted to beylerbey of Alexandria in 1565. After Turgut Reis was killed at the Siege of Malta that year, he succeeded him as bey of Tripoli. In March 1568 Sultan Selim II appointed him Pasha and beylerbey of Algiers on the recommendation of Piyale Pasha.

In July 1570 he captured four of five Maltese galleys near Cape Passaro in Sicily. At the Battle of Lepanto on 7 October 1571 he commanded the left flank of Ali Pasha's fleet, outmanoeuvred Giovanni Andrea Doria and captured the flagship of the Knights of Malta with its great banner. When the defeat was plain he extracted his ships and gathered some forty scattered galleys and fustas, arriving at Constantinople with 87 vessels. Selim II gave him the title Kılıç, meaning Sword, and on 29 October 1571 made him Kapudan Pasha.

With Piyale Pasha he began to rebuild the fleet, adding heavier ships modelled on Venetian galleasses and heavier artillery. In 1574 he sailed to Tunis with 250 galleys, taking La Goulette on 25 August and the city on 13 September. He later put down a janissary mutiny in Algiers in 1578, took part in the Ottoman–Safavid War, led an expedition to Crimea in 1584 and suppressed revolts in Syria and Lebanon in 1585.

Kılıç Ali Pasha died in Constantinople on 21 June 1587. He is buried at the Kılıç Ali Paşa Mosque, built in 1580 and designed by Mimar Sinan; he also built baths in Istanbul in 1583. Several warships and submarines of the Turkish Navy bear his name, and a statue of him stands in the central square of Le Castella.
ulysses-s-grant: Grant was born Hiram Ulysses Grant on 27 April 1822, the first child of Jesse Root Grant, a Whig supporter and fervent abolitionist, and Hannah Simpson. The family moved to Georgetown, Ohio, in 1823. When Representative Thomas L. Hamer nominated him to the United States Military Academy at West Point in 1839, Hamer altered his name, and he was enlisted as U. S. Grant. He served in the Mexican–American War and married Julia Dent on 22 August 1848. After resigning in 1854 he had no trade, and seven years of financial struggle followed; he farmed near St. Louis and sold firewood on its street corners.

When the Civil War began in April 1861 Grant became colonel of the 21st Illinois Volunteer Infantry Regiment. His victories in the western theatre in 1862 brought him prominence, and in 1863 his Vicksburg campaign gave Union forces control of the Mississippi River. After Chattanooga, Abraham Lincoln promoted him to lieutenant general and command of all Union armies. Grant fought Robert E. Lee through the Overland Campaign in 1864, and a nine-month siege of Petersburg followed. Lee abandoned Petersburg and Richmond after a general assault ordered on 2 April 1865 and surrendered at Appomattox.

Nominated unanimously by the Republicans in 1868, Grant was sworn in as president on 4 March 1869 and urged ratification of the Fifteenth Amendment. He appointed Ely S. Parker, a Seneca, as Commissioner of Indian Affairs, the first Native American in the post. His second term was beset by scandals, and the Panic of 1873 began the Long Depression. Leaving office in 1877, he toured the world for about two and a half years, meeting Queen Victoria, Otto von Bismarck, Li Hongzhang and Emperor Meiji.

Grant failed to win the Republican nomination for a third term in 1880. His savings were depleted, and a railway venture in Mexico went bankrupt in 1884. That autumn he learned that a sore throat was cancer, possibly caused by his frequent cigar smoking, and he wrote his memoirs as he was dying. He died on 23 July 1885. At his death he was the most popular American and was memorialised as a symbol of national unity. His reputation suffered for a time under the Lost Cause mythology spread by Confederate sympathisers around the turn of the twentieth century.
umar-ibn-abd-al-aziz: Umar was probably born in Medina. His father, Abd al-Aziz ibn Marwan, belonged to the ruling Umayyad family, and his mother, Layla bint Asim, was a granddaughter of the second Rashidun caliph Umar. Historians later stressed this descent to set his character apart from other Umayyad caliphs. His father governed Egypt from 685, and Umar spent part of his childhood there before being educated in Medina, where he formed ties with pious men and transmitters of hadith.

Al-Walid I appointed him governor of Medina in 706, with his jurisdiction later extended to Mecca and Taif. Traditional accounts call him a just governor. From 707 he rebuilt and enlarged the Prophet's Mosque. The Hejaz became a refuge for Iraqi exiles fleeing al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, who pressured the caliph to dismiss Umar in 712. He stayed at court and became a principal adviser to Sulayman.

According to the traditional sources, Sulayman on his deathbed at Dabiq was persuaded by Raja ibn Haywa to name Umar as his successor, though Reinhard Eisener thinks Raja's role overstated. The choice passed over the descendants of Abd al-Malik, and Umar averted conflict by naming Yazid II as his own successor. He acceded on 22 September 717 and overhauled the provincial administrations, appointing governors for their reliability and integrity.

His most significant reform was the equality of Arab and non-Arab Muslims. Converts no longer paid the jizya, but their land became the property of their villages and stayed liable to the full kharaj, a safeguard against collapse of revenue. He restricted the appropriation of crown lands as private estates and is credited with ordering the first official collection of hadith. Because of the cost of campaigns and the losses at Constantinople, he withdrew the army from the siege, though Muslim forces in al-Andalus conquered and fortified Narbonne in his reign.

Umar fell ill on a journey and died between 5 and 10 February 720 at Dayr Sim'an near Maarat al-Numan, where he was buried in a plot he had bought with his own funds. Yazid II succeeded him. Muslim tradition is unanimous, in Hugh Kennedy's words, that he was pious and ruled like a true Muslim, unlike the other Umayyads. He was widely regarded in Medina as the Mahdi, and many Muslims count him the fifth rightly guided caliph. The Abbasids spared his body from the desecration they applied to other Umayyad caliphs. Kennedy calls him the most puzzling of the Marwanid rulers.
umar-ibn-al-khattab: Umar was born in Mecca, a member of the Banu Adi, a minor clan of the Quraysh, and later became its leader. Unusually among the Quraysh, he learned to read and write, and he appreciated poetry. He at first opposed Muhammad and the new faith and even set out to kill him, but on the way was turned aside by a clansman who told him that his own sister Fatima bint al-Khattab and her husband had secretly become Muslims. Umar converted in 616 and then became the first Muslim to pray openly in the Kaaba. He took part in nearly all of Muhammad's battles, and Muhammad gave him the title al-Fārūq, the Distinguisher.

After Muhammad's death on 8 June 632, Umar helped bring about Abu Bakr's election at the gathering at Saqifa, and he served Abu Bakr as chief adviser. He urged that the Quran be compiled into a single volume after the Battle of al-Yamama. Abu Bakr named him successor, over the objection of Talha ibn Ubayd Allah that Umar was too severe. Umar was the first to take the title amir al-mu'minin, Commander of the Faithful.

Under him the caliphate expanded across Syria, Egypt, Iraq, the Jazira and deep into Persia. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas commanded against the Sasanians in Iraq, where the Battle of al-Qadisiyyah led to the fall of Mesopotamia, and Amr ibn al-As led the conquest of Egypt. The Sasanian state was shattered at the Battle of Nahavand. Umar dismissed the successful general Khalid ibn al-Walid, reportedly to show that victory comes from God and to check a cult of personality around him.

Umar picked provincial governors for ability rather than tribal standing, and never appointed one for more than two years, so that none gathered too much local power. He set up a cabinet and formalised the Bayt al-mal, the central treasury at Medina, with provincial branches. Jews and Christians continued under their own legal and judicial arrangements. He is credited with canal works in Basra and a canal linking the Nile to the Red Sea.

In 644 Umar was assassinated by a Persian slave, Abu Lu'lu'a Firuz. His motive is unclear, though medieval sources point to a tax dispute with his master al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba. Sources differ on whether the assassin was executed or killed himself. Umar left no clear successor. Sunni Muslims revere him as a just ruler and the second of the rightly guided caliphs, remembered for his plain living, while Shia Muslims view him negatively.
umar-marvi: The tale is said to date back to the 14th century and probably originated in the Soomra period, between 1050 and 1350. It was first written down in the 16th century by Shah Abdul Karim of Bulri, the great-great-grandfather of Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai, in his Bayan ul Arifeen, known to Sindhis as Karim Jo Risalo. It also appears in two chronicles, the Tarikh-i Tahiri, compiled in 1621, and the Tuhfat-al-Kiram of 1766–67.

In the story as it is told, Marvi is a young Khaskheli girl of the Panhwar tribe, and her captor is Umar Soomro, then ruler of Umerkot, who wanted to marry her for her beauty. When she refused him she was held for several years in Umarkot Fort. She resists both the ruler's overtures and the temptation to live in the palace as a queen, preferring a simple rural life among her own village people.

In the Shah Jo Risalo the tale stands among seven popular tragic romances of Sindh, with Sassui Punnhun, Sohni Mehar, Lilan Chanesar, Noori Jam Tamachi, Sorath Rai Diyach and Momal Rano. Their heroines are commonly known as the Seven Queens of Sindh, or the seven heroines of Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai. Marvi is regarded, for her courage, as a symbol of love for one's soil.

The story has been retold in modern forms. A film, Umar Marvi, directed by Shaikh Hassan and produced by Syed Hussain Ali Shah Fazlani, who also acted in it, was released on 12 March 1956 as the first Sindhi-language feature film made in Pakistan. The Pakistan Television Corporation broadcast a serial, Marvi, in 1993, which set the story in modern times. The Indian writer Ram Panjwani wrote a Sindhi play, Umar Marui, and a Sindhi song of Coke Studio's fifteenth season, Aayi Aayi, was inspired by the tale.
umayyad-caliphate: Before Islam the Banu Umayya were a leading clan of the Quraysh of Mecca, dominating its trade with Syria. Under Abu Sufyan ibn Harb they led the Meccan opposition to the Prophet Muhammad, but after Muhammad captured Mecca in 630, Abu Sufyan and the Quraysh embraced Islam. The third caliph, Uthman ibn Affan, was also an Umayyad. Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, long the governor of Syria, became caliph in 661 after emerging victorious in the First Fitna, and Damascus became the capital.

During the Second Fitna the Sufyanid line of Mu'awiya was replaced in 684 by Marwan ibn al-Hakam, who won the Battle of Marj Rahit that August. His son Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan defeated the Zubayrids in 692, centralised power and pursued Arabization of the bureaucracy; government records, kept until then in Greek, Coptic and Persian, began to be written in Arabic. The Umayyads conquered the Maghreb, the Iberian Peninsula, Central Asia and Sindh, and at its largest the caliphate covered 11,000,000 to 15,000,000 square kilometres.

Hisham (r. 724–743) curtailed expansion. Constant warfare exhausted the caliphate, and discontent among non-Arab converts, who lacked the rights of Arab Muslims, helped cause the Abbasid revolution of the 740s. In 750 the Abbasids overthrew Marwan II and most of the Umayyad family was slain. In 756 Abd al-Rahman I, a grandson of Hisham, founded an independent state in al-Andalus with its capital at Córdoba.

The early caliphs followed Byzantine administrative practice, with branches for political affairs, military affairs, tax collection and religious administration, and governors appointed by the caliph in each province. The army was mainly Arab and salaried. The Umayyads minted the first coins struck by a Muslim government. Society had four classes: Arab Muslims, non-Arab Muslim clients, dhimmis such as Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians, who paid the jizya tax, and slaves. Christians, still the majority of the population, held prominent administrative posts under the early caliphs. Umayyad monuments include the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem and the Great Mosque of Damascus.
umayyad-mosque: The site has been a place of worship since the Iron Age, when the Arameans of Aram-Damascus built a temple to Hadad-Ramman, god of thunderstorms and rain. Under the Seleucids it was dedicated to Zeus, and after Roman conquest of Damascus in 64 BCE it became a temple of Jupiter, enlarged probably from the reign of Augustus. The Roman temenos walls still form the outer walls of the mosque.

Emperor Theodosius I turned the temple into a cathedral. After the Muslim conquest of Damascus in 634 a prayer room, a musalla, was set up in part of the building, and the Christians kept the rest. Al-Walid I, the sixth Umayyad caliph, took over the cathedral, returning other properties in the city to the Christians as compensation.

The mosque was built over nine years by thousands of labourers and artisans from the Islamic and Byzantine worlds, paid for from the war booty of Umayyad conquests and taxes on the Arab troops of Damascus. Al-Walid supervised the work and told the people of Damascus that he wished to add a fifth distinction to their climate, water, fruits and baths: this mosque. The plan has a large courtyard on the north, measuring with the whole complex 97 by 156 metres, and a prayer hall along the south wall with three parallel aisles crossed by a central nave leading to the mihrab.

The architect re-used the columns and arcades of the church. Gold mosaics of vegetal motifs covered some 4,000 square metres and are likely the largest in the world. Later rulers added to it. The Abbasid governor built the Dome of the Treasury in 789–90, and a minaret, the Minaret of the Bride, is credited to the reign of al-Ma'mun. Baybars ordered extensive restoration of its marble, mosaics and gilding in 1270, and the Mamluks added the Minaret of Qaitbay.

Medieval Muslim writers regarded the mosque as a wonder of the world. It is considered the oldest mosque still in use in its original form, and one of the few early mosques to keep the general structure of the early 8th century. Its plan has served as a model for congregational mosques, among them al-Azhar and the Baybars Mosque in Cairo, the Great Mosque of Cordoba and the Grand Mosques of Bursa and Edirne.

Christians and Muslims alike hold that the head of John the Baptist is buried there, a tradition from the 6th century, and two shrines commemorate Husayn ibn Ali. One hadith places the descent of Jesus at a white minaret in Damascus, which tradition identifies with the Minaret of Isa; most Muslim theologians read this symbolically.
umberto-i: Umberto was born in Turin on 14 March 1844, the son of Victor Emmanuel II and Archduchess Adelaide of Austria. His father distrusted him and gave him no training in politics or constitutional government; he was taught to be obedient and had to kiss his father's hand before speaking to him. From March 1858 he had a military career in the Royal Sardinian Army.

He was present at the battle of Solferino in 1859 and in 1866 commanded the XVI Division at Villafranca after the Italian defeat at Custoza. On 21 April 1868 he married his first cousin Margherita of Savoy, whose cultural interests and strong personality enhanced the popularity of the monarchy. Their only son was the future Victor Emmanuel III.

Umberto came to the throne on 9 January 1878 and took the title Umberto I of Italy. In November of that year the anarchist Giovanni Passannante attacked him with a dagger during a parade in Naples; the king warded off the blow with his sabre. He approved the Triple Alliance with Austria-Hungary and Germany, formalised in 1882, though many in Italy were hostile to an alliance with their former Austrian enemies. A strong militarist, he backed colonial expansion, which began in 1885 with the occupation of Massawa in Eritrea, and Italy also expanded into Somalia.

In December 1893 he appointed Francesco Crispi prime minister, who governed in an authoritarian manner. Italian forces were defeated at the Battle of Adwa in Ethiopia on 1 March 1896, which led to demonstrations in Rome. Social unrest grew late in his reign, with the spread of socialism and crackdowns on civil liberties. On 7 May 1898, during demonstrations over the price of bread, General Fiorenzo Bava Beccaris put Milan under military rule and ordered rifle fire and artillery against the crowds. The authorities counted 82 dead, and opposition sources claimed 400. Umberto telegraphed his congratulations and later decorated the general, which outraged much of public opinion.

On the evening of 29 July 1900, as the king returned from a military parade in Monza, the Italian-American anarchist Gaetano Bresci shot him in the chest, neck and left thigh. Contemporary reports and later scholarship give Bresci's motive as revenge for the victims of the Bava Beccaris massacre. Bresci said that he had killed not Umberto but the king, a principle.

He was found hanged in his cell on 22 May 1901. Umberto was buried in the Pantheon in Rome next to his father on 9 August 1900, the last member of the House of Savoy buried there, and his son Victor Emmanuel III succeeded him. The Umbertino style of architecture is named after him.
umberto-ii: Umberto was born at the Castle of Racconigi in Piedmont, the third child and only son of King Victor Emmanuel III of Italy and Jelena of Montenegro. Because the Italian throne was limited to male descendants, he was heir apparent from birth, and a Royal Decree of 29 September 1904 formalised his title of Prince of Piedmont. On 24 October 1929, in Brussels, on the day his betrothal was announced, Fernando de Rosa fired a single shot at him with a cry of 'Down with Mussolini!' and missed. He married Princess Marie José of Belgium in Rome on 8 January 1930, and they had four children.

Umberto became commander-in-chief of the Northern Armies and then the Southern ones, but the post was formal, since his father guarded the supreme command from Benito Mussolini. In June 1940 he ostensibly commanded Army Group West in the Italian invasion of France. The offensive went only a few kilometres into French territory, and his reputation was saved only because the defeated French signed an armistice with Italy on 24 June 1940. Promoted Marshal of Italy in 1942, he turned against the war after the defeats at Stalingrad and El Alamein. In September 1943 he reluctantly obeyed his father's order to flee Rome for the south, reaching Brindisi on 9 September, and for the first time openly criticised him.

In 1944 Victor Emmanuel III, compromised by his ties to Fascism, transferred his powers to Umberto, who became Lieutenant General of the Realm. After the liberation of Rome on 6 June 1944 the political parties pressed him to dismiss Pietro Badoglio as prime minister, and Ivanoe Bonomi was appointed. The king abdicated on 9 May 1946 in the hope of strengthening the monarchy before the institutional referendum. Umberto's reign lasted 34 days, until his formal deposition on 12 June 1946, and earned him the name May King. Voters chose to abolish the monarchy.

He spent the next 37 years in exile at Cascais in Portugal. The 1948 constitution barred male heirs of the defunct throne from Italian soil until 2002. He died in Geneva on 18 March 1983 and was interred at Hautecombe Abbey in France, the burial place of the House of Savoy for centuries.
umbria: Umbria is the only Italian region with neither a coastline nor a border with another country. It lies between Tuscany, Marche and Lazio, includes part of the central Apennines, and is crossed by the Tiber. Its capital is Perugia. In antiquity a pair of shallow lakes, the Lacus Clitorius and the Lacus Umber, covered the plain; the Romans drained them, an earthquake in the 4th century let the basin refill, and Benedictine monks began draining it again in the 13th century, a work completed in the 18th.

The region is named for the Umbri, an Italic people who spoke Umbrian, a language related to Latin and Oscan. Unlike the Etruscans, they mostly lived in small dwellings in the Apennines. The Etruscans, their chief enemies, drove them towards the uplands from about 700 to 500 BCE, with the Tiber as the border. The Iguvine Tablets of Gubbio, written in Umbrian around the turn of the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE, are the longest and most important document of the Osco-Umbrian languages.

Rome defeated the Samnites and their Gallic allies at Sentinum in 295 BCE, which began a period of integration; the Romans founded colonies such as Spoletium and built the Via Flaminia in 219 BCE. Perugia took Mark Antony's side in 40 BCE and was almost completely destroyed by Octavian. After Rome's fall, Ostrogoths and Byzantines fought over the region, and the Lombards founded the Duchy of Spoleto.

When Charlemagne conquered the Lombard kingdoms, some Umbrian territories passed to the Pope. Cities gained autonomy as comuni, and families such as the Baglioni in Perugia held power as signori. By the middle of the 14th century Cardinal Albornoz had brought the region into the Papal States, and the papacy ruled it uncontested until the end of the 18th century. Umbria was part of the Napoleonic Empire from 1809 to 1814 as the department of Trasimène. In 1860 the people of Perugia destroyed the Rocca Paolina, the fortress Pope Paul III had built there, in the year the region was annexed by Victor Emmanuel II.

Umbria is divided into the provinces of Perugia and Terni. Assisi, associated with Saint Francis, is a World Heritage Site. Gubbio holds the Festival of the Ceri each 15 May, a race held every year since 1160, and the Ceri appear on the region's coat of arms. Umbria is also where the umber pigment was originally extracted.
umkhonto-we-sizwe: Umkhonto we Sizwe, meaning Spear of the Nation and abbreviated MK, was the paramilitary wing of the African National Congress, founded by Nelson Mandela in the wake of the Sharpeville massacre. Its aim was to bring armed pressure on the National Party government to abandon apartheid. In June 1961 Mandela warned newspapers that a campaign of sabotage would follow unless the government called a national constitutional convention. In his speech at the end of the Rivonia Trial he said that he and colleagues had concluded that violence was inevitable and that it would be wrong to keep preaching non-violence while the government met peaceful demands with force. The first attacks came on 16 December 1961.

MK set up regional commands in the main centres, and its high command included Nelson Mandela, Oliver Tambo, Walter Sisulu, Govan Mbeki and Joe Slovo. The first target was an electrical substation, followed over a year and a half by attacks on government posts, machines and power facilities. The organisation was banned and classified as a terrorist group by the government, which answered with laws allowing detention without trial. On 11 July 1963 nineteen leaders were arrested at Liliesleaf Farm in Rivonia, its headquarters, leading to the Rivonia Trial.

In the 1980s MK attacked police stations and, in 1980, two Sasol oil-from-coal plants. From 1985 to 1987 it laid anti-tank mines on rural roads in the Northern Transvaal, a tactic abandoned because of civilian casualties among black labourers. The ANC counted 30 explosions and 23 deaths, the government 57 explosions and 25 deaths. Abroad, MK allied itself with the Zimbabwe People's Revolutionary Army, and a joint force crossing into Rhodesia in August 1967 was largely destroyed in Operation Nickel.

MK drew nearly all its equipment from the Soviet Union, through the South African Communist Party's contacts, and kept arms depots in Botswana, Mozambique and Swaziland. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission found that torture and executions without due process were routine in ANC camps, mainly between 1979 and 1989, though not official policy, and called the Durban bombing a gross violation of human rights. It also noted that, of the three main parties to the conflict, only the ANC committed itself to the Geneva Protocols. MK was formally disbanded at Orlando Stadium in Soweto on 16 December 1993.
umm-kulthum: Fatima Ibrahim es-Sayyid el-Beltagi was born on 4 May 1904 in the village of Tamay ez-Zahayra, in the markaz of Senbellawein. Her father, Ibrahim es-Sayyid el-Beltagi, was a rural imam and her mother, Fatmah el-Maleegi, a housewife. She learned to sing by listening to her father teach her older brother Khalid, and through him she learned to recite the Qur'an, which she reportedly memorised entirely. Her father at first dressed her in boys' clothes when she sang, because singing was unacceptable for girls in the countryside at that time.

Amin El Mahdi invited her into the cultural circles of Cairo. In 1924 she was introduced to the poet Ahmed Rami, who wrote 137 songs for her and became her mentor in Arabic literature. She made her first recordings in 1924 for labels such as Odeon Records, but her recordings of 1927 truly launched her career. She studied with Abu al-Ila Muhammad from her arrival in Cairo until his death in 1927.

Her mature style in the 1940s and early 1950s is known as her golden age. In the early 1940s she asked the composer Zakariya Ahmad and the colloquial poet Mahmud Bayram el-Tunsi for songs in indigenously Egyptian styles, a departure from the romantic songs of the 1930s led by Mohammad El-Qasabgi. Their last stage collaboration was Raq el Habib in 1941. Riad Al-Sunbati became a main composer.

Around 1965 she began working with Mohammed Abdel Wahab, whose first song for her was Inta Omri. After the Six-Day War of 1967 her songs became more reflective, and she gave concerts in several Arab and European countries to raise funds for the Egyptian war effort under the slogan Art for the War Effort. She also appeared in six films, including Weddad in 1936 and Sallama in 1945.

By the late 1940s she was affected by Graves' disease, and in 1953 she travelled to the United States for surgery. She resumed singing in 1954 and wore heavy sunglasses thereafter. That year she married Dr Hasan al-Hifnawi; they had no children. She died on 3 February 1975 of kidney failure, aged 70.

About 4 million people lined the streets for her funeral procession from the Omar Makram mosque, and mourners took her coffin from its bearers and carried it to the Al Azhar mosque. She was buried near the Mausoleum of Imam al-Shafi'i in the City of the Dead in Cairo. In Egypt she is called Elsett, the Lady, and a museum in Cairo holds her belongings.
umma: Umma lay in the modern Dhi Qar Province of Iraq. It was traditionally identified with Tell Jokha, though it has more recently been suggested that it lay at Umm al-Aqarib, less than 7 kilometres to the northwest, or that the name covered both. One or both were the leading city of the Early Dynastic kingdom of Gišša, and the most recent excavators suggest that Umm al-Aqarib was prominent in the Early Dynastic III period and Jokha rose to preeminence later. Its tutelary gods were Shara and Ninura, and a lapis lazuli bead names a king of Gišša, Aka, who dedicated it to the goddess Inanna.

The site was occupied at least as far back as the Uruk period, and some proto-cuneiform tablets come from it. Umma is best known for its long frontier conflict with Lagash, as reported around 2400 BCE by Entemena. It reached its zenith about 2350 BCE under Lugal-Zage-Si, who also controlled Ur and Uruk.

Under the Akkadian Empire it was a major power and economic centre, rivalled only by Adab and Uruk. Eleven governors under Akkad are known, and a text records Naram-Sin of Akkad deciding a boundary dispute between Adab and Umma.

Under the Ur III dynasty Umma became an important provincial centre of four districts, with an economy about a third the size of that of Lagash province. Most of the more than 30,000 tablets recovered from the site are administrative and economic texts of this time. The Umma calendar of Shulgi is the immediate predecessor of the later Babylonian calendar. In the Isin-Larsa period Sumuel of Larsa named one of his years "Year Umma was destroyed".

William Loftus visited Tell Jokha in 1854, and John Punnett Peters in 1885 found it half covered with sand dunes. Many illegally excavated tablets appeared on the antiquities market in the early 1900s. An Iraqi team excavated from 1999 to 2002 and a Slovak team began work in 2016, finding the large mudbrick temple of Shara, begun in the last year of Amar-Sin and finished in the eighth year of Shu-Sin. A survey showed that in the Early Dynastic period Umma covered 400 hectares, with a city centre of 40 hectares. Looting of the site since 2003 has left it pitted with trenches.
uncle-toms-cabin: Harriet Beecher Stowe, a Connecticut-born teacher at the Hartford Female Seminary, belonged to the religious Beecher family and was an active abolitionist. She wrote a sentimental novel to depict the horrors of slavery while asserting that Christian love could overcome it. It first appeared as a 40-week serial in The National Era, an abolitionist periodical, from 5 June 1851 to 1 April 1852. It was meant to run for only a few weeks, but Stowe expanded it, and protests reached the office when she missed an issue. The character of Eliza was inspired by an account of a slave woman who crossed the frozen Ohio River in February 1838.

The book opens in Kentucky, where the farmer Arthur Shelby, facing the loss of his farm through debt, sells two of his slaves to the slave trader Mr. Haley: Uncle Tom, a middle-aged man with a wife and children, and Harry, the young son of Emily Shelby's maid Eliza. Eliza overhears the plan and flees with her son across the ice of the Ohio River. Tom is taken down the river to New Orleans, and after his owner St. Clare dies, he is sold to the plantation owner Simon Legree.

Legree beats Tom when he refuses to whip a fellow slave, and tries to crush his faith, but Tom keeps reading his Bible and comforting the others. Eliza's family reaches Canada, then France and Liberia, and George Shelby frees the slaves of the Kentucky farm. Stowe's central theme is the evil of slavery, above all the separation of families, together with the power of Christian love.

It was the best-selling novel and second best-selling book of the 19th century in the United States, after the Bible, and it is credited with helping fuel the abolitionist cause. Defenders of slavery protested, and seven Anti-Tom novels appeared in 1852 and six more in 1853. A story that Abraham Lincoln greeted Stowe in 1862 with the words 'So this is the little lady who started this great war' is likely apocryphal. Far more Americans saw the story on stage than read it, in 'Tom shows' such as George L. Aiken's version, the most popular play in the United States and Britain for 75 years.

The novel is a landmark of protest literature, and later books such as The Jungle by Upton Sinclair and Silent Spring by Rachel Carson owe it a large debt. It has also been criticised for racist descriptions of its black characters and for stereotypes it helped fix, and the Tom of the title came to mean an excessively subservient person. James Baldwin, in 1945, called it a bad novel.
underground-railroad: Enslaved people escaped from slavery as early as the 16th century, and many escapes were unaided. A network of safe houses later known as the Underground Railroad began to organise in the 1780s among abolitionist societies in the North, and it grew until the Emancipation Proclamation of 1863. The network was primarily the work of free and enslaved African Americans, helped by abolitionists and other sympathisers.

The name was first printed on 10 August 1842 by Thomas Smallwood, an African American abolitionist, who reported the Baltimore constable John Zell saying in exasperation that fugitives must be travelling by steam balloon or underground rail-road. The joke caught on and abolitionists adopted it for the whole enterprise.

The network was neither literally underground nor a railroad. John Rankin explained that it was so called because those who took passage on it disappeared from public view as if they had gone into the ground. Escapees were passengers, those who aided them conductors, and railway terms such as stations were used. Routes began at the place of enslavement and followed rivers, canals, roads and trails, and they led north to free states and Canada, but also to Mexico and the Caribbean.

Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania and most of New York were separated from Canada by water, over which transport was easy to arrange. Fugitives usually travelled on foot or by wagon, sometimes hidden under hay, in groups of one to three, though Charles Turner Torrey and his colleagues carried as many as 15 or 20 at a time.

The majority of escapes had no help from an abolitionist. Some people fled to maroon communities in wetlands such as the Great Dismal Swamp, or into Native American lands, though not all Indigenous communities welcomed them. In the South the network was informal and dangerous, since speaking against slavery risked mobs and hanging.

The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 denied suspected fugitives a jury trial or the right to testify, and of 343 seized between 1850 and 1860, 332 were returned to slavery. An estimated 30,000 to 40,000 fugitives settled in Canada, half of them between 1850 and 1860. One estimate holds that about 100,000 people had escaped through the network by 1850, and the professor J.

Blaine Hudson put the number of African Americans who self-emancipated by the end of the Civil War at 500,000 or more. Frederick Douglass criticised the openness with which some conducted it, calling it the upperground railroad. Since the 1980s some have claimed that quilt designs were used as signals, a claim that rests on advocates of the quilt theory. In 1998 the United States Congress passed the National Underground Railroad Network to Freedom Act.
unequal-treaties: The unequal treaties were agreements between East Asian countries, above all Qing China, Tokugawa Japan in the 1850s and Joseon Korea, and imperial powers including the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy, Portugal, the United States, Russia and, from the late 1870s, the Empire of Japan. They were often signed after a military defeat or under military threat. Their terms placed obligations almost entirely on the Asian party and included cession of territory, reparations, treaty ports, loss of control over tariffs and imports, and extraterritoriality for foreign citizens.

In China the earliest such agreement was the Treaty of Nanking of 1842, signed after the First Opium War. Because all of them guaranteed most favoured nation treatment, any advantage one power gained was extended to the others. Sun Yat-sen popularised the term in the 1920s, and both the Kuomintang and the Chinese Communist Party used it for the loss of sovereignty from the 1840s. The historian Dong Wang notes that the phrase lacks a clear meaning and that there is no agreement on how many treaties should be counted.

In Japan, Matthew Perry's fleet reached the country in 1854 and compelled it to sign the Convention of Kanagawa under threat of violence, ending 220 years of seclusion. The Harris Treaty of 1858, negotiated by Townsend Harris, established extraterritoriality and became the model for further treaties, the Ansei Treaties, which opened five ports and set fixed, low tariffs. The tariffs hampered the development of domestic industries and caused economic disruption and political outrage. The shock of curtailed sovereignty helped end the shogunate in 1868.

Korea's first such treaty was with Japan, not the West. After the Ganghwa Island incident of 1875, in which Japan sent the warship Un'yō, Korea signed the Treaty of Ganghwa Island in 1876. The China–Korea Treaty of 1882 stipulated that Korea was a dependency of China and gave the Chinese extraterritoriality. Japan imposed further treaties, beginning with the 1882 Treaty of Chemulpo, and its annexation of Korea in 1910 made the treaties with the Western powers largely null and void.

Japan's victory in the First Sino-Japanese War of 1894–95 convinced many in the West that such treaties could no longer be enforced on it. The Anglo-Japanese Treaty of Commerce and Navigation of 1894, negotiated by Mutsu Munemitsu, was the first successful step towards ending extraterritoriality, which was fully achieved in 1899. Japan then began to impose such treaties on China itself. In China the concept became bound up with the idea of a century of humiliation, and the historian Immanuel Hsu writes that the Chinese saw the treaties as unequal because they were imposed after a war and encroached on sovereign rights.
unesco: The organisation's mandate for international cooperation can be traced to a League of Nations resolution of 21 September 1921, which asked for a commission to study whether nations could freely share cultural, educational and scientific achievements. The resulting International Committee on Intellectual Cooperation was created in 1922. Its members included Henri Bergson, Albert Einstein, Marie Curie, Robert A. Millikan and Gonzague de Reynold, and it was a small body centred largely on Western Europe.

The International Institute for Intellectual Cooperation was set up in Paris in September 1924 as the committee's executing agency. The International Bureau of Education began work in December 1925 as a non-governmental body; it formed a joint commission with UNESCO in 1952 and joined it in 1969. World War II largely interrupted the work of the predecessor bodies, and UNESCO was founded in 1945 as their successor.

UNESCO is governed by a General Conference of member states and associate members, which meets every two years to set its programmes and budget. The conference elects an executive board of 58 members who hold office for four years, and appoints a Director-General every four years. The headquarters stand at the Place de Fontenoy in Paris, built by a group of architects including Bernard Zehrfuss, Marcel Breuer and Luigi Nervi. The grounds hold a Garden of Peace, given by the government of Japan and designed by Isamu Noguchi in 1958.

Its work falls under five programme areas: education, natural sciences, social and human sciences, culture, and communication and information. It adopted the Convention against Discrimination in Education in 1960 and the Seville Statement on Violence in 1989, and it designates places and projects of significance, among them biosphere reserves, begun in 1971, and the Memory of the World register, begun in 1997.

In the 1970s and 1980s UNESCO's support for a New World Information and Communication Order was condemned in the United States, the United Kingdom and Singapore as an attempt to curb freedom of the press. The United States withheld its contributions and withdrew in 1984, and the United Kingdom followed in 1985. Singapore also left at the end of 1985, citing rising membership fees. The United Kingdom rejoined after a change of government in 1997, the United States in 2003 and Singapore on 8 October 2007.
unesco-world-heritage-site: The programme grew out of a rescue operation. In 1954 the government of Egypt decided to build the Aswan High Dam, whose reservoir would flood a stretch of the Nile valley containing the cultural treasures of ancient Egypt and ancient Nubia. In 1960 UNESCO's Director-General launched the International Campaign to Save the Monuments of Nubia, which led to the excavation and recording of hundreds of sites and the relocation of several temples, among them Abu Simbel and Philae. Its success led to campaigns for Venice, the ruins of Mohenjo-daro and the Borobodur Temple Compounds.
The Convention Concerning the Protection of the World Cultural and Natural Heritage was adopted by the General Conference of UNESCO on 16 November 1972 and came into force on 17 December 1975.

A site is nominated by its host country and decided on by UNESCO's World Heritage Committee, whose 21 states parties are elected by the United Nations General Assembly. A country first lists its sites on a Tentative List and then submits a Nomination File, evaluated by the International Council on Monuments and Sites and the World Conservation Union. A site must be of outstanding universal value and meet at least one of ten criteria.

A site may be placed on the List of World Heritage in Danger when threats such as armed conflict, pollution or uncontrolled development endanger it. Three sites have been removed from the list altogether: the Arabian Oryx Sanctuary in Oman in 2007, the Dresden Elbe Valley in Germany in 2009 and Liverpool Maritime Mercantile City in 2021.

A listed site gains international recognition and legal protection and can obtain money from the World Heritage Fund. UNESCO counts the restorations of Angkor, the Old City of Dubrovnik, the Wieliczka Salt Mine and the Ngorongoro Conservation Area among its successes. The programme has also drawn criticism for the under-representation of sites outside Europe, for disputed selections, and for the effects of mass tourism.
unilever: Unilever was formed by a merger of the Dutch margarine producer Margarine Unie and the British soapmaker Lever Brothers. The name Unilever is a blend of the names of the two companies. In the 1930s the business grew and launched new ventures in Africa and Latin America. During this period it acquired the United Africa Company, created from a merger of the African & Eastern Trade Corporation and the Royal Niger Company, which had overseen British trade interests in present-day Nigeria during the colonial era.

The Nazi occupation of Europe during the Second World War meant that Unilever could not reinvest its capital in Europe, so it acquired new businesses in the United Kingdom and the United States instead. After 1945 its American businesses, Lever Brothers and T. J. Lipton, began to decline, and Unilever adopted a hands-off policy towards the subsidiaries and left American management to its own devices. By the end of the 1970s, through acquisitions, it held 30 per cent of the Western European ice cream market.

In 1982 its management decided to reposition it from an unwieldy conglomerate into a more concentrated fast-moving consumer goods company. In 1984 it acquired Brooke Bond, the maker of PG Tips tea, for £390 million, its first successful takeover. It bought Pond's in 1986 and Calvin Klein Cosmetics, Fabergé and Elizabeth Arden in 1989. In 1993 it acquired Breyers from Kraft, which made it the largest ice cream manufacturer in the United States, and in 1996 it purchased Helene Curtis, adding the Suave and Finesse hair-care brands and the Degree deodorant brand. It sold its speciality chemicals businesses to Imperial Chemical Industries in 1997. In 2001 it split into two divisions, one for foods and one for home and personal care.

Unilever's registered office is at Port Sunlight in Merseyside, and its head office is at Unilever House in London. It is listed on the London Stock Exchange, with secondary listings on Euronext Amsterdam and the New York Stock Exchange. Its largest brands include Dove, Axe or Lynx, Lifebuoy, Lux, Persil or Omo, Rexona or Sure, Sunlight and Sunsilk, and it is the largest producer of soap in the world. From 2000 to 2012 it sponsored the Turbine Hall commissions at Tate Modern, which became known as the Unilever Series.
union-flag: In 1603 James VI of Scotland inherited the Kingdom of England as James I, uniting the crowns in a personal union. He often described himself as ruler of a unified kingdom, although the parliaments of England and Scotland did not unite until the Kingdom of Great Britain was formed in 1707.

Several designs for a common flag were drawn up after 1603, some placing the cross of St George and the saltire of St Andrew side by side, but none was acceptable to him. On 12 April 1606 a royal decree specified a flag that joined the English red cross on white and the white saltire of Scotland on blue. This became the flag of Great Britain and the first union flag.

The present flag dates from 1 January 1801 and the Act of Union 1800, which merged the Kingdom of Great Britain and the Kingdom of Ireland. The new design added a red saltire, the cross of St Patrick, for Ireland. The cross of St Patrick takes its origin from the arms of the Old English FitzGerald family rather than directly from the saint. George III's proclamation described the flag only in heraldic terms, with the saltires counterchanged, so that the red always follows the white clockwise.

A white fimbriation separates the red cross and the red saltire from the blue field and from each other. Because of this counterchange the flag has no reflection symmetry, and there is a correct side up. The Irish saltire is slightly depressed at the hoist end, which gives seniority to the cross of St Andrew. Wales is not represented, because the flag of 1606 was designed when Wales was part of the Kingdom of England. The Admiralty set the usual proportion of 1:2 around 1837, and flags on land are normally 3:5. The design was unchanged after the Irish Free State seceded in 1922.

Commissioned warships of the Royal Navy fly the Union Jack from the jackstaff at the bow, and it is worn at the masthead to show an Admiral of the Fleet. It was the flag of the empire's colonies as well. Many colonial flags carried it in the canton, on a Red or Blue Ensign.

It was the official national flag of Canada until 1965 and of Australia until 1953, and it became the flag of New Zealand after the Treaty of Waitangi in February 1840. It was kept as the flag of the Union of South Africa after 1910. In Hong Kong its official use ended with the handover to China in July 1997. No law makes it the national flag of the United Kingdom; it has become so by precedent.
union-island: Union Island has an area of 9 square kilometres and lies about 200 km west-southwest of Barbados, within view of Carriacou and of Grenada, which lies directly to the south. It is roughly 4.8 kilometres long and 1.6 kilometres wide. Its volcanic outline has earned it the name Tahiti of the West Indies, and its highest peak, Mount Taboi, rises 304 metres above sea level. The climate is semi-arid, because the hills are not high enough to bring the rainfall that turns the northern coast of Grenada into rainforest. In the dry season, from December to June, the island depends on water stored during the rainy season. Nearby islands include Mayreau, Palm Island, Petit Saint Vincent and the Tobago Cays.

After the original Arawak and Carib settlers, the island passed into the hands of French and English slave traders and plantation owners. They brought hundreds of Africans there, mostly from regions that are now Nigeria, Cameroon, Angola and Ghana, and sea island cotton was an important export crop. When slavery was abolished, people still lived by farming and fishing, and many men went to sea to work on freighters to support their families.

In the late 1970s Union Island was the centre of political unrest, when a group of residents favoured seceding from Saint Vincent and the Grenadines and joining Grenada, their neighbour to the south. The government of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines put down the insurrection with its forces. In July 2024 Hurricane Beryl, an extremely powerful storm, devastated the island, leaving most of its residents homeless and most of its infrastructure in ruins.

Union Island is part of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, and Clifton and Ashton are its two principal towns. It has just under 3,000 residents, and English is the official language, with French and German spoken by some merchants in Clifton. The island has an airport with flights to Saint Vincent and other Grenadines, Barbados, Carriacou, Grenada and Martinique, and ferries link Clifton with Saint Vincent. Yacht services and tourism provide many jobs, since many yachts call on their way to the nearby Tobago Cays National Marine Park. The Union Island gecko, discovered in 2005, is found only on the island.
union-of-arras: After the Pacification of Ghent the whole Habsburg Netherlands stood united against King Philip II of Spain. The provinces formed the Union of Brussels, with a government of the States General and a governor-general, the archduke Matthias, in competition with the royal governor-general, Don Juan of Austria. The Pacification gave the Calvinists freedom of religion in Holland and Zeeland, while the other 15 provinces officially kept the Catholic Church as the dominant one.

Calvinists elsewhere soon claimed freedom of religion too, and in Flanders and Brabant they used force to change the governments of Ghent, Bruges and Antwerp, to the dismay of Catholic politicians in the south. William of Orange tried to promote a religious peace allowing worship to Catholics and Protestants alike.

Don Juan died in October 1578 and was replaced by Alexander Farnese, Duke of Parma, an able diplomat who drove wedges between the southern Catholic nobles and the regime of Orange and the States General. A group of Catholic nobles known as the Malcontents formed under Philip de Lalaing, stadtholder of Hainaut, and Emanuel Philibert de Lalaing.

Parma negotiated with them, and on 6 January 1579 Hainaut, Artois and the city of Douai subscribed to a declaration rejecting Orange's religious peace without naming him. They swore to maintain the Catholic faith, due obedience to the king and the Pacification of Ghent. The declaration made no plan for a defensive alliance of the kind the northern provinces formed later in January 1579 in the Union of Utrecht, since its signers considered themselves the true defenders of the Union of Brussels.

The members soon opened peace talks with Parma, which led to the Treaty of Arras on 17 May 1579. It reaffirmed the Pacification of Ghent, the Perpetual Edict and the Union of Brussels, ended foreign garrisons, reinstated the privileges of the time of Charles V and abolished later taxes. It allowed Catholicism as the only religion. Hainaut, Artois and Lille, Douai and Orchies signed, and Namur, Luxembourg and Limburg favoured the peace and acceded later. Parma used these reconciled counties as a base to begin the reconquest of the disobedient provinces, the members of the Union of Utrecht.
union-of-brest: Rome-oriented and Byzantium-oriented Christians had formally severed connections from 1054, and several attempts at reunion followed, among them the Union of Florence of 1439, which the deposed Metropolitan of Kiev, Isidore, endorsed. In 1588 and 1589 the Patriarch of Constantinople, Jeremias II, travelled through the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and the Tsardom of Russia. In Moscow he recognised the Russian Orthodox Church and consecrated Job as Patriarch. In the Commonwealth he deposed the Metropolitan of Kiev, Onesiphorus Divochka, and, with the approval of King Sigismund III, consecrated Michael Rohoza as the new Metropolitan of Kiev, Halych and all Rus'.

After Jeremias II left, some of the Orthodox bishops of the Ruthenian lands gathered in synod at Brest and signed a declaration of readiness to reunite with Rome. Several others joined later, among them Hypatius Pociej, Bishop of Volodymyr-Brest, and Michael Rohoza, while Hedeon Balaban and Mykhailo Kopystenskyi withdrew their signatures in 1595. Prince Konstanty Wasyl Ostrogski held that the Metropolitan of Kiev should first reach agreement with the eastern patriarchs.

The union was proclaimed in the Hall of Constantine in the Vatican. The bishops' letter to the pope, dated 12 June 1595, was read in Ruthenian and Latin, Pociej and Bishop Cyril Terlecki of Lutsk read the formula abjuring the schism of 1054, and Pope Clement VIII promised his support. The bull Magnus Dominus et laudabilis nimis announced the union, and on 7 February 1596 the pope called a synod of the Ruthenian bishops.

The 33 articles of union were accepted in Rome. The Ruthenians kept their own rite, apart from customs opposed to Catholic doctrine. It was agreed that the filioque would not be inserted into their Nicene Creed. The bishops asked to be excused from introducing the Gregorian Calendar, to avoid popular discontent, and asked that the king of Poland grant them the dignity of senators by right. A bull of 23 February 1596, Decet Romanum pontificem, defined the rights of the Ruthenian episcopate and their subjection to the Holy See.

Sigismund III Vasa strongly supported the union. Some bishops, prominent nobles led by Ostrogski, and the nascent Cossack movement for Ukrainian self-rule opposed it, and the Church of Rus' split into Greek Catholic and Greek Orthodox jurisdictions. Enforcement on Orthodox parishes provoked several large uprisings, and the union lost some of its early support within decades. In 1620 a Metropolis of Kiev, Galicia and all Ruthenia was set up under the Patriarchate of Constantinople for dissenting Orthodox, which produced parallel successions of metropolitans in the Commonwealth. The Ruthenian Uniate Church survives as the Ukrainian and Belarusian Greek Catholic Churches.
union-of-krewo: In the strict sense the Union of Krewo comprised a set of prenuptial promises made at Kreva Castle on 14 August 1385 by Jogaila, Grand Duke of Lithuania, concerning his prospective marriage to the underage reigning Queen Jadwiga of Poland. Louis I of Hungary had died in 1382 leaving only two daughters, and Poland faced a succession crisis. Jadwiga was crowned King of Poland, not queen, to stress her rights, on 15 October 1384. She was betrothed to William of Austria, whom Polish nobles forcibly removed from Wawel when he arrived in summer 1385. Nobles of Lesser Poland proposed that she marry Jogaila instead.

Jogaila ruled a large state of pagan Lithuanians and Orthodox Ruthenians, which had defended itself for a century against the Teutonic Knights, a crusading order. He understood that conversion was inevitable. In 1384 he considered converting to Orthodoxy and marrying Sophia, daughter of Dmitry Donskoy, but Catholics held Orthodoxy no better than paganism. The Polish proposal avoided the pitfalls of both.

In mid-1385 Jogaila sent a delegation including his brother Skirgaila to Kraków and then to Queen Elizabeth in Buda, and a Polish delegation went to Lithuania. On its return Jogaila confirmed in writing all the promises made for him. The document of 560 words is addressed to Elizabeth and the Polish delegation. In exchange for the marriage Jogaila agreed to convert himself, the Lithuanian nobles and all pagan Lithuanians to Roman Catholicism. He promised 200,000 florins to William of Austria for ending the engagement, the return of lands Poland had lost in wars, and the release of 40,000 or 45,000 Christian prisoners of war. He also agreed to attach (Latin applicare) Lithuanian and Ruthenian lands to the Crown of Poland.

Jogaila was elected king at Lublin on 1 February 1386 and baptised at Wawel Cathedral, taking the name Wladislaus. He married Jadwiga on 18 February and was crowned on 4 March. He then returned to Vilnius to convert Lithuania, setting up the first seven parishes. New converts were baptised en masse with little teaching, a haste later criticised at the Council of Constance. A civil war ended with the Ostrów Agreement, which made Vytautas Grand Duke of Lithuania, with Jogaila as overlord. Only the Union of Lublin of 1569 created the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth.

The original document was found in 1835 in a register of the Cracow Cathedral Chapter. Historians have long argued about applicare, a Latin term without a legal definition. Some read it as turning Lithuania into a Polish province, others as a fief of Poland, and the Lithuanian historians Adolfas Šapoka and Zenonas Ivinskis as a personal union under one monarch.
union-of-lublin: Lithuania had been increasingly on the losing side of the Muscovite-Lithuanian Wars, and by the second half of the sixteenth century it faced the threat of total defeat in the Livonian War and incorporation into the Tsardom of Russia. Lithuanian magnates feared losing power, since the union would make their legal status equal to that of the far more numerous Polish lower nobility. The Polish nobility, the szlachta, were reluctant to give more help without return: as much as 70% of the taxes collected in Poland in the 1560s went to support Lithuania against Moscow.

Sigismund II Augustus, the last of the Jagiellons, had no children or brothers to inherit the throne and pressed for the union, in part to preserve the continuity of his dynasty's work. The union was one of the constitutional changes needed to establish a formal elective monarchy reigning over both domains.

The Sejm met near Lublin in January 1569 but reached no agreement; one point of contention was the right of Poles to settle and own land in the Grand Duchy. After most of the Lithuanian delegation under Mikołaj Radziwiłł left on 1 March, the king annexed the Podlachie, Volhynian, Bracław and Kiev Voivodeships to the Crown on 6 June, with wide approval from the local gentry.

The Lithuanians returned under Jan Hieronimowicz Chodkiewicz. Although the szlachta wanted full incorporation of the Grand Duchy, the Lithuanians agreed only to a federal state. The last objections were overcome on 28 June 1569, and the king then signed the act at Lublin Castle.

The union provided for a merger in which each state kept its own army, treasury, laws and administration. A single ruler, freely elected by the nobility of both nations, would be crowned King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania in Wawel Cathedral in Kraków. The common Sejm met in Warsaw, with 114 deputies from the Polish lands and 48 from Lithuania, and the Senate had 113 Polish and 27 Lithuanian senators. A common coin, the złoty, was introduced. Lithuania lost the Podlaskie, Volhynia, Podolia and Kiev voivodeships to the Polish Crown.

The union accelerated the Polonization of the Ruthenian nobility, who were initially Ruthenian-speaking and Eastern Orthodox. It also brought increasing enserfment of the Ruthenian peasantry. The Commonwealth endured for over 200 years and ended in the partitions of 1772, 1793 and 1795. The original act was included by UNESCO in the Memory of the World International Register in 2017.
union-of-the-crowns: In August 1503 James IV of Scotland married Margaret, eldest daughter of Henry VII of England, the outcome of the Treaty of Perpetual Peace of the year before. The marriage brought the Scottish Stuarts into the Tudor line of succession, though no Scottish prince was then likely to inherit the English throne.

The peace did not last. In 1513 James invaded northern England in support of France and died at the Battle of Flodden, which England won decisively. In the decades after, England repeatedly invaded Scotland. By the end of Elizabeth I’s reign it was clear to all that James VI of Scotland, great-grandson of James IV and Margaret, was the only generally acceptable heir.

From 1601 Elizabeth’s chief minister, Sir Robert Cecil, kept up a secret correspondence with James to prepare a smooth succession. In March 1603, with the queen dying, Cecil sent him a draft proclamation and London was placed under guard. Elizabeth died in the early hours of 24 March, and within eight hours James was proclaimed king in London without protest or disturbance. James left Edinburgh on 5 April 1603, promising to return every three years; he came back only once, in 1617. His English coronation took place on 25 July.

In his first speech to the English Parliament, on 19 March 1604, James likened himself to a husband to the whole island and said he should not be a polygamist with two wives. Parliament feared the loss of the name of England, and legal opinion held that a union would end the established laws of both countries. On 20 October 1604 James took the title King of Great Britain, France and Ireland by proclamation, which deepened the offence.

In October 1604 English and Scottish commissioners were appointed to explore a union. They made limited progress on border laws, trade and citizenship, but free trade and equal rights before the law proved contentious.

The Scottish Parliament feared the lesser being drawn by the greater, and anti-English satires proliferated. James devised new coats of arms and a uniform coinage, and on 12 April 1606 proclaimed the Union Flag. Scots who saw in it the cross of St George laid over the saltire of St Andrew made a design of their own with the reverse arrangement.

England, Scotland and Ireland stayed separate states with separate parliaments until the Acts of Union of 1707 united England and Scotland into the Kingdom of Great Britain. Ireland kept a legally separate Crown and Parliament, as a practical dependency, until 1801.
union-of-utrecht: The Union of Utrecht came during the Eighty Years' War, after a series of earlier unions. At the Union of Dordrecht on 4 July 1575, William of Orange was appointed stadholder of Holland, and Holland and Zeeland decided to cooperate. After Spanish troops sacked Antwerp on 4 November 1576, the States of Holland, the States of Zeeland and the other, mostly Catholic, regions reconciled on 8 November in the Pacification of Ghent, agreeing to resist interventions by Philip II of Spain while remaining obedient to him.

The first Union of Brussels, of 6 January 1577, confirmed it, and Don Juan of Austria accepted it in the Eternal Edict of 12 February. William of Orange then urged Guelders to form a further alliance with Holland and Zeeland, but the predominantly Catholic province saw little point.

The treaty was concluded on 23 January 1579 and signed by Holland, Zeeland, Utrecht, though not all of it, and the province, but not the city, of Groningen. It was a reaction to the Union of Arras, in which two southern provinces and a city declared their support for Catholic Spain.

It aimed to force Philip II to stop his harsh administrative measures and regulated defence, taxation and religion, which is why it is seen as a precursor of a later constitution. It allowed complete personal freedom of religion, making it one of the first unlimited edicts of religious toleration, and an additional declaration let provinces and cities that wished to remain Catholic join. Further signatories followed, including Ghent, Antwerp, Breda and Brussels in 1579, and Overijssel and Drenthe in April 1580.

Antwerp was the capital of the union until it fell to the Spanish, and Spanish troops conquered almost all of Flanders and half of Brabant. The union worsened relations between the provinces and their lord, and in 1581 the United Provinces declared their independence in the Act of Abjuration.

It is regarded as the foundation of the Republic of the Seven United Provinces, which Spain did not recognise until the Twelve Years' Truce of 1609. Until the early 20th century historians such as Henri Pirenne held it to be a Calvinist alliance of the northern provinces, but the Flemish researcher Leo Delfos argued from 1929 that it sought to uphold the Pacification of Ghent and to include all the provinces.
unita: Jonas Savimbi and António da Costa Fernandes founded UNITA on 13 March 1966 at Muangai in Moxico province, in Portuguese Angola, with some 200 other delegates present. It launched its first attack on the Portuguese colonial authorities on 25 December 1966. Savimbi had originally been affiliated with Holden Roberto's National Liberation Front of Angola (FNLA), and UNITA fought alongside the FNLA and the MPLA in the war for independence that lasted from 1961 to 1975. Its leadership came heavily from the Ovimbundu, Angola's majority ethnic group. Its policies were at first Maoist, and it received aid from the People's Republic of China until 1975.

After the Portuguese withdrew in 1974 and 1975, the MPLA and UNITA clashed and a civil war began that lasted until 2002. The MPLA leader Agostinho Neto became the first president. Backed by Soviet and Cuban money, weapons and troops, the MPLA defeated the FNLA militarily and forced it largely into exile. UNITA was nearly destroyed in November 1975 but survived and set up a second government at Huambo. It recovered with South African aid and was strengthened by United States support in the 1980s. The MPLA was strongest in the cities, the coast and the oil fields, while UNITA held much of the interior highlands. Until 1996 it was funded through diamond mines in the Cuango River valley.

Cuba withdrew its troops in 1989. After the Bicesse Accords of 1991 elections were held in 1992 with Savimbi and José Eduardo dos Santos as presidential candidates. When no one won an overall majority in the first round and UNITA questioned the vote, fighting resumed in October 1992. The United Nations imposed an embargo on UNITA, and the Lusaka Protocol of 1994 sought a government of national unity. An MPLA offensive in 1999, Operation Restore, ended UNITA as a conventional army. Both sides were criticised for human rights abuses.

Savimbi was killed in an ambush on 22 February 2002. Six weeks later, in April 2002, UNITA agreed to a ceasefire, and about 350,000 soldiers and family members were gathered in 33 demobilisation camps. In August 2002 UNITA formally gave up its armed wing, and it has since taken part in electoral politics as a party. Isaías Samakuva, elected to lead it after Savimbi's immediate successor António Dembo died, was in turn succeeded by Adalberto Costa Júnior in 2019.
united-arab-republic: Pan-Arab sentiment was strong in Syria, and Nasser was a popular figure across the Arab world after the 1956 Tripartite Aggression. The Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party was the leading advocate of union. In mid-1957 Western powers feared a Communist takeover in Syria, which led to the Syrian Crisis of 1957, and Syrians then intensified their efforts to unite with Egypt. On 11 January 1958 a Syrian delegation of military officers led by the chief of staff Afif al-Bizri arrived in Cairo uninvited and petitioned for union.

Nasser, who is reported to have first favoured a federal union, agreed to a full merger on terms he called non-negotiable: a plebiscite, the dissolution of parties and the withdrawal of the army from politics. Syrian elites thought the terms unfair but saw no better option. Referendums were held on 21 February 1958, and the results, announced on 22 February, approved the merger and Nasser as president.

Nasser issued a provisional constitution creating a National Assembly of 600 members, 400 from Egypt and 200 from Syria, and disbanding all political parties, the Ba'ath among them. He gave each region two vice-presidents. Over time he squeezed prominent Syrians out of positions of influence, and in the Syrian Ministry of Industry seven of the top thirteen posts went to Egyptians. In Syria Army officers resented serving under Egyptians, and Egyptian-style land reform was resented too. In 1960 Nasser nationalized the Egyptian press.

From July 1961 he nationalized the cotton trade and import-export firms, and on 23 July he announced the nationalization of banks, insurance companies and heavy industry. In August 1961 he replaced regional governments with a single central authority. On 28 September 1961 a group of Syrian officers staged a coup and declared Syria independent of the UAR. Nasser refused to renegotiate a union on equal terms and chose not to send troops.

After Syria's withdrawal, Egypt kept the official name United Arab Republic until 2 September 1971, when it became the Arab Republic of Egypt. The union had been a member of the United Arab States, a loose confederation with the Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen that was dissolved in 1961. The UAR flag, based on the Arab Liberation Flag of 1952, had two stars for the two parts of the union, and Iraq later adopted a similar flag with three stars, for the hope that it would join.
