Gaza was administered by the UAR until 1967. The republic is recognized as the first genuine integrated union between two Arab states in the modern era.
united-fruit-company: In 1871 the American railroad entrepreneur Henry Meiggs contracted with Costa Rica to build a railroad from San José to the port of Limón. His nephew Minor C. Keith took over his business after Meiggs died in 1877 and began planting bananas as cheap food for his workers. In 1884 President Próspero Fernández Oreamuno gave him 800,000 acres of tax-free land along the line and a 99-year lease on the railway. The railroad opened in 1890, but passengers could not pay Keith's debt, whereas bananas carried to Limón and shipped to the United States proved very lucrative.

In 1899 Keith merged his Tropical Trading and Transport Company in Boston with the rival Boston Fruit Company, founded by the sailor Lorenzo Dow Baker and Andrew W. Preston. The new United Fruit Company had Preston as president and Keith as vice-president, with the lawyer Bradley Palmer on its executive committee. It was capitalised at $11.23 million and soon bought or took shares in 14 competitors, giving it 80% of the banana import business of the United States.

The company held huge tracts in the Caribbean lowlands and dominated regional transport through its International Railways of Central America and its Great White Fleet of refrigerated steamships. It built enclave economies in which export earnings were largely not shared with the host country. It kept market dominance by controlling arable land, holding extra land in reserve against hurricanes and blight, which in practice kept governments from distributing land to peasants. This political involvement helped give rise to the term banana republic, coined by the American writer O. Henry.

In Colombia it acquired land in Urabá and Magdalena through deals with elites and the government, displacing small farmers. In Guatemala it built railroads, ports and schools but left much land uncultivated and discouraged highway building that would have lessened its railway monopoly. Its holdings in Cuba, including sugar mills in Oriente, were expropriated by the revolutionary government in 1959. Panama disease, black sigatoka and Moko struck its plantations.

Critics accused the company of exploitative neocolonialism, and Latin American journalists called it el pulpo, the octopus. Writers including Pablo Neruda, Gabriel García Márquez and Miguel Ángel Asturias denounced it in their work.

Eli M. Black bought a large stake in 1968 and merged United Fruit with his company AMK in June 1970 to form the United Brands Company. In 1975 the Securities and Exchange Commission exposed a scheme, called Bananagate, to bribe Honduran president Oswaldo López Arellano. Carl Lindner Jr. took control in August 1984 and renamed it Chiquita Brands International.
united-kingdom-of-great-britain-and-irel: The Kingdom of Ireland had enjoyed a brief period of limited independence, which ended after the Irish Rebellion of 1798, during the war with revolutionary France. Fear that an independent Ireland might side with France led the Kingdom of Great Britain to decide on union, passed by the parliaments of both kingdoms and in effect from 1 January 1801. The Irish had been led to believe that the loss of their legislature would be offset by Catholic emancipation. George III held that it would violate his coronation oath to uphold the Protestant faith, and his refusal led the prime minister, William Pitt the Younger, to resign.

Britain was at war with France almost until 1815. Napoleon's plans to invade failed, chiefly because of his weaker navy, and a fleet under Nelson defeated the French and Spanish navies at Trafalgar in 1805. The War of 1812 with the United States ended in a stalemate and a negotiated peace at the end of 1814 that restored the prewar boundaries. From the defeat of Napoleon to the First World War, Britain was almost continuously at peace with the other Great Powers, and its Royal Navy supported what was later called Pax Britannica. By the Great Exhibition of 1851 it was described as the workshop of the world, and it exercised influence through free trade and investment as well as through a formal empire.

Catholic emancipation came in 1829 after a campaign by Daniel O'Connell, and the Test Acts were repealed in 1828. Reform legislation followed in 1832, 1867 and 1884. The Great Irish Famine of the mid-19th century, worsened by government inaction, led to a collapse in population in much of Ireland. Queen Victoria reigned from 1837 to 1901. The First World War followed in 1914, after Germany invaded France through Belgium, whose neutrality London had guaranteed, and it ended in an Allied victory in 1918 at a massive cost.

The Easter Rising of 1916 was suppressed after a week, and the execution of 15 leaders alienated nationalist opinion and moved it from home rule toward independence. The Irish War of Independence ended in British recognition of the Irish Free State in 1922. As a dominion, the Free State was no longer part of the United Kingdom and ceased to be represented at Westminster. Six north-eastern counties, which had been governed under home rule since 1920, stayed in the Union. Self-governing dominions such as Canada, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa had also grown out of the empire. The present United Kingdom is a direct continuation of the state that remained.
united-kingdom-of-portugal-brazil-and-th: The United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves was a pluricontinental monarchy: the State of Brazil was raised to a kingdom and united with the Kingdom of Portugal and the Kingdom of the Algarves in a single state of three kingdoms. It came into being in the wake of Portugal's war with Napoleonic France, when the Prince Regent, the future John VI, with his incapacitated mother Queen Maria I and the royal court, fled to Brazil.

After Napoleon's defeat in 1815 there were calls for the monarch's return to Lisbon, but the Prince Regent enjoyed life in Rio de Janeiro, where the monarchy was more popular. Brazilian courtiers and nationalists pressed for Brazil to be raised in rank, to enjoy equal status within a transatlantic monarchy.

By a law of 16 December 1815 the Prince Regent raised Brazil to a kingdom and united the three kingdoms under one title. The royal styles changed accordingly, a new flag and coat of arms were adopted, and in 1817 the title Prince of Brazil gave way to Prince Royal. Maria I died in Rio de Janeiro on 20 March 1816, and the Prince Regent became John VI. After the Liberal Revolution of 1820 in Portugal the king left Brazil and reached Lisbon on 4 July 1821, leaving his heir, Prince Pedro, as Regent of Brazil with delegated powers over its government.

The Cortes assembled in Lisbon after the revolution to draft a constitution was composed mostly of Portuguese delegates, as the Brazilian delegates were elected later, and Brazilians were under-represented and often mistreated in the streets. The king, limited to the executive, had no influence over the constitution. Attempts by the government in Lisbon to end Brazil's home rule and undermine its unity led to the proclamation of Brazilian independence in 1822, which de facto dissolved the union. Portugal formalised the dissolution in 1825, when it recognised the independent Empire of Brazil.
united-malays-national-organisation: After the British returned to Malaya following the Second World War, they formed the Malayan Union, which met opposition because its constitutional framework was held to threaten Malay sovereignty. The party grew out of that opposition, which began as a combination of 41 Malay associations that submitted a memorandum rejecting the proposal. UMNO is the oldest national political party in Malaysia.

Its constitution states its objectives as the promotion of Malay nationalism, the concept of Ketuanan Melayu (Malay overlordship), the preservation of the dignity of the Malay people, recognition of Islam as the religion of the federation and the protection of Malay culture as the core national culture. The party advocates the special status of the Bumiputera recognised in Article 153 of the constitution.

UMNO was a founding and principal member of the Alliance Party and of its successor, the Barisan Nasional coalition. Every prime minister from independence until the defeat of 2018 also served as UMNO president. In the general elections of 1959 the Alliance won 51.8% of the votes and 74 of 104 seats, a two-thirds majority, though a dispute over seats cost it some when supporters of the Malayan Chinese Association leader Lim Chong Eu ran as independents.

After Singapore left the federation, UMNO sought to reduce reliance on English in government, while the Democratic Action Party, taking up the call for a Malaysian Malaysia, opposed it. When Abdul Razak succeeded Tunku Abdul Rahman in 1970 he asserted UMNO’s leadership of the Alliance more strongly, so that UMNO became the base of the government.

Mahathir Mohamad stepped down as president in 2003 and was succeeded by Abdullah Ahmad Badawi. The coalition won a landslide in 2004, but in 2008 it fell short of a two-thirds majority for the first time and lost Selangor, Perak, Penang and Kedah. Abdullah resigned in 2009 and Najib Razak succeeded him.

After its defeat in 2018 the party kept considerable influence. During the political crisis of 2020 to 2022 it returned to power twice, first as part of a government led by another coalition and then as the leading party of a Barisan Nasional administration, in which the UMNO vice president Ismail Sabri Yaakob was prime minister from 2021 to 2022. In 2022 its president, Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, became deputy prime minister in a government led by the Pakatan Harapan coalition.
united-nations: In the century before its creation, bodies such as the International Committee of the Red Cross were formed to protect and assist victims of armed conflict. During the First World War several leaders, above all the American president Woodrow Wilson, advocated a world body to guarantee peace, and the League of Nations came into being on 10 January 1920 when its Covenant, ratified by 42 nations in 1919, took effect.

The United States never joined. Most of the League's substantive decisions required unanimity, and it failed to act against Japan in Manchuria and against Italy in the Second Italo-Ethiopian War, despite the appeal of Emperor Haile Selassie I at Geneva in 1936. It effectively closed down when the Second World War broke out in 1939. The United Nations was established by the signing of its Charter on 26 June 1945.

The UN has six principal organs: the General Assembly, the Security Council, the Economic and Social Council, the International Court of Justice, the Secretariat and the Trusteeship Council, which suspended its work on 1 November 1994 on the independence of Palau, the last trust territory. The International Court of Justice sits at The Hague, and the other organs have their main seat in New York City, with major offices at Geneva, Vienna and Nairobi. Its six official languages are Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian and Spanish.

Membership has 193 states, the most recent being South Sudan, which joined on 14 July 2011; the Holy See and Palestine are observer states. Indonesia is the only state to have tried to withdraw, in 1965, and it resumed membership in 1966. Because the UN keeps no military of its own, peacekeepers are provided voluntarily by member states and approved by the Security Council. The UN has carried out 71 peacekeeping operations since 1947, and its Truce Supervision Organization has been in the Middle East since 1948.

Peacekeeping forces received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1988, and the UN and Kofi Annan shared it in 2001. The UN High Commissioner for Refugees won it in 1954 and 1981. Political scientists such as Virginia Page Fortna have found that UN-led conflict resolution usually resulted in long-term peace, while critics describe the Security Council veto as undemocratic and a main cause of inaction on genocides. There is also a divide between richer Northern and developing Southern states over how strong the UN should be. A Hymn to the United Nations, with words by W. H. Auden, was performed by Pau Casals on 24 October 1971.
united-nations-charter: The framework of the United Nations was worked out in a series of wartime conferences. The Declaration of St James's Palace, issued in London on 12 June 1941, was the first joint statement of the aims of the Allies. About two months later the United States and the United Kingdom issued the Atlantic Charter, many of whose principles inspired the Charter. On 1 January 1942 representatives of thirty nations at war with the Axis powers signed the Declaration by United Nations. The Declaration of the Four Nations, signed in Moscow on 30 October 1943, was the first formal announcement that a general international organisation was contemplated to replace the League of Nations.

From 21 August to 7 October 1944 the United States hosted the Dumbarton Oaks Conference, where many of the Charter's provisions were proposed, including the Security Council. The Yalta Conference of February 1945 settled the debate over the Council's voting structure and called a conference at San Francisco.

The San Francisco Conference opened on 25 April 1945. About 850 delegates attended, with advisers and organisers making 3,500 participants, and committees held more than 400 meetings. After a final full meeting on 25 June the text was unanimously approved, and it was signed on 26 June 1945 by 50 of the 51 original member countries.

The Charter consists of a preamble and 111 articles in 19 chapters. Chapter I states the purposes of the United Nations, above all the maintenance of international peace and security. Chapters III to XV set out the principal organs: the General Assembly, the Security Council, the Economic and Social Council, the Trusteeship Council, the International Court of Justice and the Secretariat. Chapter VII lets the Security Council impose sanctions or authorise the use of force to deal with threats to the peace. Article 103 gives the Charter's obligations precedence over those of other agreements.

The Charter entered into force on 24 October 1945, after ratification by the five permanent members of the Security Council, the United States, China, France, the Soviet Union and the United Kingdom, and a majority of the other signatories. That date is considered the official start of the United Nations. The first session of the General Assembly, with all 51 original members, opened in London in the following January. Amendments need a two-thirds vote of the Assembly and ratification by two-thirds of member states, including all the permanent members of the Council. It is an important part of public international law.
united-nations-convention-on-the-law-of-: The Convention replaced the older freedom of the seas, dating from the 17th century. National rights were limited to a belt of water, usually three nautical miles, and all waters beyond were open to every nation, the mare liberum principle of Hugo Grotius. A League of Nations conference at The Hague in 1930 reached no agreement, and in 1945 Harry S. Truman extended United States control to all the natural resources of its continental shelf. Between 1946 and 1950 Chile, Peru and Ecuador claimed 200 nautical miles to cover their Humboldt Current fishing grounds.

The first United Nations Conference, at Geneva in 1958, produced four treaties but left open the breadth of territorial waters. Arvid Pardo of Malta raised the varying claims at the United Nations in 1967, and the Third Conference convened in New York in 1973. It used consensus rather than majority voting, with more than 160 nations taking part, and lasted until 1982. The Convention came into force on 16 November 1994, a year after Guyana became the 60th state to ratify it.

Zones are measured from a baseline, normally the low-water line. The territorial sea extends 12 nautical miles, where the coastal state has sovereign rights, but ships have a right of innocent passage, which excludes fishing, polluting, weapons practice and spying. A contiguous zone reaches a further 12 nautical miles, where a state may enforce customs, taxation, immigration and pollution laws. Exclusive economic zones extend 200 nautical miles, within which the coastal state has sole rights over natural resources; they were introduced to halt clashes over fishing rights, though oil was also becoming important. Archipelagic states may draw baselines between their outermost islands.

Waters beyond these areas are the high seas, and the seabed there is called the Area. Part XI created the International Seabed Authority to authorise seabed exploration and mining, under the principle of the common heritage of mankind, and Part XII places duties on states to protect the marine environment. The Convention established the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea in Hamburg and gives landlocked states a right of access to the sea. It does not settle territorial disputes or issues of sovereignty.

The Convention codifies the principles of international maritime law, which rest on centuries of maritime experience, and strengthens and expands much of the 1958 Geneva law. A number of states signed but did not ratify it, among them the United States, and others did not sign. In 2023 agreement was reached on the High Seas Treaty, an instrument under the Convention for conserving marine biodiversity in international waters.
united-nations-emergency-force: The United Nations General Assembly approved the force by Resolution 1001 (ES-I) of 7 November 1956, largely as a result of efforts by the Secretary-General, Dag Hammarskjöld, and of a proposal by the Canadian Minister of External Affairs, Lester B. Pearson, who later won the Nobel Peace Prize for it. The Good Faith Accords between the Egyptian government and the Secretary-General placed it in Egypt with Egypt's consent, and since the resolutions were not passed under Chapter VII of the Charter, the deployment needed the approval of Egypt and Israel.

Its task was to enter Egyptian territory, with the consent of the Egyptian government, to help maintain quiet during and after the withdrawal of non-Egyptian forces, over an area from the Suez Canal to the armistice lines between Egypt and Israel. Contingents came from Brazil, Canada, Colombia, Denmark, Finland, India, Indonesia, Norway, Sweden and Yugoslavia. The first troops reached Cairo on 15 November 1956, and the force was at its full strength of 6,000 by February 1957. Israel refused the Secretary-General's request to station some of it on the Israeli side of the 1949 armistice lines.

The mission had four phases. In November and December 1956 the force oversaw the departure of British and French forces from the Suez Canal area. From December 1956 to March 1957 it helped to separate the Israeli and Egyptian forces and the Israeli evacuation of the areas captured in the war except Gaza and Sharm-el-Sheik, and in March 1957 it covered Israel's departure from those too, when Israel withdrew its last forces from Rafah on 8 March. Then it was deployed along the borders for observation, until May 1967.

On 16 May 1967 the Egyptian government ordered all United Nations forces out of Sinai; they were then mostly Brazilian, Canadian and Indian, with a smaller Swedish contingent. Secretary-General U Thant tried to redeploy UNEF on the Israeli side of the border, but Israel rejected this. Before the war began the Canadian contingent had been flown out, while the other contingents were still preparing to leave, when Israel invaded Egypt on 5 June 1967, beginning the Six-Day War. Israeli forces attacked a UNEF convoy, camps and the headquarters in Gaza, killing one Brazilian peacekeeper and 14 Indian officials. The last peacekeeper left on 17 June.

UNEF was the first United Nations military force of its kind. After the Yom Kippur War the General Assembly established a second force, the United Nations Emergency Force II, to supervise the ceasefire between Egyptian and Israeli forces.
united-nations-general-assembly: The first session was convened on 10 January 1946 in the Methodist Central Hall in London, with representatives of 51 nations. Until it moved to its permanent home in Manhattan, the Assembly met at the former New York City Pavilion of the 1939 New York World's Fair in Flushing, and on 29 November 1947 it voted there to adopt the United Nations Partition Plan for Palestine. It moved to the permanent headquarters in New York at the start of its seventh regular session, on 14 October 1952. In December 1988 it held its 43rd session in Geneva in order to hear Yasser Arafat.

Its powers and procedures are set out in Chapter IV of the United Nations Charter. It is the only United Nations organ in which all member states have equal representation, each with one vote. Most questions are decided by a simple majority; important questions, such as recommendations on peace and security, budgetary matters and the admission of members, need a two-thirds majority. The Assembly approves the budget and decides how much each member state must pay. It elects the non-permanent members of the Security Council and, with the Council, judges of the International Court of Justice, and it appoints the secretary-general on the Council's nomination. The main annual session begins in September and runs for about three months.

Apart from budgetary measures, Assembly resolutions are not binding on members. Under the Uniting for Peace resolution of November 1950 it may consider a threat to the peace at once and recommend collective measures if the Security Council fails to act because of the negative vote of a permanent member. Membership grew from 51 in 1945 to 193, more than two thirds of them developing countries. In the 1980s the Assembly became a forum for a North–South dialogue between industrialised and developing countries.
united-nations-general-assembly-resoluti: The Republic of China was one of the 51 original members of the United Nations in 1945. Civil war between the Kuomintang and the Chinese Communist Party ended in 1949 with the proclamation of the People's Republic of China in Beijing and the retreat of the Kuomintang government to Taiwan. Both governments claimed to be the only legitimate government of China, and each refused relations with states that recognised the other. Votes on the People's Republic's membership between 1950 and 1970 did not pass.

On 15 July 1971 seventeen members, among them Albania, Algeria, Cuba and Tanzania, asked for the restoration of the People's Republic's lawful rights to be placed on the Assembly's agenda. On 17 August the United States asked for a second item, arguing that the United Nations should take account of both governments. The Assembly debated the matter at twelve plenary meetings between 18 and 26 October.

The vote came on 25 October 1971. The Assembly first rejected a motion by the United States that expelling the Republic of China's representatives was an important question needing a two-thirds majority. It then rejected, by 61 votes to 51, a motion to remove the clause on expelling the representatives of Chiang Kai-shek. The Republic of China's foreign minister, Chow Shu-kai, announced that his delegation would take no further part. The Assembly adopted the Albanian draft as Resolution 2758 by 76 votes to 35, with 17 abstentions. Delegates of the People's Republic began representing China from 15 November 1971.

The resolution says nothing of Taiwan, and its meaning has been disputed ever since. The People's Republic holds that it settled the question of China's representation and, with it, Taiwan's status under the one-China principle. Its critics, among them the Republic of China, the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia and the European Union, answer that the text concerns only who represents China in the United Nations and does not establish Chinese sovereignty over Taiwan.

The Republic of China's government has called the expulsion illegal, since the Charter requires a Security Council recommendation to expel a member. Taiwan's governments sought to return in later decades, applying under the name Taiwan from 2007, and two referendums on membership in 2008 failed to reach the required turnout. In 2024 and 2025 several parliaments rejected the People's Republic's reading of the text.
united-nations-security-council: In the century before the United Nations, treaty organisations and conferences such as the International Committee of the Red Cross and the Hague Conventions of 1899 and 1907 had tried to regulate conflict between states. After the First World War the Paris Peace Conference created the League of Nations, which lacked representation for colonial peoples, then half the world's population, and several major powers, including the United States, the USSR, Germany and Japan, took little part.

It failed to act against the Japanese invasion of Manchuria in 1931, the Second Italo-Ethiopian War in 1935 and the Nazi expansion that led into the Second World War. The Security Council was created in 1945 to succeed it, and held its first session on 17 January 1946 at Church House, Westminster, in London.

In its early decades the council was largely paralysed by the Cold War and could generally act only in conflicts unrelated to the rivalry of the United States and the Soviet Union. A notable exception was the resolution of 1950 authorising a US-led coalition to repel the North Korean invasion of South Korea, passed while the Soviet Union boycotted the council. In 1956 the first United Nations peacekeeping force was set up to end the Suez Crisis, but the council could not act against the simultaneous Soviet invasion of Hungary.

After the Cold War the United Nations took on more peacekeeping missions in ten years than in the previous four decades. Between 1988 and 2000 the number of resolutions more than doubled and the peacekeeping budget grew more than tenfold. In 1991 the council condemned the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait on the day of the attack and later authorised a US-led coalition that repulsed the Iraqi forces.

The council has 15 members: five permanent members, Russia, China, the United States, the United Kingdom and France, who were the great powers among the Allies of the Second World War or their recognised successor states, and ten non-permanent members elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms. Each permanent member can veto a substantive resolution. The non-permanent seats rose from six to ten in 1965, the only enlargement. The presidency rotates monthly in English alphabetical order. Under Chapter VII of the Charter its resolutions, such as economic sanctions, are binding on all members.
united-nations-transitional-authority-in: The United Nations Transitional Authority in Cambodia (UNTAC) was formed after the Paris Peace Accords of October 1991 and established in February 1992 by Security Council Resolution 745, in agreement with the State of Cambodia, the de facto government. It was the first occasion on which the United Nations directly took responsibility for administering an independent state, rather than only monitoring it. Its aim was to restore peace and civil government in a country ruined by decades of civil war, to hold elections leading to a new constitution and to begin rehabilitation.

The mandate was wide: supervision or control of foreign affairs, defence, finance, public security and information, the disarming and demobilising of the fighting factions, the promotion of human rights, the repatriation of refugees and mine clearance. UNTAC had its own radio station and jail. Yasushi Akashi of Japan headed it, with Lieutenant-General John Sanderson of Australia as force commander, and personnel came from 46 countries. The operation cost more than 1.6 billion dollars.

The Khmer Rouge sabotaged the mission and refused to take part in the election, and its forces were never disarmed or demobilised. Critics argued that UNTAC disarmed the State of Cambodia's local militias more thoroughly than the Khmer Rouge, which gained territory. In May 1993 more than 4 million Cambodians, about 90 percent of eligible voters, voted. Prince Norodom Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC won 45.5 percent, ahead of Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party. A constitution was promulgated on 24 September 1993, establishing a constitutional monarchy under Norodom Sihanouk, with Ranariddh and Hun Sen as first and second prime ministers.

UNTAC lost 78 people. Two Japanese personnel were killed in April and May 1993, which led to calls in Japan's Diet for withdrawal, refused by Prime Minister Miyazawa. Sihanouk had reservations about the operation, and the number of sex workers in Cambodia rose from about 6,000 in 1991 to over 20,000 after UNTAC arrived, with a possible link to the spread of HIV. The coalition between FUNCINPEC and the Cambodian People's Party stayed tense and ended in FUNCINPEC's attempted coup of July 1997, which the Cambodian People's Party defeated. The effort to try senior Khmer Rouge leaders led to an agreement ratified on 4 October 2004; the first trials took place in 2007.
united-states: The United States is the third or fourth largest country by total area, with figures ranging between 9,629,091 and 9,866,624 square kilometres. The coastal plain of the Atlantic seaboard gives way to the Piedmont plateau, and the Appalachian Mountains separate the East Coast from the Great Lakes and the grasslands of the Midwest. The Mississippi River System runs north to south through the centre of the country, the Great Plains stretch to the west, and the Rocky Mountains extend across the country beyond them. Alaska is a semi-exclave whose Denali, at 6,190 metres, is the highest peak in the country, while the Hawaiian archipelago lies entirely outside North America.

The first inhabitants of North America migrated from Siberia at least 15,000 years ago. The Clovis culture, which appeared around 11,000 BCE, is believed to be the first widespread culture in the Americas, and later the Mississippian culture developed agriculture, architecture and complex societies. Estimates of the native population before the arrival of European colonizers range from around 500,000 to nearly 10 million. Spain chartered Spanish Florida in 1513 and founded Saint Augustine in 1565. France, the Dutch colony of New Nederland and the Swedish colony of New Sweden also settled parts of the continent, and British colonization began with the Virginia Colony in 1607 and the Plymouth Colony in 1620.

Clashes with the British Crown over taxation without parliamentary representation sparked the American Revolution. Independence was formally declared in the Lee Resolution of 2 July 1776, two days before the Declaration of Independence, and victory in the Revolutionary War of 1775 to 1783 confirmed international recognition. The country expanded westward through purchase, settlement and conquest. A sectional division over slavery led 11 Southern states to secede and form the Confederate States of America, which fought the Union in the Civil War of 1861 to 1865. Slavery was abolished after the Union's victory.

The United States is a federal republic of 50 states and a federal capital district. Its Constitution created a separation of powers among legislative, executive and judicial branches. Congress consists of the Senate, with 100 members, and the House of Representatives, with 435 voting members. The Census Bureau's 2025 estimate of the population was 341,784,857. About 82% of Americans live in metropolitan areas. By 1900 the country had emerged as a great power.
united-states-bill-of-rights: The Bill of Rights followed the often bitter debate of 1787 and 1788 over ratification of the Constitution. Anti-Federalists such as Patrick Henry, Samuel Adams and Richard Henry Lee objected that it contained no bill of rights, and Elbridge Gerry's objections went through 46 printings. Federalists largely opposed adding one. Alexander Hamilton argued in The Federalist No. 84 that the Constitution was itself a bill of rights, since the people surrendered nothing and so needed no particular reservations.

The Massachusetts convention broke the impasse when Samuel Adams and John Hancock agreed to ratification on condition that amendments also be proposed. Its proposals included a grand jury requirement and a reservation of powers to the states, which later shaped the Fifth and Tenth Amendments. James Madison first opposed a list of rights, fearing that anything left off it would seem unprotected, but he agreed to support one and became its author, including a Ninth Amendment to meet that fear. His sources included Magna Carta, the English Bill of Rights of 1689 and the Virginia Declaration of Rights.

Congress approved twelve articles of amendment on 25 September 1789 and sent them to the states on 2 October. Articles Three to Twelve were ratified on 15 December 1791 and became the First to Tenth Amendments. Article Two became the Twenty-seventh Amendment on 5 May 1992, and Article One is still pending. They were added as supplements, not worked into the body of the Constitution as Madison had proposed.

The First Amendment bars laws respecting an establishment of religion or abridging speech, the press, assembly and petition. The Second protects the right to keep and bear arms, and the Third limits the quartering of soldiers in private homes. The Fourth to Eighth cover searches, grand juries, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, due process, trial by jury, bail and cruel and unusual punishment. The Ninth says the listing of certain rights does not deny others, and the Tenth reserves unlisted powers to the states or the people.

The amendments applied only to the federal government, a limit affirmed in Barron v. Baltimore in 1833. The Bill had little judicial effect for about 150 years, and the Court made no important decision protecting free speech until 1931. After the Fourteenth Amendment was ratified in the 1860s, federal and state courts began from the early 20th century to apply parts of the Bill to state and local governments, a process called incorporation. George Washington had fourteen handwritten copies made; the copy kept by the First Congress has been on display at the National Archives in Washington since 13 December 1952.
united-states-capitol: Before the national capital was established, Congress and its predecessors met in several places, including Independence Hall and Congress Hall in Philadelphia, Federal Hall in New York City, and York, Lancaster, Annapolis, Princeton and Trenton. The Capitol's original wings were designed in 1793 and occupied in 1800. The Senate wing was completed in 1800, and the 6th Congress convened in the building on 17 November 1800, moving the national capital from Philadelphia to Washington.

President John Adams had urged the move, in the hope of securing enough Southern votes in the Electoral College to be re-elected. The Senate and House first shared the north wing. The House moved early into its own south wing in 1807, and that wing was finally completed in 1811.

The building was partly destroyed in the burning of Washington by British forces in 1814, and was fully restored within five years. During the 19th century the wings were extended for the chambers of the two houses as more states joined the union, and the massive dome was completed around 1866, just after the American Civil War. The present Senate Chamber opened in 1859. The old House chamber, used from 1807 to 1857, was repurposed in 1864 as the National Statuary Hall.

The Old Senate Chamber served the Senate from 1810 to 1859 and the Supreme Court from 1860 until 1935. Frederick Law Olmsted planned the expansion and landscaping of the grounds from 1874 to 1892 and proposed marble terraces to give the building a base, because it had been built too far westward on the crest of the hill. The East Front was rebuilt in 1904, and the East Portico was extended by 33.5 feet from 1958.

C. and its four quadrants. It is built in the neoclassical style and has a white exterior. Its central dome rises over a rotunda, with the Senate in the north wing and the House of Representatives in the south wing. The Crypt on the ground floor was intended as the tomb of George Washington, who was buried at Mount Vernon under the terms of his will. Constantino Brumidi painted murals in the corridors of the Senate side from 1856. The Capitol Visitor Center, below the East Front, opened on 2 December 2008.
united-states-congress: The First Continental Congress was a gathering of representatives from twelve of the Thirteen Colonies. On 4 July 1776 the Second Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence. The Articles of Confederation of 1781 created the Congress of the Confederation, a unicameral body with equal representation among the states, in which each state had a veto over most decisions. It had executive but not legislative authority, and it lacked authority to collect taxes, regulate commerce or enforce laws. The Constitution's First Article created the present two-chamber Congress, which replaced it in its legislative function.

Congress is bicameral. It has 535 voting members, 100 senators and 435 representatives, and the House also has six non-voting members. The Reapportionment Act of 1929 fixed the House at 435 seats, apportioned among the states by population every ten years, with each state having at least one. Representatives serve two-year terms, each corresponding to one Congress. Each state has two senators, who serve staggered six-year terms. Article One sets a minimum age of 25 for the House and 30 for the Senate, citizenship of seven and nine years respectively, and residence in the state represented.

Article One vests all legislative powers in Congress, and legislation cannot be enacted without the consent of both chambers. The Senate approves treaties and presidential appointments, while the House initiates revenue-raising bills and impeachments, and a two-thirds vote of the Senate is needed to remove an impeached person from office. Work is divided among committees, and Congress is helped by bodies such as the Library of Congress, established by an act of 1800 and burnt by British forces in 1814. Members enjoy freedom of speech in debate and freedom from arrest except for treason, felony and breach of the peace.
united-states-declaration-of-independenc: After the Coercive Acts of 1774, called the Intolerable Acts in the colonies, the First Continental Congress met in Philadelphia and organised a boycott of British goods. The Revolutionary War began in April 1775, and George III proclaimed the colonists to be in rebellion on 23 August 1775. The Second Continental Congress initially lacked clear authority to declare independence, since its delegates were bound by instructions from thirteen different governments. Historian Pauline Maier counts more than ninety state and local declarations of independence from April to July 1776. On 7 June Richard Henry Lee presented a resolution that the United Colonies ought to be free and independent states.

On 11 June 1776 Congress appointed the Committee of Five, John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Thomas Jefferson, Robert R. Livingston and Roger Sherman, to draft a declaration. Adams persuaded the committee to charge Jefferson with the first draft, which he largely wrote between 11 and 28 June and which Congress then edited. The text is often discussed as five parts: introduction, preamble, indictment of King George III, denunciation of the British people, and conclusion. It cites 27 grievances against the king and asserts natural and legal rights, including a right of revolution. Jefferson's most immediate sources were his own draft of the preamble of the Virginia constitution and George Mason's draft of the Virginia Declaration of Rights.

Congress adopted the Declaration on 4 July 1776, and John Dunlap printed about 200 broadsides that night. The first public readings took place on 8 July in Philadelphia, Trenton and Easton. The engrossed copy was ordered on 19 July and signed mostly on 2 August by fifty-six delegates. In the years after the Revolution the text drew little attention, and interest revived only in the 1790s with the first political parties. The French Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen of 1789 drew largely on American ideals. Abraham Lincoln saw the Declaration as the moral standard to which the United States should strive and made it the centrepiece of the Gettysburg Address in 1863.
united-states-invasion-of-panama: The United States kept numerous military bases and a substantial garrison in the Canal Zone to protect the Panama Canal. On 7 September 1977 President Jimmy Carter and General Omar Torrijos, Panama's de facto leader, signed the Torrijos-Carter Treaties, which began the handover of the canal to Panama by 2000. General Manuel Noriega, Torrijos's successor, had been a paid informant of the Central Intelligence Agency from 1967.

In the mid-1980s relations deteriorated after the murder of Hugo Spadafora and the resignation of President Nicolas Ardito Barletta, and in 1988 federal grand juries indicted Noriega on drug-related charges. Several neighbouring leaders tried in secret to persuade him to resign and go into exile in Spain, without success. After the general election of 7 May 1989, which the opposition candidate Guillermo Endara appeared to have won, Noriega annulled the result.

S. Marine lieutenant, Robert Paz, was shot dead by the Panama Defense Forces. President George H. W. Bush ordered the execution of Operation Just Cause on 17 December. m. S. citizens, defending democracy and human rights, combating drug trafficking and protecting the integrity of the Torrijos-Carter Treaties. Forces of the Army, Navy, Marines, Air Force and Coast Guard took part. Panamanian forces were quickly overwhelmed, although operations went on for several weeks.

Endara was sworn in as president, in hiding, on the night before the invasion. Noriega took refuge in the diplomatic mission of the Holy See in Panama City and surrendered on 3 January 1990. He was flown to the United States, tried, convicted and sentenced to 40 years in prison.

S. S. civilians. About 20,000 people lost their homes in the urban fighting, and the United States paid $6,500 each to about 2,700 families displaced by the El Chorrillo fire. The Panama Defense Forces were dissolved. On 29 December 1989 the United Nations General Assembly voted 75 to 20, with 40 abstentions, to condemn the invasion as a flagrant violation of international law, and the Organization of American States denounced it on 22 December.

A draft Security Council resolution demanding withdrawal was vetoed on 23 December by the United States, the United Kingdom and France. S. government invoked self-defence, while several scholars have argued that the invasion was illegal.
united-states-marine-corps: The Corps traces its roots to the Continental Marines, formed by Captain Samuel Nicholas under a resolution of the Second Continental Congress on 10 November 1775, which is marked as its birthday. John Adams nominated Nicholas, who was commissioned a captain on 28 November 1775 and by December had raised one battalion of 300 men by recruitment in Philadelphia.

The Marines were founded to serve as infantry aboard naval vessels. They guarded the ship and its crew in boarding actions and defended the officers against mutiny. The first American amphibious assault came on 3 March 1776, when Marines took Fort Montagu and Fort Nassau, a British ammunition depot and naval port on New Providence in the Bahamas. The Corps has legally been part of the Department of the Navy since 30 June 1834.

In the War of 1812 Marine detachments took part in frigate duels, and they held the centre of General Andrew Jackson's line at the Battle of New Orleans in 1815. At the Battle of Bladensburg on 24 August 1814, 120 marines under Captain Samuel Miller were among the only effective American resistance. In the Civil War about a third of the officers left to form the Confederate States Marine Corps. The Marines mainly performed blockade duty and took part in the capture of New Orleans in 1862.

In the First World War the Corps grew from 511 officers and 13,214 enlisted personnel to 2,400 officers and 70,000 enlisted by 11 November 1918. Opha May Johnson became the first woman to enlist in 1918. Two manuals of the 1930s, the Small Wars Manual and the Tentative Landing Operations Manual, set doctrine for counterinsurgency and for the amphibious operations of the Second World War.

In the Pacific War the Marines fought at Guadalcanal, Tarawa, Saipan, Peleliu, Iwo Jima and Okinawa, and some 600,000 Americans served in the Corps in that war. In the Korean War Marines spearheaded the landing at Inchon, and the 1st Marine Division fought its way out from the Chosin Reservoir. In Vietnam 13,091 Marines were killed in action.

The Marines are organised around the Marine Air-Ground Task Force, which joins ground, aviation and logistics elements under a common command. In the aftermath of the Second World War, Army leaders including Dwight D. Eisenhower and George C. Marshall sought to dissolve the Corps and fold its capabilities into the other services.

The Corps excluded African Americans from 1798 to 1942, and a presidential order forced it to begin recruiting them in 1942. Integration advanced from segregated battalions in 1942 to unified training in 1949 and full integration in 1960. Its traditions include nicknames such as Leatherneck, from a leather collar once part of the uniform, and the phrase Once a Marine, always a Marine.
united-states-mexico-canada-agreement: The agreement is based substantially on the North American Free Trade Agreement, which came into effect on 1 January 1994. The formal process to renegotiate NAFTA began on 18 May 2017, when the United States Trade Representative, Robert Lighthizer, notified Congress of the American intent to open talks. Negotiations commenced on 16 August 2017, with eight formal rounds held until 8 April 2018.

By 2 May 2018 no resolution had been reached, and Lighthizer warned that talks would pause until 2019 without a deal, citing concerns over Mexico's incoming president, Andrés Manuel López Obrador, who opposed parts of the negotiated terms. The parties reached an agreement on 1 October 2018, and it was signed on 30 November 2018 at the G20 summit in Buenos Aires.

Much of NAFTA was kept or updated, and the agreement is sometimes called NAFTA 2.0. Its rules of origin for automobiles raised the share of a vehicle's value that must come from within the region from 62.5 percent to 75 percent. The initial American proposal of 85 percent was not included in the final text. It also required 40 to 45 percent of automobiles made in North America to come from a factory paying at least US$16 an hour, phased in over five years.

Canada gave American dairy farmers tariff-free access to 3.6 percent of its dairy market and raised its de minimis thresholds for courier goods, while Mexico agreed to pass legislation improving the collective bargaining of labour unions. Copyright in Canada was extended to life plus 70 years, and the dispute settlement system of NAFTA was retained.

Continued disputes over labour rights, steel and aluminium prevented ratification of the 2018 text, and a revised agreement was signed on 10 December 2019. All three countries had ratified it by 13 March 2020, and it came into effect on 1 July 2020. It requires a joint review every six years and has a 16-year sunset clause, which an extension at a review can renew.

At the first review, in the summer of 2026, Canada asked on 1 June for a renewal of 16 years, and on 1 July the United States announced it would not renew. The parties will review annually until the agreement expires in 2036 or one of them gives six months' notice of withdrawal. The AFL-CIO called its labour standards unenforceable, and an International Monetary Fund working paper of March 2019 found its effects on the broad economy would be negligible.
united-states-navy: The Navy originates from the Continental Navy, established in the American Revolutionary War. After the war the United States was without a navy for nearly a decade, which exposed American merchant ships to attacks by the Barbary pirates. The sole armed maritime presence between 1790 and the launching of the first warships in 1797 was the Revenue-Marine, the main predecessor of the Coast Guard, and its operations against the pirates were far outstripped by their depredations.

On 27 March 1794 Congress passed the Naval Act, which established a permanent standing navy and ordered the construction and manning of six frigates. By October 1797 the first three, USS United States, USS Constellation and USS Constitution, were in service. John Adams, who argued strongly for a standing navy, is often called the father of the American Navy.

In the American Civil War the Navy blockaded the Confederacy and seized control of its rivers. A modernisation programme beginning in the 1880s, in which the first steel-hulled warships stimulated the American steel industry, produced what was called the new steel navy. Its decisive victory over the outdated Spanish Navy in 1898 brought a new respect for American technical quality, and the building of pre-dreadnoughts, then dreadnoughts, brought it in line with the navies of Britain and Germany. In 1907 President Theodore Roosevelt ordered most of the battleships, dubbed the Great White Fleet, on a 14-month circumnavigation of the world to demonstrate the Navy's reach.

In the Second World War the Navy was central in defeating the Imperial Japanese Navy in the Pacific War and the German U-boats in the Battle of the Atlantic, and it supplanted the Royal Navy as the world's largest navy. During the Cold War, rivalled by the Soviet Navy, it began providing nuclear deterrence through ballistic missile submarines. It took a major part in the Korean and Vietnam Wars and later in the Gulf War and the Yugoslav Wars.

The Navy is part of the Department of the Navy, alongside the coequal Marine Corps, and is headed by the Secretary of the Navy. The most senior officer is the Chief of Naval Operations, a four-star admiral who is a member of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. The uniforms were based on those of the Royal Navy of the time, and the predominant colours remain navy blue and white.
united-states-senate: The drafters of the Constitution debated how to award representation in the Senate more than any other part of the document. Bicameralism and a proportional people's house were widely popular, but Senate representation proved contentious. Some small states, unwilling to give up the equal power they held under the Articles of Confederation, threatened to secede in 1787, and they won by a vote of 5 to 4 in what became known as the Connecticut Compromise. It provided that each state, whatever its population, would have two senators. The Senate's composition and powers are set out in Article One of the Constitution, which has been in effect since 4 March 1789.

From 1789 until 1913 senators were appointed by the legislatures of their states. By the early 20th century the legislatures of as many as 29 states had provided for popular election of senators by referendum, and in 1913 the ratification of the Seventeenth Amendment made election by statewide popular vote the national rule. The Senate has expelled fifteen senators in its history: William Blount for treason in 1797, and fourteen in 1861 and 1862 for supporting Confederate secession. In 1837 it chose the vice president, Richard Mentor Johnson, after a deadlock in the Electoral College, the only time it has done so.

The Senate has two senators from each state who serve staggered six-year terms. A senator must be at least 30 years old, a citizen for at least nine years and an inhabitant of the state represented. James Madison argued in Federalist No. 62 that this called for a greater extent of information and stability of character. The vice president is president of the Senate and votes only to break a tie, and in the vice president's absence the president pro tempore presides. Much of the work is done in committees, and a characteristic practice is the filibuster and its remedy, the vote on cloture.

The Senate must consent to treaties by a two-thirds vote of the senators present, confirms judges, ambassadors, Cabinet members and many other officials, and tries impeachments brought by the House of Representatives, where conviction needs a two-thirds majority. Bills for raising revenue must originate in the House, a rule based on the practice of the Parliament of the United Kingdom. Critics such as the political scientist Robert Dahl have called its equal representation of states a profound violation of political equality among citizens, while defenders argue that it gives stability and protects the voice of smaller states.
united-states-virgin-islands: The United States Virgin Islands lie in the Leeward Islands of the Lesser Antilles, about 64 kilometres east of Puerto Rico and immediately west of the British Virgin Islands. The territory consists of the three main islands, Saint Croix, Saint John and Saint Thomas, and 50 other minor islands and cays, with a land area of about 346 square kilometres. Columbus named them in 1493 Santa Úrsula y las Once Mil Vírgenes, after the legend of Saint Ursula and the 11,000 virgins, and the name was later shortened to the Virgin Islands.

Arawakan-speaking peoples originally inhabited the islands, possibly from as early as 1000 BCE, and the Kalinago arrived around the mid-15th century. Columbus is thought to have been the first European to see them, in 1493. The Spanish settled in 1555, and English and French settlers arrived on Saint Croix from 1625, followed by a period in which Spain, France, Great Britain and the Netherlands disputed the islands.

The Danish West India Company settled Saint Thomas in 1672 and Saint John in 1694 and bought Saint Croix from France in 1733. The islands became royal Danish colonies in 1754. Sugarcane produced by enslaved Africans drove their economy in the 18th and early 19th centuries, alongside cotton and indigo. Denmark sold the islands to the United States for 25 million dollars in the 1917 Treaty of the Danish West Indies, and the United States took possession on 31 March 1917, when the population was about 26,000. Transfer Day is kept each year as a holiday.

The territory is an organised, unincorporated territory of the United States, governed under the Revised Organic Act of 1954. Its capital is Charlotte Amalie on Saint Thomas. People born on the islands are United States citizens by statute, and the territory elects a delegate to the House of Representatives who may speak in debates but not vote. Tourism is the main industry.
universal-declaration-of-human-rights: During the Second World War the Allies, formally known as the United Nations, adopted the Four Freedoms as their basic war aims: freedom of speech, freedom of religion, freedom from want and freedom from fear. The United Nations Charter reaffirmed faith in fundamental human rights, but when the atrocities of Nazi Germany became fully apparent after the war, the world community judged that the Charter did not sufficiently define the rights it referred to. A declaration that specified the rights of individuals was thought necessary to give effect to its provisions.

In June 1946 the Economic and Social Council created the Commission on Human Rights, with 18 members of varied national, religious and political backgrounds. In February 1947 the Commission set up a Drafting Committee chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt of the United States. The Canadian John Peters Humphrey, Director of the Division of Human Rights in the UN Secretariat, became the principal drafter. P. C. Chang of China was vice-chairman, René Cassin of France prepared the second draft, and Charles Malik of Lebanon was rapporteur. The committee was soon enlarged to include Australia, Chile, the Soviet Union and the United Kingdom, and it met in two sessions over two years.

The structure of the Declaration, a preamble followed by general principles, was influenced by the Code Napoléon. Articles 1 and 2 establish dignity, liberty and equality for all humans. Articles 3 to 5 deal with the right to life and the prohibition of slavery and torture, and articles 6 to 11 with legal remedies when rights are violated. Articles 12 to 17 cover the individual's rights towards the community, including freedom of movement, property, nationality and asylum, and articles 18 to 21 the freedoms of thought, conscience, religion, expression and assembly. Articles 22 to 27 set out economic, social and cultural rights, among them work, health, housing and education, and articles 28 to 30 describe how the rights are to be exercised and their limits.

The General Assembly adopted the Declaration on 10 December 1948. Roosevelt told it that the text was not a treaty or a statement of legal obligation but a declaration of basic principles, a common standard of achievement for all peoples. It remains non-binding, yet it was the first step towards the International Bill of Human Rights, completed in 1966 and in force from 1976, and its contents have been elaborated in later treaties, regional instruments and national constitutions.

The Declaration was officially adopted as a French document, with official translations in English, Chinese, Russian and Spanish. It has been translated into more languages than any other document: 298 translations when the Guinness Book of Records recorded the fact in 1999, and more than 500 by 2016.
universal-house-of-justice: Baháʼu'lláh ordained the House of Justice in the Kitáb-i-Aqdas and set out its functions there and in other writings. He wrote that it would assume authority over the religion and consider matters he had not covered, and that its members would be assured of divine inspiration. His son and successor ʻAbdu'l-Bahá elaborated on its composition and election in his Will and Testament. He wrote that it would be freed of error and that obedience to it would be obligatory, and he first used the term Universal House of Justice to distinguish it from the local Houses of Justice and the secondary Houses of Justice, which are now the National Spiritual Assemblies.

Neither ʻAbdu'l-Bahá nor Shoghi Effendi established it. Shoghi Effendi held that the existing institutions were too weak, with very few national and local assemblies, and prepared for it by building a strong administrative structure. In 1951 he appointed the International Baháʼí Council, which he called an embryonic international House of Justice. After his unexpected death in 1957 the Hands of the Cause directed the religion's affairs.

In 1961 the International Baháʼí Council became an elected body. In April 1963 the first Universal House of Justice was elected by 56 National Spiritual Assemblies. The election coincided with the end of the Ten Year Crusade, a teaching plan begun by Shoghi Effendi, and with the centenary of Baháʼu'lláh's declaration in the Garden of Ridván in April 1863. Its constitution was published in 1972. Members have authority only as an assembly.

Elections take place every five years at a convention of National Spiritual Assembly members, by secret ballot, without nominations or campaigning. Each voter names nine adult male Baháʼís. In April 2013, more than 1,000 Baháʼís from 157 countries took part, and in 2023 some 1,300 representatives from 176 countries. Membership is limited to men; ʻAbdu'l-Bahá wrote that the wisdom behind this would become apparent in the future, while women and men are spiritually equal.

The House of Justice may legislate on matters the sacred texts do not address and may change its own legislation, but it cannot alter laws written in the texts. It has used this power rarely. It guides the community mainly through multi-year plans, letters and annual messages on the first day of Ridván, which Baháʼís regard as authoritative. Its statements include The Promise of World Peace of 1985, presented to over 160 heads of state and government, and a Letter to the World's Religious Leaders of 2002.

It has also published the Kitáb-i-Aqdas in English in 1992 and set up research departments and archives at the Baháʼí World Centre. Its duties include preserving and translating the sacred texts, administering funds such as Huqúqu'lláh, and defending Baháʼís against persecution.
universal-postal-union: Before the Union, every pair of countries that exchanged mail had to negotiate a postal treaty, and without one mail had to be forwarded through an intermediate country. Negotiations could drag on for years: the United States drafted a treaty with France in 1852 but did not sign one until 1857, and exchanged ratifications of a later one only in July 1874, three months before the Union made it unnecessary.

United States Postmaster General Montgomery Blair called an International Postal Congress in 1863, which met in Paris but reached no agreement. After the Franco-Prussian War the new German Empire's Reichspost set uniform rates inside Germany, but the uniformity ended at the border. German Postmaster-General Heinrich von Stephan called another congress in 1874, and at Bern the delegates agreed to all his proposals.

The Treaty of Bern, signed on 9 October 1874, established the General Postal Union. It provided for a uniform flat rate to mail a letter anywhere in the world, equal treatment of foreign and domestic mail, and the retention by each country of the money it collected for international postage. Stamps of countries a mailpiece passed through no longer had to be affixed. The treaty was signed by 21 countries, 19 of them European, and membership grew rapidly. The second Congress in 1878 renamed it the Universal Postal Union.

French was the sole official language until English was added as a working language in 1994. Late in the 19th century the Union issued rules for stamp design, such as giving values in numerals and using the same colours for post cards (green), letters (red) and international mail (blue). It became a specialized agency of the United Nations in 1948.

The Union has four bodies: the Congress, the Council of Administration, the Postal Operations Council and the International Bureau. The Congress, held every four years, examines proposals to amend the Union's acts. The Union is headquartered in Bern.

The 1874 treaty let the originating country keep all postage revenue, on the assumption that each letter would bring a reply, but other mail flowed one way. Remailing through a third country was banned in 1924. After decolonisation, developing countries received more mail than they sent, and in 1969 the Union introduced terminal dues, paid by the country sending more mail to the one receiving more.
university-of-al-qarawiyyin: In the 9th century Fez was the capital of the Idrisid dynasty, the first Islamic state based in present-day Morocco. According to the Rawd al-Qirtas of Ibn Abi Zar, one of the main early sources, the mosque was founded by Fatima al-Fihri, daughter of a wealthy merchant, Mohammed al-Fihri. Her family had migrated from Kairouan in Tunisia to Fez, which gave the mosque its name, and she vowed to spend her whole inheritance on a mosque suitable for her community. Her sister Mariam is reputed to have founded the al-Andalusiyyin Mosque in the same year.

It is unclear when the mosque began to act formally as an educational institution. Major mosques of the early Islamic period were multi-functional buildings where teaching took place alongside other activities. The earliest clear evidence of teaching, according to the historian Abdelhadi Tazi, dates from 1121.

Many scholars place its high point in the 13th and 14th centuries, when the curriculum was broadest. Subjects taught around then or soon after included the Quran and fiqh, grammar, rhetoric, logic, medicine, mathematics, astronomy and geography, though alchemy was never officially taught as too unorthodox. The Marinid dynasty built madrasas around the mosque, the Saffarin Madrasa in 1271, al-Attarine in 1323 and the Mesbahiya in 1346. They housed students from other towns, many of them poor.

The institution declined with Fez in later centuries and its curriculum narrowed to the traditional Islamic sciences and Arabic linguistics. In 1788–89 the Alawi sultan Muhammad ibn Abdallah regulated the programme but excluded logic, philosophy and the more radical Sufi texts. By the early 20th century its library had been reduced to around 1,600 manuscripts and 400 printed books.

After Morocco became a French protectorate in 1912, the French administration reformed its structure between 1914 and 1947 without modernising the content of teaching. Many Moroccan nationalists were educated there, and in 1937 the mosque was a rallying point for demonstrations. It was incorporated into the state university system in 1963 and renamed two years later. Women were first admitted in the 1940s.

UNESCO and Guinness World Records have cited it as the oldest university or oldest continually operating higher-learning institution. Many scholars hold that the term university applies only to the institutions that took form in medieval Christian Europe, and they treat al-Qarawiyyin as a madrasa until its reorganisation in 1963. Its alumni and teachers are said to include Maimonides, Ibn Arabi, Ibn Khaldun and Leo Africanus.

The mosque has grown over more than a thousand years under successive dynasties into the largest in Africa, with a capacity of 22,000 worshippers. Its present teaching still concentrates on Islamic religious and legal sciences, Classical Arabic grammar and Maliki law, delivered with students seated in a semi-circle around a sheikh.
university-of-alcala: On 20 May 1293 King Sancho IV of Castile granted Gonzalo Pérez Gudiel, archbishop of Toledo, a licence to create a Studium Generale, as university studies were then called across Europe, in Alcalá de Henares. It was to have the same freedoms for teachers and students as the General Study of Valladolid. These studies were modest but survived, and on 17 July 1459 Pope Pius II granted a bull, requested by Archbishop Alfonso Carrillo de Acuña, for three chairs of arts and grammar at the study of Alcalá. Cardinal Cisneros later integrated these chairs into his new university.

In 1499 Cardinal Cisneros founded a university at Alcalá de Henares. Historians call it by several names, among them the Complutense University and the Cisneriana University, and together with the University of Salamanca it reached a pre-eminent place among Castilian universities during the Golden Age. Alumni and teachers over the centuries included Antonio de Nebrija, who held a chair of poetry and grammar and is best known for his grammar of Castilian, Ignatius of Loyola, who studied theology and Latin there, Tirso de Molina, and the humanist Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda. Pedro Calderón de la Barca studied logic and rhetoric there, and Andrés Manuel del Río, who discovered compounds of vanadium, studied at the university too. It later entered a period of decline.

By a royal order of 29 October 1836 Queen Regent Maria Christina ordered the university moved to Madrid. There it took the name Literary University and, in 1851, Central University of Madrid, until the name Complutense was restored in the 1970s. The buildings in Alcalá passed between various businesses for years. In 1975 the Complutense University opened a branch in Alcalá, and in 1977 the university was founded anew as the University of Alcalá de Henares, a name shortened to University of Alcalá in 1996.

The Complutense University of Madrid regards itself as continuous with the university Cisneros founded in 1499, while the present University of Alcalá, founded in 1977, uses the historic buildings in the city centre that the older university once occupied. UNESCO named the site a World Heritage site in 1998. The university keeps its traditional humanities faculties and promotes the Spanish language through its teaching and through the Cervantes Prize, which the King and Queen of Spain award each year in the sixteenth-century Paraninfo, the Great Hall.
university-of-cape-town: The University of Cape Town was founded at a meeting in the Groote Kerk in 1829 as the South African College, a high school for young men. A small tertiary facility was introduced in 1874 and grew substantially after 1880, when the discovery of gold and diamonds in the north created a demand for mining skills and gave the college the financial boost it needed. It built its first science laboratories and started departments of mineralogy and geology to supply skilled personnel to the mining industry, and it began to admit women.

The college developed into a fully fledged university between 1880 and 1900, and was incorporated by a private act of Parliament, passed in 1916, in 1918. Its crest was designed in 1859 by Charles Davidson Bell, the Surveyor-General of the Cape Colony.

From 1960 to 1990 the university earned the nickname Moscow on the Hill for its sustained opposition to apartheid, particularly in higher education. In 1968 it withdrew the appointment of a black lecturer, Archie Mafeje, under government pressure, since the government had declared it a white educational institution. This led to a nine-day protest by hundreds of students.

The university admitted its first small group of black students in the 1920s, and their numbers remained relatively low until the 1980s and 1990s, when it committed itself to a planned process of internal transformation. In 2015 the Rhodes Must Fall protest movement began against a statue of Cecil Rhodes on the campus, and the statue was removed on 9 April 2015 after a vote of the university council.

The main teaching campus, Upper Campus, stands on the Rhodes Estate on the slopes of Devil's Peak, and its original buildings and layout were designed by J. M. Solomon and built between 1928 and 1930. It is centred on Sarah Baartman Hall, which is used for graduation. The university is organised in six faculties with 57 departments and teaches in English. College House, established in 1887, is the oldest university residence in Africa. The sports teams, particularly the rugby union team, are known as the Ikey Tigers or the Ikeys. The nickname arose in the 1910s as an antisemitic epithet used by students of Stellenbosch University, the university's traditional rugby opponent, because of the supposed large number of Jewish students at Cape Town.
university-of-chicago: The first University of Chicago was founded by a small group of Baptist educators and incorporated in 1857 after a land endowment from Senator Stephen A. Douglas. It closed in 1886 after decades of financial struggle, worsened by the Great Chicago Fire and the Panic of 1873, when its creditors foreclosed on its property. In 1890 its trustees renamed it the Old University of Chicago so that a new university could take the name of the city.

The American Baptist Education Society incorporated the new University of Chicago in 1890 as a coeducational institution. It used $400,000 donated to the society to supplement a $600,000 donation from John D. Rockefeller, co-founder of Standard Oil, and land given by Marshall Field. Wealthy Chicagoans financed the Hyde Park campus: Silas B. Cobb gave its first building, Cobb Lecture Hall.

After the death of the first president in 1906, Harry Pratt Judson became president in 1907. His financial austerity renewed Rockefeller's confidence and brought large gifts between 1906 and 1910, including $10 million in 1910 that balanced the budget.

In 1929 Robert Maynard Hutchins, the 30-year-old dean of Yale Law School, became president. In 1930 he organised the graduate departments into four divisions and united the undergraduate colleges into one college, and in 1931 a two-year general education curriculum called the New Plan formed the basis of the core curriculum. The Metallurgical Laboratory produced the first human-made, self-sustaining nuclear reaction in Chicago Pile-1, beneath the viewing stands of Stagg Field. In 1978 Hanna Holborn Gray became the first woman in the United States appointed to a full-term presidency of a major research university.

The university's scholars helped develop economics, law, literary criticism, mathematics, physics, religion, sociology and political science, and established the Chicago schools of thought in several fields. Its students, faculty and staff have included 102 Nobel laureates. It operates Fermilab and Argonne National Laboratory, and the University of Chicago Press is the largest university press in North America. The undergraduate college introduced a widely adopted model of liberal arts education that featured the Socratic method, the Great Books program and the core curriculum.
university-of-chile: In 1841 the minister of public education, Manuel Montt, conceived the idea of founding a corporation for the advancement and development of the sciences and humanities. The Venezuelan poet and humanist Andrés Bello drew up the project, which became law on 19 November 1842 with small changes. The university was formally opened on 17 September 1843. It answered the need to modernise a country that had become independent from Spain a little more than two decades earlier, and it replaced the colonial Royal University of San Felipe, established in 1738.

At its opening the university had five faculties: Humanities and Philosophy, Physical and Mathematical Sciences, Law and Political Sciences, Medicine, and Theology. In its first years it supported education, institutional organisation, including the Civil Code, the building of roads that joined the territory, and energy and production works. By 1931 the number of colleges had risen to six. Many Chilean presidents and people in politics, business and culture studied there.

During the military regime of Augusto Pinochet, from 1973 to 1989, the university changed profoundly. A decree of 2 October 1973 provided that the regime would appoint its presidents. Another decree of 3 January 1981 restructured it completely: its provincial campuses were separated and, together with those of the Universidad Técnica del Estado, made into separate universities, among them Talca, Valparaíso and Antofagasta. Advisers to the regime designed these changes to moderate the university's influence on national politics and intellectual life, which the regime considered leftist.

Several firsts are linked to the university: Eloísa Díaz Insunza graduated as a doctor in 1887, the first woman to attend university in Chile and in South America, and the first woman lawyer, Matilde Throup, graduated in 1892. The Student Federation (FECH), founded in 1906, is the oldest student organisation in the country. The first kidney transplant in Chile was performed at its clinical hospital in 1966, and in 1987 it registered the first domain under .cl.

The university also runs national services, among them the National Astronomical Observatory, working since 1852, and the official seismological service, since 1908. Gabriela Mistral and Pablo Neruda are the university's Nobel laureates: Mistral received the title of Spanish teacher in 1923, and Neruda entered the Pedagogical Institute in 1921. Its Main House on the Alameda in Santiago, opened in 1872, has a neoclassical façade.
university-of-dublin: The university was modelled on Oxford and Cambridge as a collegiate university. Queen Elizabeth I named Trinity College as the mater universitatis, the mother of the university, and the founding charter of 3 March 1592 gave the college a general power to make provision for university functions. The charter named the first provost, the first fellows and the first scholars, and also named the first Baron Burghley as the first chancellor of the university. It was established to consolidate Tudor rule in Ireland, and it has had an academic partnership with Oxford and Cambridge since 1636.

No other college was ever established. The idea of a second college was seriously considered at least twice, but the money or endowment was never available. Queen Victoria's letters patent of 24 July 1857 gave formal legal foundation to the senate and other university authorities. In a High Court case of 1898 the court held that Trinity College and the University of Dublin were one body, and the two names are usually synonymous in practice.

The university is governed by its senate, chaired by the chancellor or a pro-chancellor, which the letters patent made a body corporate with the title The Chancellor, Doctors, and Masters of the University of Dublin. Each meeting is headed by a caput of the chancellor, the provost of Trinity College and the senior master non-regent, any of whom can veto its decisions. Degrees are conferred at public commencements, usually in the Public Theatre in Parliament Square, in a formal ceremony conducted in Latin, in which the senators answer Placet or non-placet. Business meetings are held in English and in private.

The university also elected members to the Irish parliament. Its representatives in Seanad Éireann have included Edward Gibson, W. E. H. Lecky, Edward Carson, Noel Browne, Conor Cruise O'Brien and Mary Robinson. The franchise was at first restricted to the provost, fellows and scholars of Trinity College; it was extended in 1832 to those with an MA and in 1918 to all who had received a degree from the university. Sports clubs traditionally use the name Dublin University rather than Trinity College.

The Universities Act 1997 defines the University of Dublin as the university established by the charters and letters patent incorporating Trinity College. It belongs to the Irish Universities Association, Universities Ireland, the League of European Research Universities and the Coimbra Group, and is one of the seven ancient universities of Great Britain and Ireland. Graduates of liberal degrees receive an honours Bachelor of Arts after four years of study in Trinity College.
university-of-freiburg: The university began as Albrechts University with four faculties: theology, philosophy, medicine and law. Its foundation belongs to the second wave of university foundings in the German-speaking world in the late Middle Ages, like Tübingen and Basel, and it was the second university in Habsburg territory after Vienna. It was established by papal bull, and so, like most medieval universities, was a corporation of the church: the bishop of Basel was its chancellor and the bishop of Constance its patron. Its real founder was the sovereign, Archduke Albert VI of Austria, brother of Emperor Frederick III, who gave it land, endowments and its own jurisdiction. It remained the territorial university until it was handed over to the Habsburgs in 1490.

In 1679 Freiburg temporarily became French. Louis XIV gave the Jesuits a free hand in the university, a bilingual programme began on 6 November 1684, and from 1686 to 1698 the faculty fled to Konstanz. After Freiburg was reconquered and made capital of Further Austria, Empress Maria Theresa's reforms of 1767 opened it to students who were not Roman Catholics, added the natural sciences and public administration, and made the university a state institution despite the Church's protests.
