The suppression of the Jesuits in 1773 ended the Church's predominant influence, and Johann Georg Jacobi became the first Protestant professor in 1784.

Grand Duke Ludwig I of Baden rescued the university with an annual contribution in 1820, and it has since been named the Albert Ludwig University. In 1900 it became the first German university to accept women. Under the Nazi dictatorship it went through political alignment; under the rector Martin Heidegger all Jewish faculty members were forced to leave. After the Second World War it reopened, and the Freiburg School of economists, among them Walter Eucken and Franz Böhm, developed the ordoliberal ideas that influenced Germany's social market economy.

The university seal, in use since 1462, shows Christ on a gothic throne offering the gospel to Jewish scholars, with the arms of the Austrian duchies, the Habsburgs and the city of Freiburg. Its scholars have included Edmund Husserl, Martin Heidegger, Hannah Arendt, Edith Stein, Max Weber, Friedrich Hayek and Hans Spemann. The Jugendstil Kollegiengebäude I, built in 1911 by Hermann Billing, stands in the historic centre, and the university has offered German language courses to foreign students since 1911.
university-of-giessen: The University of Giessen is among the oldest institutions of higher education in the German-speaking world. It was founded in 1607 as a Lutheran university in Giessen because the nearby University of Marburg, in Hesse-Kassel, had become Reformed. Louis V, Landgrave of Hesse-Darmstadt, gave it its original name, Ludoviciana, and intended it above all to educate pastors and civil servants. A charter issued by Emperor Rudolf II on 19 May 1607 allowed it to begin instruction in October 1607. During the Thirty Years' War, when Hesse-Darmstadt took the area around Marburg, instruction at Giessen ceased and the university moved to Marburg in 1624/25. The Peace of Westphalia restored the old arrangement, and in 1650 the university returned to Giessen.

In the 17th and 18th centuries it was a typical small state university with four faculties, theology, law, medicine and philosophy, and about 20 to 25 professors teaching several hundred students. Reforms in the 18th century followed the Enlightenment models of Halle and Göttingen but were limited by the finances of Hesse-Darmstadt. Financial hardship also produced a Faculty of Economics between 1777 and 1785, which brought together veterinary medicine, forestry and cameral sciences and offered one of the earliest courses in forestry in Europe. In the early 19th century Giessen was, with Jena, a prototype of the politicised Vormärz university, marked by the Giessener Schwarzen with Karl Follen and Georg Büchner.

In 1824 the Grand Duchy appointed the 21-year-old Justus von Liebig, against the university's will and on the recommendation of Alexander von Humboldt, opening a new era in the natural sciences. Other scholars there included the lawyer Rudolf von Jhering, the theologian Adolf von Harnack, the mathematician Moritz Pasch and the physicist Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen. A central building was inaugurated in 1880, with new facilities for chemistry and physics. The student body passed one thousand in 1902. Women were admitted as guest students from 1900 and for regular study from 1908. After the Hessian states were reunited in 1929, Giessen and Marburg became public universities of the same state.

The university, officially Justus Liebig University Giessen, is named after Liebig, its best-known faculty member, the founder of modern agricultural chemistry and inventor of artificial fertiliser. It has no defined campus: buildings are grouped by subject around the city, as at Philosophikum II on the edge of the city forest. Its eleven faculties range from law and economics to veterinary medicine and agricultural sciences. Among its professors was the physician Georg Haas, who carried out the first human hemodialysis in Giessen in 1924, and among its students the chemist August Kekulé, Georg Büchner and Ernest Rutherford. Carl A. Schenck, who took his doctorate in forestry there, founded the Biltmore Forest School in the United States.
university-of-gottingen: In 1734 George II of Hanover ordered Gerlach Adolph von Münchhausen, a member of the privy council of the Electorate of Hanover, to establish a university at Göttingen to spread Enlightenment ideals. It began admitting students in 1737. The first infrastructure was modest, a riding hall and a fencing house, with lectures held in the Paulinerkirche, a Dominican monastery or professors' homes, and no university auditorium stood until the 19th century. Napoleon is reported to have said that Göttingen belongs neither to a state nor to Germany, and is the university of Europe.

In the 18th century Göttingen was known among German universities for its free spirit and scientific exploration. Georg Christoph Lichtenberg held one of the first German professorships in experimental physics from 1769 to 1799, and by 1812 the library held over 200,000 volumes. It became known first for its Faculty of Law, where Johann Stephan Pütter taught public law for half a century, and by the centenary in 1837 law students often made up more than half of the student body. The Brothers Grimm taught there and compiled the first German dictionary. In 1837 seven professors, among them the Brothers Grimm, were expelled for protesting against the revocation of Hanover's liberal constitution of 1833 by King Ernest Augustus.

Around the turn of the 20th century Göttingen reached its academic peak in mathematics and physics. Carl Friedrich Gauss began the tradition, followed by Dirichlet and Riemann, and by 1900 David Hilbert and Felix Klein had made it a leading centre of mathematics. Ludwig Prandtl developed fluid mechanics and aerodynamics there from 1904, and Max Born led the theory group from 1921 to 1933, when quantum mechanics was developed. American students such as Edward Everett and George Bancroft studied there. In the purge of 1933 after Adolf Hitler's rise to power, many professors, including Born, James Franck, Emmy Noether and Richard Courant, were dismissed or fled. The university reopened in 1945 under British control.

The Göttingen State and University Library, with around 9 million media units, is among the largest libraries in Germany. The university counts 47 Nobel Prize winners among its affiliates by its own count. A tradition holds that new doctors are driven in a decorated wagon to the Marktplatz, where they kiss the statue of the Gänseliesel, the goose girl of a fairy tale. An old inscription on the Ratskeller wall reads Extra Gottingam non est vita, which means there is no life outside Göttingen.
university-of-graz: During the Reformation many citizens and nobles of Styria emigrated to universities in Protestant principalities of the Holy Roman Empire. The Catholic rulers of Styria wanted to counter this by founding a university at Graz under the leadership of the Jesuits. Archduke Charles II of Inner Austria founded it on 1 January 1585. The foundation charter, with the sceptre and seal, was presented on 14 April 1586 in the Graz parish church of St. Ägidius, now the cathedral, to the provincial superior of the Jesuits and to the first rector, Father Heinrich Blyssem.

Discussion of adding law and medical faculties began early in the 17th century, but the Jesuits opposed them for more than a century, though from 1648 the Styrian estates financed a one-year course in Roman law. After the abolition of the Jesuit Order in 1773 the state took over the university and secular clergy replaced the Jesuits in theology. Education aimed to train loyal civil servants and teach exclusively practical knowledge, and the Faculty of Law was founded in 1778. The university was re-established in 1827, with few changes at first, and had only 23 teachers until 1848.

From the winter semester of 1933 to 1934 the Austro-Fascist government controlled Austria's universities, and purges affected a third of the professors at Graz. After the Anschluss in 1938 the rector Josef Dobretsberger resigned under pressure from National Socialist students and teachers. After 1945 the Nazi era was long suppressed: a fresco honouring National Socialist students was hastily painted over, and the denazification of the late 1940s brought little change.

At the turn of the 20th century Graz was the centre of the Graz School of psychology and philosophy, founded by Alexius Meinong and Christian von Ehrenfels. It developed object theory, which holds that objects of thought can have properties even if they do not exist, and influenced Gestalt psychology and phenomenology. Among its Nobel laureates were Fritz Pregl, Erwin Schrödinger, Otto Loewi and Victor Franz Hess, and Ludwig Boltzmann was professor of physics from 1876 to 1890. The Faculty of Medicine became the separate Medical University of Graz in 2004.
university-of-greifswald: The university was founded on 17 October 1456 with the approval of the Holy Roman Empire and the Pope. It owed most to the commitment of the lord mayor Heinrich Rubenow, who became its first rector, and to the support of Duke Wartislaw IX of Pomerania and Bishop Henning Iven. The founding took place in the local cathedral. A decree restricting teaching at the University of Rostock, founded in 1419, made it possible, and several professors left Rostock for Greifswald. At first it had the four traditional faculties of theology, philosophy, medicine and law.

In 1604 Greifswald founded the first centralised university library in Germany. The jurist Joachim Stephani of Greifswald is credited with the phrase cuius regio, eius religio. Because the Duke of Pomerania could not pay the professors, he gave the university the Amt Eldena, 140 square kilometres of land. When Swedish Pomerania passed to Prussia in 1815, Greifswald became the oldest university on Prussian territory, and building and funding grew. In 1856 a monument marked the 400th anniversary in the presence of King Frederick William IV. In the 19th century it drew many Polish students, the third-largest group in Germany after Breslau and Berlin.

In 1933 the university was named after Ernst Moritz Arndt, a name proposed by the professor Walther Glawe, and it was brought into line with Nazi aims. It reopened on 15 February 1946 after activity stopped at the end of the Second World War. The name Arndt was removed at first and restored in 1954. Land reform after the war ended its status as a large landowner.

The university is a public research university in Greifswald, in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, and the fourth oldest in Germany. It has five faculties, among them arts and humanities, and law and economics. Its research emphasis lies in plasma physics, landscape ecology, medicine, biotechnology, the Middle Ages and the languages and cultures of the Baltic region. It joined the Bologna system of bachelor's and master's degrees from 1999. Part of its former land has been returned since reunification, including a forest near Eldena open to the public.
university-of-hohenheim: The University of Hohenheim lies in the district of Plieningen, on the southern edge of Stuttgart, and is the city's oldest university. Between 1770 and 1794 the Karlsschule had been the only university in Stuttgart. The eruption of the Indonesian volcano Mount Tambora in 1815 triggered a global climate change and was one of the causes of the famine that struck the Kingdom of Württemberg early in the nineteenth century. In 1818 King William I of Württemberg set up an Agricultural Academy at Hohenheim to improve nutrition in the kingdom radically through teaching, experiment and demonstration. It began with 18 students and three professors. Its first director was Johann Nepomuk Schwerz, and it was housed in Hohenheim Palace, built by Charles Eugene, Duke of Württemberg.

In 1847 the institution was given the rank of an Academy of Agriculture and Forestry, and in 1904 its name became Agricultural College. It won the right to confer doctorates in 1918 and habilitations in 1919. In 1923 Margarete von Wrangell was appointed to the chair for plant nutrition, becoming the first female full professor at a German university. Under National Socialism the college was brought into line with the party's ideology, and it was forced to close in 1945.

The college reopened in 1946, having survived the war relatively undamaged. In 1964 the faculties of Agricultural Sciences and Natural Sciences were created, followed in 1968 by the Faculty of Business, Economics and Social Sciences. Hohenheim has had university status since 1967, when it took the name Universität Hohenheim. It is not connected to the University of Stuttgart, which was founded in 1829, although the two collaborate.

The baroque palace is the university's emblem and main building, and it stands among historic parkland and the botanical Hohenheim Gardens, which include the historic Landesarboretum Baden-Württemberg. The university runs several museums open to the public: the German Agricultural Museum, which has 5,700 square metres of covered exhibition space, the Zoological and Veterinary Museum, housed in the palace, and the Hohenheim History Museum in the Spielhaus, which tells the history of the municipality, the palace and the university. Its research has centred on agriculture, nutrition and environmental protection, and it was a co-founder in 2001 of the Euroleague for Life Sciences, a network of European universities.
university-of-jena: Elector John Frederick of Saxony first thought of a university at Jena upon Saale in 1547, while he was held captive by Emperor Charles V. His three sons put the plan into motion, and after obtaining a charter from Emperor Ferdinand I the university was established on 2 February 1558. It was maintained jointly by the Saxon duchies derived from the partition of John Frederick's duchy, and was named the Ducal Pan-Saxon University, or Salana, after the river Saale. It was founded as a home for the new religious opinions of the sixteenth century and has since been one of the most politically radical universities in Germany.

Enrolment peaked in the 18th century, and the university's reputation reached its height under Duke Charles Augustus, the patron of Goethe, between 1787 and 1806, when Gottlieb Fichte, G. W. F. Hegel, Friedrich Schelling, Friedrich von Schlegel and Friedrich Schiller were on its teaching staff. Jena was noted for allowing students to duel and for their passion for Freiheit, regarded as necessary characteristics of German student life. A historical detention room, the Karzer, survives with caricatures by the Swiss painter Martin Disteli.

In the later 19th century its zoology department taught evolutionary theory, with Carl Gegenbaur and Ernst Haeckel publishing detailed theories, and the term Haeckelism was in some European countries more common than Darwinism. In 1905 Jena had 1,100 students and 112 teachers. After the end of the Saxon duchies in 1918 and their merger into Thuringia in 1920, it became the Thuringian State University in 1921, and in 1934 it was renamed the Friedrich Schiller University. Cooperation with the Zeiss corporation in the 20th century brought new prosperity and a dramatic increase in funding and enrolment.

With Karl Leonhard Reinhold, Fichte, Hegel, Schelling and Schlegel on its staff, the university stood at the centre of the emergence of German idealism and early Romanticism. It is counted among the ten oldest universities in Germany and is affiliated with six Nobel Prize winners. During the Third Reich leading posts went to staunch Nazis, many professors had to leave in 1933 under the Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service, and air raids in 1945 damaged the library and main building. It is the only comprehensive university in Thuringia.
university-of-konigsberg: Albert, former Grand Master of the Teutonic Order and first Duke of Prussia since 1525, bought land behind Königsberg Cathedral on the Kneiphof island in the Pregel River and had an academic gymnasium built there in 1542. He issued the deed of foundation of the Collegium Albertinum on 20 July 1544, and the university was inaugurated on 17 August. It was the world's second Protestant academy, after Marburg, and served as a Lutheran counterpart to the Catholic Kraków Academy. Its first rector was the poet Georg Sabinus, son-in-law of Philipp Melanchthon, and all professors swore an oath on the Augsburg Confession. Emperor Charles V and Pope Paul III withheld approval, but King Sigismund II Augustus of Poland granted the royal privilege on 28 March 1560.

The university first had four colleges, Theology, Medicine, Philosophy and Law, with natural sciences added later. The Prussian lands escaped the Thirty Years' War, which increased its popularity with students. The first book in Lithuanian was printed in Königsberg in 1547, and the university had a deep effect on Lithuanian culture. Tsar Peter I of Russia visited in 1697, and Russian officials afterwards studied cameralist theory there. The 18th century, known as the Königsberg Century of the Enlightenment, brought Johann Georg Hamann and Johann Gottfried Herder among its alumni, and Immanuel Kant, rector in 1786 and 1788.

A botanical garden opened in 1811, and Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel built his observatory beside it two years later. In the 19th and 20th centuries the university was best known for mathematics, in a school founded by Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi and later associated with Hermann Minkowski, Adolf Hurwitz and David Hilbert. A new main building in neo-Renaissance style by Friedrich August Stüler was inaugurated in 1862, and in 1900 the university had 900 students.

The university marked its 400th anniversary on 10 July 1944. In August the city was heavily bombed by the Royal Air Force, and the Red Army's offensive and the Battle of Königsberg followed. When General Otto Lasch signed the capitulation on 9 April 1945, 80 per cent of the campus lay in ruins, and many of the faculty, who had fled, were received at the University of Göttingen. Under the Potsdam Agreement the city became Kaliningrad in the Soviet Union and the Albertina was closed. In 1947 a new institution resumed work as the Kaliningrad State Pedagogical Institute, which became Kaliningrad State University in 1967. Today the Immanuel Kant Baltic Federal University claims to maintain the Albertina's traditions.
university-of-marburg: Landgrave Philip I founded the university by decree on 30 May 1527, and on 1 July the landgravial chancellor Johann Feige formally inaugurated it. It then had eleven professors and 88 students. Its first rector was Johannes Eisermann, known as Ferrarius Montanus, a professor of law. Philip granted it academic freedoms and privileges, including the right to send a representative to the regional assembly and exemptions from tolls and levies for its members. It first used the former monastic buildings of the Dominicans, Franciscans and Brethren of the Common Life.

In 1541 the university gained financial independence through a deed of endowment, and the following year Philip received the university privilege from Emperor Charles V. In 1529 the landgrave hosted the Marburg Colloquy, a religious debate between Martin Luther, Ulrich Zwingli and Philip Melanchthon.

Epidemics, among them English sweating sickness and plague, repeatedly forced the university to move temporarily to nearby towns in its first century. When Landgrave Maurice of Hesse-Kassel converted to Calvinism, the university had to adopt the reformed confession too, which drove many Lutheran professors to the newly founded University of Giessen in 1607. The philosopher Christian Wolff, expelled from Halle by Frederick William I, held a chair at Marburg from 1723 to 1740.

In 1807 the Electorate of Hesse became part of the Kingdom of Westphalia, a French satellite state. Marburg was spared closure and gained from resources redistributed after the closure of the universities of Rinteln and Helmstedt. After Prussia annexed Hesse in 1866, the university had 264 students and 51 professors and became part of the Prussian system. Formal admission of women began in the winter semester of 1908/09 with 26 female students.

After the Nazi rise to power in 1933, 21 professors, more than a tenth of the teaching staff, were dismissed for political or racial reasons. They included the economist Wilhelm Röpke, the Romance philologist Erich Auerbach and the philosopher Karl Löwith. Quotas limited Jewish enrolment to 1.5% overall.

Eleven people associated with Marburg through study or teaching won the Nobel Prize between 1901 and 2011, among them Emil von Behring, Otto Hahn and Boris Pasternak. Its alumni and faculty include Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, Robert Bunsen, Rudolf Bultmann, Hannah Arendt, Martin Heidegger and Alfred Wegener. Today it is a public university of the state of Hesse, without religious affiliation, and one of Germany's oldest.
university-of-nantes: The university of Brittany was founded by Bertrand Milon on 4 April 1460, at the initiative of Francis II, Duke of Brittany, under a bull of Pope Pius II. It embodied the duke's wish to affirm his independence towards the French king, at a time when universities had been created in the neighbouring cities of Angers in 1432, Poitiers in 1432 and Bordeaux in 1441. Founded as a studium generale, it taught the traditional disciplines of Arts, Theology, Law and Medicine. Between the end of the 15th century and the following two centuries it enrolled a thousand or, by the highest estimates, 1,500 students.

At the end of the 16th century Henry IV tried to punish Nantes, which had been loyal to the Catholic League and had supported Philippe Emmanuel, Duke of Mercœur, by moving the university to Rennes, a city loyal to the monarchy. A royal letter of 8 August 1589 ordered the move, but financial problems prevented it, and a second letter of 5 September 1591 repeated the order with the same result. In April 1598 a letter from the king settled the matter by confirming the university's place in Nantes. The original university was abolished during the French Revolution.

Among its notable alumni were René Laennec, the physician and musician who invented the stethoscope, and Georges Clemenceau, Prime Minister of France in 1906–1909 and 1917–1920. The botanist and physician François Bonamy, who lived from 1710 to 1786, served as regent of its medical faculty and as academic rector.

A university of Nantes was re-established in the early 1960s, and the present institution was founded in 1970 under the terms of the 1968 law that reformed French higher education. It is a public university with campuses in Nantes and satellite campuses at Saint-Nazaire and La Roche-sur-Yon, and its faculties include medicine, pharmacy, dentistry, law, psychology, and science and technology. Since 2004 it has followed the European system of Licence, Master and Doctorat degrees, with credits counted under the European Credit Transfer System.
university-of-naples-federico-ii: Frederick II had specific aims in founding the university. He wanted to train administrators and skilled bureaucrats for the curia regis, the kingdom's ministries and governing apparatus, and to prepare lawyers and judges who would help the sovereign draft laws and administer justice. He also wanted promising young scholars to avoid expensive trips abroad. By creating a state university he kept students from completing their training at the University of Bologna, in a city hostile to imperial power. It was arguably the first university formed from scratch by a higher authority, not based on an existing private school. Its motto, Ad scientiarum haustum et seminarium doctrinarum, comes from a circular letter of Frederick II.

The first studies were in law, the liberal arts, medicine and theology. Theology was taught in religious institutions, in particular the convent of San Domenico Maggiore, where Thomas Aquinas taught from 1271 to 1274. Its structure remained substantially unchanged in the Angevin period, from 1265 to 1443. With Aragonese rule in 1443 the university was closed for about twenty years, reopened in 1465 until 1490, and from 1443 to 1501 the humanities became the main focus of higher education in Naples. Only from 1507 did it enjoy lasting stability, remaining open in the Monastery of San Domenico Maggiore.

After the arrival of the Spaniards in the early sixteenth century it was no longer closed, except briefly by riots, epidemics and famines, but its conditions stayed precarious, with no stable headquarters and some of the lowest salaries in Italy and Europe. A papal bull of 1564 imposed an oath of fidelity to the Catholic faith on all professors and doctors. At the turn of the 19th and 20th centuries its prestige grew in the sciences, and it was a pioneer in genetics, with the first chair in Italy.

The university has no main campus; its colleges and departments are scattered through Naples and Portici, and its central campus lies in the Historic Centre along Corso Umberto I. With over 90,000 students in 2022 it is among the largest universities in Europe. Alumni include Thomas Aquinas, Giordano Bruno, the jurist Gaetano Filangieri, the historian Pietro Giannone, the philosopher Benedetto Croce and the Italian presidents Enrico De Nicola, Giovanni Leone and Giorgio Napolitano. Giambattista Vico, Ettore Majorana and Giuseppe Mercalli were among its professors.
university-of-paris: In 1150 the future University of Paris was a student–teacher corporation operating as an annex of the cathedral school of Paris. Three schools were especially well known in the city: the palace school, the school of Notre-Dame and that of Sainte-Geneviève Abbey. Victor and Richard of St. Victor among its professors.

King Philip II formally recognised the corporation as a universitas in an edict of 1200, which placed students under ecclesiastical law and followed a violent incident between students and the king's officers at a pub. Pope Innocent III recognised it in 1215, when the papal legate Robert de Courçon issued rules governing who could become a professor: to teach the arts a candidate had to be at least 21, and for a chair in theology thirty years old.

The university had four faculties: Arts, Medicine, Law and Theology. The Faculty of Arts ranked lowest but was the largest, since students had to graduate there before entering a higher faculty. Humanistic instruction covered the trivium and quadrivium: grammar, rhetoric, dialectics, arithmetic, geometry, music and astronomy. The theological College of Sorbonne, founded by Robert de Sorbon and chartered by King Louis IX around 1257, gave the university its popular nickname.

The Hundred Years' War damaged its colleges. The National Convention suppressed the faculties and colleges on 15 September 1793, and Napoleon re-established the university on 1 May 1806 as a single University of France, which a decree of 1808 divided into five faculties. A new University of Paris was inaugurated on 19 November 1896.

After the student revolts of May 1968, a law adopted on 12 November 1968 led to the division of the university in 1970 into 13 universities, now reduced to 11 by mergers. The university introduced doctoral degrees and student nations, standards that spread widely, and educated three popes: Innocent III, Celestine II and Adrian IV.
university-of-pavia: An edict of the Frankish king of Italy Lothar I mentions a higher education institution at Pavia as early as 825, mainly devoted to ecclesiastical and civil law and divinity, and chosen as the prime educational centre for northern Italy.

In 1361 the Holy Roman emperor Charles IV officially established it as a studium generale, granting the privileges of the universities of Paris and Bologna, so that it could teach canon and civil law, philosophy, medicine and the liberal arts. The duke of Milan, Gian Galeazzo Visconti, then expanded and renovated it, and in 1389 he obtained permission from Pope Boniface IX to teach advanced theology.

The institution was divided into a university of jurisprudence and a university of arts, and a rector, normally a student over twenty, was elected each year. It offered bachelor, licentiate and doctoral degrees and drew foreign students. In 1412 Filippo Maria Visconti invited scholars to teach and issued an edict penalising students who went elsewhere.

In the fifteenth century teachers included Baldo degli Ubaldi, Lorenzo Valla and Giasone del Maino, and from 1490 Hebrew was taught. Leonardo da Vinci probably studied anatomy with Marcantonio della Torre there in 1511. The university closed in 1524 during the Italian War of 1521–6, and when it reopened Andrea Alciato and Gerolamo Cardano taught there.

While the kings of Spain governed the duchy of Milan research stagnated, and Maria Theresa and Joseph II renewed it in the late eighteenth century. Alessandro Volta held the chair of natural philosophy from 1769 to 1804 and Lazzaro Spallanzani that of natural history from 1768 to 1799. In 1858 students protested against Austrian rule, and the authorities closed the university temporarily. Camillo Golgi, who taught there from 1861, received the Nobel Prize in Physiology in 1906, and in 1912 Carlo Forlanini discovered artificial pneumothorax as a cure for tuberculosis there.

The university remained the only one in the greater Lombardy region until the end of the nineteenth century. It has no main campus, and its buildings are scattered across the city. Its central palace on Strada Nuova dates to the fifteenth century, when Ludovico il Moro assigned it a building that had belonged to Azzone Visconti, and it was remodelled between 1661 and 1671 and the eighteenth century. The Collegio Borromeo and the Collegio Ghislieri, built in the sixteenth century, are its oldest colleges.
university-of-rostock: The university grew out of the prosperity that Rostock had gained as a member of the Hanseatic League. Pope Martin V confirmed its foundation in 1419, making it the fifth university established in the Holy Roman Empire and the oldest in continental northern Europe and the Baltic Sea area. In Germany five universities are older, but only Heidelberg and Leipzig have operated continuously since their foundation, which makes Rostock the third oldest German university in continuous operation. Throughout the 15th and 16th centuries it had about 500 students a year and was among the most important universities in Germany and northern Europe, with many students from the Low Countries, Scandinavia and other lands around the Baltic.

Political struggles and pressure from the church drove the university to Greifswald in 1437, where it remained until 1443, and teaching took place in Lübeck from 1487 to 1488. A few years after the city, the university became Protestant in 1542, and Humanism and Lutheranism became its defining characteristics. In the 16th century Rostock was the first university to teach Copernicanism, introduced by Professor Duncan Liddel. After the Thirty Years' War it played only a regional role for about two centuries. When ownership passed from the city to the state of the Grand Duchy of Mecklenburg-Schwerin in 1827, its position improved, and the second half of the 19th century saw much building and a return of its reputation.

On the 500th anniversary, on 12 November 1919, Albert Einstein and Max Planck received honorary doctorates, which made Rostock the first institution of higher learning to honour Einstein in this way. Einstein's doctorate was not revoked under Nazi rule, for reasons that remain unknown. The psychologist David Katz and the dean of the medical faculty Hans Moral were among those who lost their posts in 1933. After the Second World War, in the Soviet zone, the university reopened on 24 February 1946. From 1976 until German reunification it bore the name Wilhelm-Pieck-Universität.

Many notable students and teachers have had ties with Rostock. They include the astronomer Tycho Brahe, who studied there in 1566, the humanist Ulrich von Hutten, who wrote his first important work there in 1509, the Swedish statesman Axel Oxenstierna, who studied from 1599 to 1601, and the archaeologist Heinrich Schliemann, who took his doctorate in 1869. Four Nobel laureates are associated with it: Albrecht Kossel, Hans Spemann, Karl von Frisch and Otto Stern, who both held professorships in the early 1920s. The university's botanical garden and a zoological collection founded in 1775 by Oluf Gerhard Tychsen are among its collections.
university-of-salamanca: Salamanca had a cathedral school known to exist by 1130. King Alfonso IX of León founded the university as a studium generale in 1218, as the scholas Salamanticae, and the actual creation of the university, or the transformation of the older school, took place between August 1218 and the following winter. A charter of King Alfonso X dated 8 May 1254 set rules for its organisation and financial endowment and for the first time called it by that name. A papal bull of Alexander IV in 1255 confirmed the charter and gave its degrees universal recognition. The sayings Quod natura non dat, Salmantica non praestat and Multos et doctissimos Salmantica habet reflect the prestige it quickly gained.

Under Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile, the Spanish state employed many university graduates as bureaucrats and lawyers, called letrados, among them graduates of Salamanca and of the newly founded University of Alcalá. They staffed the councils of state, including the Consejo de Indias and the Casa de Contratacion, the two highest bodies in Spain for governing the New World. While Columbus lobbied the monarchs, he argued his case before a council of geographers at Salamanca, who doubted his calculations, though the university supported the idea of unknown territories to the west.

In the 16th century the School of Salamanca debated the morality and laws of colonisation in the Indies. The faculty renovated theology, laid foundations for modern law, international law and economic science, and took part in the Council of Trent. Its mathematicians studied the calendar reform commissioned by Pope Gregory XIII and proposed the solution later adopted. By 1580, 6,500 new students arrived each year. Beatriz Galindo and Luisa de Medrano were probably the first women admitted, and Medrano probably the first woman to teach at a university.

The colleges, the Colegios Mayores, were founded as charities so that poor scholars could attend. By the 18th century they had become closed corporations controlled by the families of their founders, and they dominated the university. Napoleon's troops destroyed most of them. In the 19th century the government dissolved the faculties of canon law and theology, which were reestablished in the 1940s as the Pontifical University of Salamanca. In popular belief the university was linked with sorcery, and a cave in Salamanca was thought to hold a school of black magic. Among its students and teachers were Miguel de Cervantes, Francisco de Vitoria, Bartolomé de Las Casas, Fray Luis de León and Miguel de Unamuno. Its eighth centennial fell in 2018.
university-of-sydney: In 1848 two members of the Legislative Council, William Wentworth, an alumnus of the University of Cambridge, and Sir Charles Nicholson, a graduate of the University of Edinburgh Medical School, proposed expanding the existing Sydney College into a university. Wentworth argued that it would give the child of every class the chance to become great and useful in the destinies of his country, and that a state secular university was imperative for a society aspiring to self-government. The university was founded in 1850. It was one of the world's first universities to admit students solely on academic merit, and it opened its doors to women on the same basis as men.

The Grant of Arms was made by the College of Arms in 1857, with the motto Sidere mens eadem mutato. The arms show an open book on a blue cross between four eight-pointed stars, with a lion above. Eight-pointed stars were unusual in arms at the time, though they had been used unofficially as emblems of New South Wales since the 1820s. Extension lectures began in 1886, 36 years after the founding, making the university's continuing education programme the longest running in Australia.

The university began teaching for the PhD research degree in 1947 after discussing it from 1944. The first PhD was awarded on 28 April 1951 to William H. Wittrick of the Faculty of Engineering, and the next two on 2 May 1951 to Eleanora C. Gyarfas and George F. Humphrey of the Faculty of Science. The New England University College, founded as part of the university in 1938, separated in 1954 to become the University of New England. The Sydney Conservatorium of Music became a faculty of the university in the 1990s.

The main campus lies across the inner-city suburbs of Camperdown and Darlington and is noted for its architecture and quadrangle. Five denominational colleges, one Jewish college and one women's college are affiliated with the university, and unlike some residential colleges elsewhere they are not tied to any discipline. The University Library, with 11 individual libraries, holds rare items including a first edition of Isaac Newton's Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica. The University of Sydney Union is the oldest and largest university union in Australia.

The university has educated eight Australian prime ministers, two governors-general, 13 premiers of New South Wales and 26 justices of the High Court. Since 2000 the Dr Charles Perkins Oration has honoured its first Aboriginal graduate, Charlie Perkins. The Chau Chak Wing Museum, opened in November 2020, houses the Nicholson Collection of antiquities, the Macleay Collections and the University Art Collection.
university-of-tartu: King Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden signed the foundation act of the new university in Dorpat, now Tartu, on 30 June 1632, while leading a military campaign in Germany, a few months before his death at Lützen. The university was called Academia Dorpatensis after its location or Academia Gustaviana after its founder, and its first chancellor was Baron Johan Skytte, governor-general of the Swedish provinces of Livonia, Ingria and Karelia. It was the third oldest university in the Kingdom of Sweden, after Greifswald and Uppsala. A Jesuit grammar school founded by Stefan Batory in 1583 had existed until 1601. The first students matriculated in April 1632, and the opening ceremony took place on 15 October.

It had philosophy, law, theology and medical faculties with the privileges of the University of Uppsala. Because of the Russo-Swedish war of 1656 to 1658 it moved to Tallinn, closed in 1665 and reopened in Tartu in 1690 as Academia Gustavo-Carolina. It then moved to Pärnu in 1699 and was closed after the surrender of that city in 1710 during the Great Northern War.

The university was relaunched by Baltic German nobles and officially opened in April 1802, with a charter confirmed by Tsar Alexander I, as the first German-speaking university in the Russian Empire. Georg Friedrich Parrot was a prominent organiser and its rector. Over half of the professors came from Germany. German was the language of instruction until 1893, and russification between 1882 and 1898 drove out virtually all distinguished German scholars; in 1898 the town and university were renamed Yuryev. In 1918 Russian staff and students took refuge in Voronezh, which led to the founding of Voronezh State University.

After Estonia became independent in 1918, the University of Tartu was an Estonian-language institution from 1919. It was renamed Tartu State University in 1940 to 1941 and again from 1944 to 1989 under Soviet occupation, and was called the Ostland-Universität in Dorpat during the German occupation of 1941 to 1944. Estonia regained independence in 1991, and the university's full academic autonomy can be dated to 1992. Lectinology was founded there in 1888 with Peter Hermann Stillmark's thesis on the isolation of ricin. Its historical buildings are included in the European Heritage Label list.
university-of-tehran: The first official step towards the present university came on 31 March 1931, when the Minister of Court, Abdolhossein Teymourtash, wrote to Isa Sedigh, who was completing his doctoral dissertation at Columbia University in New York, to ask what establishing a university in Tehran would require. Sedigh took the letter as an invitation to outline a comprehensive scheme for a new university.

In 1933 the subject was raised in a cabinet meeting. The acting minister of education, Ali Asghar Hekmat, said that the only obvious deficiency of the capital was that it had no university. The proposal was accepted, and the Ministry of Education was authorised, with an initial budget of 250,000 tomans, to find suitable land and take the necessary steps to build it.

The university began with eight colleges and faculties, among them theology and Islamic studies, letters and humanities, and, in 1934, science, medicine and pharmacy. Dentistry followed in 1939, and the College of Fine Arts in 1941. In 1942 the College of Engineering and the Faculty of Law and Political Science were added, and veterinary medicine in 1943. In 1935 the university, until then for men only, opened its doors to women as part of the country's policy of universal education.

In 1986 the Iranian parliament, the Majlis, ordered that the overcrowded College of Medicine be separated as the independent Tehran University of Medical Sciences, under the new ministry of health and medical education.

Its central place in Iranian elite circles made the university the setting for many political events. It played a central role in the overthrow of the Pahlavi government in the revolution of 1978 and 1979, and the shah's army opened fire on dissident students at its gates. Its curricula, staff and student intake were revised in the early 1980s as part of Iran's Cultural Revolution. In July 1999 a smaller number of dissident students confronted the police there.

Many leading figures of Iranian political, academic and social life have been associated with the university, among them the nationalist leader Mohammad Mosaddegh, Ayatollah Mohammad Beheshti and the Nobel Peace Prize laureate Shirin Ebadi. Its central library, with over a million books, periodicals, manuscripts and documents, is the largest academic library in Iran.
university-of-tubingen: Count Eberhard V, called the Bearded, later the first Duke of Württemberg as Eberhard I, founded the university in 1477. He was a civic and ecclesiastical reformer who set up the school after becoming absorbed in the Renaissance revival of learning during his travels to Italy. Its first rector was Johannes Nauclerus.

During a plague outbreak in 1482 the staff and students took refuge in a series of towns, Dornstetten, Rottenburg, Urach and finally Waiblingen, and returned to Tübingen only in 1483. Duke Carl Eugen gave the university its present name in 1769 by adding his own first name to that of the founder. It later became the principal university of the Kingdom of Württemberg.

The university has a long history of innovative thought, particularly in theology, in which it and the Tübinger Stift are known. Philip Melanchthon, a chief figure of the Protestant Reformation, helped establish its direction. Hölderlin, Hegel and Schelling, called the Tübingen Three, were roommates at the Stift, and the astronomer Johannes Kepler was among its students.

In the middle of the 19th century the Protestant theologian Ferdinand Christian Baur and his circle, the Tübingen School, pioneered the historical-critical analysis of biblical and early Christian texts. The university founded the first faculty of economics and business in Germany in 1817 and the first faculty of natural sciences in 1863, and Friedrich Miescher discovered DNA there in 1868.

In the Nazi period the university played a leading role in efforts to present the policies of the Third Reich as scientific. It dismissed the fewest Jewish employees of any German university in 1933, because it had hardly any Jewish scholars or students. The physicist Hans Bethe was dismissed on 20 April 1933 as non-Aryan, and at least 1,158 people were sterilised at the university hospital. There was no significant resistance. Theologian Helmut Thielicke helped revive the university after the war from 1947. In 1966 Joseph Ratzinger, later Pope Benedict XVI, took a chair in dogmatic theology.

The university is not a campus university but is spread through the town of Tübingen, in buildings of the old town, the Wilhelmstraße area, the Morgenstelle science campus built in the 1970s and the teaching hospitals. Schloss Hohentübingen houses the collections of the Museum of the University of Tübingen, among them mammoth ivory figures and bone flutes from the Vogelherdhöhle, among the oldest figurative works of art and musical instruments. It is the only university in Germany with a faculty of rhetoric, founded by Walter Jens. Eleven Nobel laureates are associated with it, among them Eduard Buchner, Hans Bethe and Christiane Nüsslein-Volhard.
university-of-turin: At the start of the fifteenth century, instability in Lombardy and the death of Gian Galeazzo Visconti led the teaching staff of the universities of Pavia and Piacenza to propose a new studium generale to Ludovico di Savoia-Acaia. Turin was chosen because it lay at the crossroads of the Alps, Liguria and Lombardy, was an episcopal seat, and because the Savoy prince was willing to found a university on his own land. In autumn 1404 a bull of the Avignon pope Benedict XIII marked its birth. Emperor Sigmund confirmed it in 1412, and the antipope John XXIII in 1413.
At first it taught only civil and canon law and could confer the licentia and doctoratus. The bishop, as rector of studies, proclaimed and conferred the title on new doctors.

The early decades were discontinuous, marked by epidemics and crises and by difficult relations with the local administration. The university moved to Chieri and then to Savigliano in the 1420s and 1430s. Returning to Turin in 1436, it was reordered under ducal licences that set up faculties of Theology, Arts and Medicine, and Law, with twenty-five chairs. The invasion of Savoy by France closed it in 1536, and it was re-established in Turin in 1566 by Duke Emmanuel Philibert.

Plague, famine and war caused decline in the second half of the seventeenth century. The new premises in via Po opened for the academic year 1720 to 1721, the first of the reform of studies by Victor Amadeus II, who held that a university directly controlled by the state would train a faithful and capable ruling class. The reform created the Collegio delle Province, housing one hundred young people of low social origin at the state's expense, and a chair of Italian rhetoric beside that of Latin.

In 1864 Filippo de Filippi gave the first lecture in Italy on the theories of Charles Darwin. Giulio Bizzozero founded the Laboratory of General Pathology in 1873 and discovered blood platelets, and in 1884 Carlo Forlanini tried out the first artificial lung in Turin. Under French imperial rule it became the second largest university in the empire after Paris. The first Italian chair of psychology was held there by Friedrich Kiesow in 1905.

In the twentieth century it was a centre of Italian anti-fascism. In the 1930s Giuseppe Levi trained Salvador Luria, Renato Dulbecco and Rita Levi-Montalcini, each of whom won a Nobel Prize in Medicine or Physiology. Antonio Gramsci, Piero Gobetti, Palmiro Togliatti, Primo Levi and Italo Calvino are among its graduates, and Giuseppe Peano and Umberto Eco taught there.
university-of-utah: Soon after the Mormon pioneers arrived in the Salt Lake valley in 1847, Brigham Young began organising a Board of Regents to establish a university. It was established on 28 February 1850 as the University of Deseret by the General Assembly of the provisional State of Deseret, with Orson Spencer as its first chancellor. Early classes were held in private homes or wherever space could be found. The university closed in 1853 because of a lack of funds and a lack of feeder schools.

After years of intermittent classes in the Salt Lake City Council House, the university began to be re-established in 1867 under David O. Calder, followed by John R. Park in 1869. It moved to the Union Academy building in 1876 and onto Union Square in 1884. In 1892 its name was changed to the University of Utah, four years before Utah became a state. Park then arranged to obtain land belonging to the army's Fort Douglas on the east bench of the Salt Lake Valley, where the university moved permanently in 1900. Park left his entire fortune to the university on his death in 1900.

Further Fort Douglas land was granted to the university over the years, and the fort was officially closed on 26 October 1991. The campus covers 1,534 acres, about 2 miles east of downtown Salt Lake City, close to the Wasatch Range, and includes the Health Sciences complex, Research Park and Fort Douglas.

The university is governed by a Board of Trustees of ten members, eight of them appointed by the Governor of Utah with the consent of the Utah Senate. Together with the other public colleges of Utah it falls under the Utah Board of Higher Education. It organises its academic departments and programmes into 17 colleges and schools. Its School of Medicine was Utah's first medical school.

The long-term genealogy work of the LDS Church has allowed researchers to trace genetic disorders through several generations, and the university has contributed to the study of genetics. The Department of Ballet was founded in 1951 by William F. Christensen. The athletic teams are called the Utes, and the men's basketball team won the NCAA title in 1944.
university-of-vienna: The university was founded on 12 March 1365 by Rudolf IV, Duke of Austria, and is therefore called the Alma Mater Rudolphina. After Charles University in Prague (1347) and Jagiellonian University in Kraków (1364) it is the third oldest university in Central Europe and the oldest in the contemporary German-speaking world, though Charles University was German-speaking at its founding too. Pope Urban V did not ratify the foundation as sanctioned by Rudolf, in particular regarding theology, presumably under pressure from the Holy Roman Emperor Charles IV, who wished to avoid competition for Prague. The pope granted an endowment in 1365, and papal assent came in 1384, giving the university and its Faculty of Catholic Theology full status. The first university building opened in 1385.

The Rector stood at the top, the masters and doctors formed the four faculties, and students and all other members were divided into four Academic Nations, whose elected boards chose the Rector. By the mid-15th century, with the advent of Humanism, it was the biggest university of the Holy Roman Empire, with more than 6,000 students.

As a papal institution the university suffered a setback during the Reformation, and epidemics, economic stagnation and the first Ottoman siege of Vienna sharply reduced enrolment. Emperor Ferdinand I installed the Jesuit Order there in 1551, and in 1623 Ferdinand II incorporated the Jesuit College into the university. In the mid-18th century Empress Maria Theresa placed it under the control of the monarchy, and her successor Joseph II abolished official attire, allowed Protestants and Jews to enrol by 1782 and made German the compulsory language of instruction the next year.

After the Revolution of 1848 the Philosophical Faculty was given equal status with Theology, Law and Medicine, and the reforms of Leopold, Count von Thun und Hohenstein, brought greater academic freedom.

In the late 1920s anti-democratic and antisemitic activity among students caused turmoil, and Professor Moritz Schlick was killed by a former student on the university steps. After the Anschluss of 1938 a huge number of teachers and students were dismissed for political and racial reasons.

The University of Vienna has about 85,000 students and is one of the largest institutions of higher learning in Europe. It is associated with 17 Nobel Prize laureates and has been home to scholars including Erwin Schrödinger, Karl Popper, Friedrich Hayek, Sigmund Freud and Gregor Mendel. Its library, founded in 1365, is the oldest university library in the German-speaking world.
university-of-zagreb: The beginnings of the university lie in a decree of 23 September 1669, by which the Holy Roman Emperor Leopold I granted the establishment of the Jesuit Academy of the Royal Free City of Zagreb. The study of philosophy at Zagreb thereby gained a formal and legal status as a public institution of higher education. The Jesuits ran the academy for more than a century, until Pope Clement XIV dissolved the order in 1773. In 1776 Empress Maria Theresa issued a decree founding the Royal Academy of Science, with three faculties of philosophy, theology and law. During the Austro-Turkish War of 1788 to 1791 the academy asked for university status, but it kept its form until 1874 and educated most of the Croatian intelligentsia.

Bishop Josip Juraj Strossmayer proposed a university at Zagreb to the Croatian Parliament in 1861. Emperor Franz Joseph signed a decree for its establishment during a visit in 1869, and the Act of Founding was passed by Parliament and ratified by the Emperor on 5 January 1874. The Royal University of Franz Joseph I was opened on 19 October 1874, the third university in the Hungarian realm of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Its Faculty of Medicine did not begin to function until 1917, and the Faculty of Philosophy served as the general scientific faculty, with geology, botany, physics, mathematics and chemistry taught from 1876.

Further schools were added in the 20th century: a School of Technology and a School of Veterinary Medicine in 1919, which became university faculties in 1926 and 1925. During the Independent State of Croatia from 1941 to 1945 the university was called the Croatian University. In 1956 the Faculty of Technology was divided into four faculties, and in 1999 the university adopted the European Credit Transfer System; Croatia's later adherence to the Bologna declaration led all its universities to follow.

The university is a public research university made up of 29 faculties, three art academies and one university centre, with more than 70,000 students. Its rectors have included Matija Mesić, the first, in 1874 and 1875. Since 1874 more than 200,000 students have received a bachelor's degree, more than 18,000 a master's and more than 8,000 a doctorate. The Faculty of Philosophy and Religious Sciences remains a work of the Society of Jesus and traces its origins to 1662.
unna: Unna lies on the Westphalian Hellweg, an ancient salt-trading route, at the eastern extremity of the Ruhr district and about 15 kilometres east of the centre of Dortmund. Trade along the Hellweg, including trade in the period of the Hanseatic League, reached it from as far as London. The River Ruhr runs just south of the town. Its districts include the city centre, Königsborn, Massen, Afferde and several more rural villages; Massen and Königsborn are former industrial and mining areas.

Human settlement in the area can be traced back to the Neolithic. In the Middle Ages Unna gained significance as a way station on the Hellweg. It is first recorded by name in an ecclesiastical document of 1032. Around 1200 the archbishop-electorate of Cologne invested Count Friedrich von Altena-Isenberg with the fiefdom of Unna, among other estates. Over the next few centuries the town was repeatedly fought over and burned down several times.

In the 14th century it grew wealthy, with a mint and flourishing regional trade. Excavation in 1952 found about 70 gold coins from various countries, thought to have been buried around 1375. From the mid-15th century Unna was a notable trade centre and a member of the Hanseatic League. In 1597 more than half its people died of bubonic plague. In the early 17th century the town changed hands several times in the religious wars, and in 1666 it fell under the control of Prussia.

Its economy rested largely on agriculture until the 19th century, when better roads, railways and waterways brought industry. Coal mining began in 1870, with industries that depended on it, and the population rose from about 2,500 at the start of the century to 15,000 in 1900. Königsborn became known early in the century as a spa with mineral springs. Major air attacks in 1943-45 struck the barracks and other military installations. After the war the artisan district that had survived the bombing was largely torn down for modern development, though many of its buildings have been restored.

Unna is a city of about 59,000 people in North Rhine-Westphalia and the seat of the Unna district. Many half-timbered buildings from the 16th to the 19th centuries stand in the old town, together with parts of the city wall and its towers. The medieval castle houses the Hellweg Museum, a regional history museum. The Centre for International Light Art, in a former brewery, is described as the only art museum devoted exclusively to light art. Unna is twinned with Pisa, among other towns.
unstrut: The Unstrut rises in northern Thuringia near Dingelstädt, in the Eichsfeld area, and its catchment is the whole of the Thuringian Basin. It leaves the basin through the Thuringian Gate west of Heldrungen and in its lower reaches flows through Saxony-Anhalt, before emptying into the Saale near Naumburg. Its total length is 192 kilometres. Towns along it include Mühlhausen, Sömmerda, Bad Frankenhausen, Artern, Roßleben and Freyburg, and its main tributaries are the Gera, Wipper, Helme and Lossa. The name goes back to Old High German Strödu, boggy thicket, with the prefix un- to intensify it, so the region was very swampy. The river is recorded as Onestrudis in 575, as Unestrude in the seventh century and as Vnstruod in 994.

According to the Decem Libri of Gregory of Tours, the decisive battle between the Franconians and the Thuringians took place along the Unstrut in 531. It ended in the destruction and annexation of the early medieval Thuringian kingdom by the Frankish empire. In 933 King Henry I fought a Hungarian army in the Battle of Riade, at a place near the Unstrut that is now unknown, after a ten-year truce. His victory brought a period of peace, until the Hungarians returned in 955 and were defeated again.

Memleben on the Unstrut was one of Henry's favourite places, and a royal residence was built there. He died there in 936, and so did his son Otto I in 973. A monastery built in the following years became for a short time one of the most important in the German realm, and its ruins can still be seen, although the exact site of the palace is no longer known.

Because the river was marshy, it was long unnavigable for ships. In the years 1790–94 it was made navigable on the orders of the Elector of Saxony, and for a century it was an important shipping lane, carrying sandstone and limestone in particular. The Unstrut Railway, built beside it from 1889, greatly reduced its importance as a transport route. The countryside around the Saale and the Unstrut forms the Saale-Unstrut wine-growing region, one of the smallest, with an area of 300 hectares. The sparkling wine brand Rotkäppchen is made in the cellars of Freyburg. Sights along the river include the town of Mühlhausen, the ruined castle of Wendelstein and Neuenburg Castle at Freyburg.
unye: Ünye is a municipality and district of Ordu Province, on the Black Sea coast 76 km west of the city of Ordu. The district covers 569 square kilometres. The town has a small port in a bay on one of the flatter stretches of the coast, and because its hinterland is flatter than most of the coastline it has less rainfall than much of the region. Its name evolved from the Greek Oinoe through Oinaion, Unieh, Unie and Unia to the present Ünye.

The history of the place goes back to the Hittite period in the 15th century BCE, followed by the Kashkas, Scythians, Milesians and Persians, and then by Pontus and the Roman and Byzantine eras. In Greco-Roman times it was called Oenoe and was a port of Pontus at the mouth of the river Genius.

Later rule changed often. The Danishmends held it between 1086 and 1098, 1141 and 1144, and 1150 and 1157. The Sultanate of Rum held it in 1188-1204, 1214-1228 and 1230-1243, and the Empire of Trebizond in 1204-1214, 1228-1230, 1243-1297 and 1302-1346. The Emirate of Hacıemiroğlu held it between 1297 and 1302 and again from 1346 to 1461. The Ünye fortress was built in the 1290s by the Trebizond emperor Ioanni II. In 1806 the Laz attacked the town, which was evacuated under the guidance of Bishop Meletios and resettled in Sinope.

Agriculture is the basis of the local economy, above all the growing, trading and processing of hazelnuts. The town also has a cement factory, flour mills and local handicrafts, and it serves the surrounding countryside with schools and other services. It has a population of 132,432 (2022). Its sights include an 18th-century town hall, Ünye Castle, which dates back to the Pontus era, and Uzunkum, a long beach on the Black Sea.
upanishads: The Upanishads are Sanskrit texts of the late Vedic and post-Vedic periods. They are the most recent addition to the Vedas, whose earlier parts dealt with mantras, benedictions, rituals, ceremonies and sacrifices. The word Upaniṣad is understood as "sitting near a teacher", from upa "by" and ni-ṣad "sit down", though it first meant "connection" or "equivalence". Most authors are unknown, but the early texts credit sages such as Yajnavalkya, Uddalaka Aruni and Shvetaketu, and women such as Maitreyi and Gargi take part in the dialogues.

Scholars are uncertain about when they were composed. The Indologist Patrick Olivelle holds that no dating of the early texts can be closer than a few centuries. The early Upanishads are generally placed in northern India, in the region of Kuru-Panchala and Kosala-Videha, where King Janaka of Videha features prominently in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad.

Of 108 Upanishads known from the Muktika list, about a dozen are the oldest and are called the principal or mukhya Upanishads. The Brihadaranyaka and the Chandogya are the oldest of these. They were memorised and passed down orally for centuries. Each Upanishad is attached to one of the four Vedas: the Rigveda, Samaveda, Yajurveda or Atharvaveda. New Upanishads continued to be composed into the modern era, and in 1908 four previously unknown ones were found in manuscripts.

Their central concern is the relation between ritual, cosmic realities and the human person, with Atman, the self, and Brahman, the ultimate reality, at the summit of the universe. The older texts attack ritual with increasing intensity: the Brihadaranyaka calls anyone who worships a divinity other than the self a domestic animal of the gods. The ideas are plural. Some texts are monistic, while the Katha Upanishad is dualistic and the Maitri inclines towards the dualism that grounds the Samkhya and Yoga schools.

The mukhya Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita and the Brahmasutra together form the three main sources of all schools of Vedanta. Their varied teaching allowed divergent readings. Adi Shankara, in the 8th century CE, wrote commentaries on eleven principal Upanishads and is linked with the non-dual Advaita school, while Ramanuja (1017 to 1137 CE) read them as teaching qualified monism and Madhvacharya (1199 to 1278 CE) as strongly theistic. Modern scholars differ on how far Shankara's views follow the texts.

Translations of the early 19th century drew the attention of Western readers. The German philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer was deeply impressed and called them the most profitable and elevating reading possible in the world.
upolu: Upolu was formed by a massive basaltic shield volcano that rises from the seafloor of the western Pacific Ocean. The island is 75 kilometres long and 1,125 square kilometres in area, which makes it the second largest of the Samoan Islands by area. It lies to the southeast of Savai'i, the big island. Apia, the capital, stands in the middle of the north coast, and Faleolo International Airport is at the western end. There are no historically recorded eruptions, though three lava flows show activity between a few hundred and a few thousand years ago. In the Samoan branch of Polynesian mythology, Upolu was the first woman on the island.

In 1841 the island was the site of the Bombardment of Upolu, an incident during the United States Exploring Expedition. In the late 19th century the Scottish writer Robert Louis Stevenson owned a 400-acre estate at the village of Vailima. He died there in 1894 and is buried at the top of Mount Vaea overlooking it.

The Vailima estate was bought in 1900 to serve as the official residence of the German governor of German Samoa. When British and Dominion authorities took over the government of the islands, they confiscated the estate and used it in the same way. It later housed the New Zealand administrator and, after independence, the Samoan head of state. During the Second World War the US Navy built Naval Base Upolu on the island. A tsunami struck Upolu on 29 September 2009 and reportedly destroyed twenty villages on its south side.
Upolu has about 145,000 inhabitants and is by far the most populous of the Samoan Islands. The Samoan moss spider, Patu marplesi, an extremely small species, lives on the island.
upper-austria: Upper Austria is one of the nine states of Austria, with its capital at Linz. It borders Germany and the Czech Republic and the Austrian states of Lower Austria, Styria and Salzburg, and has an area of 11,982 square kilometres. Historically it was divided into four regions: the Hausruckviertel, Innviertel, Mühlviertel and Traunviertel. Under Roman rule the parts south of the Danube belonged to the province of Noricum.

In the early Middle Ages the Avars and Slavs expanded as far as the Enns, while the lands further west belonged to the Old Bavarians. Bavaria came under Carolingian rule by 788, and after the Treaty of Verdun in 843 the region belonged to the East Frankish Realm, though Hungarian raids devastated it in the first half of the tenth century. After the Battle of Lechfeld in 955 it was consolidated within the Duchy of Bavaria.

In 1156 the March of Austria became a duchy under the House of Babenberg, and by the mid-thirteenth century the region was known as the Principality above the Enns, a name first recorded in 1264. By the end of the century the House of Habsburg ruled the duchy, which became an archduchy in 1453.

In 1490 the area above the Enns, centred on Linz, received a measure of provincial autonomy. By 1550 it had a Protestant majority, and the Counter-Reformation was introduced under Emperor Rudolf II and his successor Matthias. Bavaria controlled the area for some years in the early seventeenth century. The Innviertel was ceded from Bavaria in the Treaty of Teschen in 1779. French armies occupied the land more than once in the Napoleonic Wars.

The two archduchies, above and below the Enns, kept separate administrations through the nineteenth century, and after Austria-Hungary collapsed in 1918 the name Upper Austria was officially adopted. After Austria was annexed by Nazi Germany it formed part of Reichsgau Oberdonau, and in 1945 it was divided between an American zone to the south and a Soviet zone to the north.

Upper Austria has about 1.5 million inhabitants and is Austria's leading industrial region. It is divided into 15 districts, the three statutory cities of Linz, Steyr and Wels, and 438 municipalities. Its state constitution defines it as an independent state of the Republic of Austria. After World War II it received a million refugees.
upper-bavaria: Upper Bavaria lies in the southern part of Bavaria and is centred on Munich, the state capital and seat of the district government. It is by far the most populous administrative division in Bavaria. The name refers to the relative position on the Danube and its tributaries: downstream, Upper Bavaria is followed by Lower Bavaria, then Upper Austria, and then Lower Austria. The region has 20 districts and 500 municipalities, including three district-free cities, Ingolstadt, Munich and Rosenheim, and is divided into four planning regions.

The duchy of Upper Bavaria was first created by the First Bavarian partition in 1255 under Duke Louis II, though it did not correspond exactly to the present territory. After the reunification of 1340 Bavaria was divided again in 1349, and in 1392 the duchies of Bavaria-Munich and Bavaria-Ingolstadt were created in Upper Bavaria. Bavaria was permanently reunited in 1505. For administration it was split into Rentämter, and Upper Bavaria consisted of the Rentamt Munich and the Rentamt Burghausen.

After the Kingdom of Bavaria was founded the state was reorganised, and in 1808 it was divided into 15 districts, created in the fashion of the French departments and named after their main rivers. Territorial changes, among them the loss of Tyrol and the addition of the Palatinate, reduced them to eight, one of which was the Isarkreis. In 1837 King Ludwig I renamed the districts after historical names and tribes, and the Isarkreis became Upper Bavaria. These districts were predecessors of modern regional self-government, linking the Bavarian state to the local authorities.

Upper Bavaria is one of the seven administrative regions of Bavaria. Former residence cities include Munich, Ingolstadt and Neuburg an der Donau, and the diocesan towns are Freising and Eichstätt. The Zugspitze is its highest mountain, and its lakes include the Tegernsee, the Starnberger See, the Ammersee and the Chiemsee. The monasteries of Andechs, Ettal and Benediktbeuern and the Wieskirche hold sacred art, the royal castles of Ludwig II stand at Linderhof and Herrenchiemsee, and Altötting and Tuntenhausen are the most important places of pilgrimage.
upper-egypt: Upper Egypt is the Nile valley in the south of the country. Today it is counted from Beni Suef to the First Cataract, which precedes Lake Nasser, the lake formed by the Aswan High Dam. Its northern part, between Sohag and El-Ayait, is also known as Middle Egypt.

In ancient Egypt it was called tꜣ šmꜣw, the Land of Reeds or Sedgeland, after the sedges that grow there. The Arabic name Sa'id means uplands, from a root meaning to go up. Its people are known as Sa'idis and generally speak Sa'idi Egyptian Arabic. In Biblical Hebrew and Akkadian it was known by names that come from the Egyptian for the southern land.

By about 3600 BCE Neolithic societies along the Nile based their culture on crops and the domestication of animals. A new pottery appeared, related to Levantine ceramics, and copper implements became common. The towns of Upper Egypt then politically unified, as did those of the Delta, which led to warfare between the two new kingdoms. The main city of prehistoric Upper Egypt was Nekhen, and its patron deity was the goddess Nekhbet, depicted as a vulture.

During his reign in Upper Egypt King Narmer defeated his enemies in the Delta and became sole ruler of the two lands. It is believed that the rulers of the supposed Thinite Confederacy had united Upper Egypt by absorbing rival city states during the Naqada III period, and its unification with Lower Egypt ushered in the Early Dynastic period. In royal symbolism Upper Egypt was represented by the tall White Crown, the flowering lotus and the sedge, and after unification its patron Nekhbet was shown with the patron of Lower Egypt as the Two Ladies.

For most of ancient history Thebes was its administrative centre. After the Assyrians devastated it, Egypt's importance declined, and under the Ptolemies Ptolemais Hermiou became the capital of Upper Egypt. In the eleventh century large numbers of pastoralists, known as Hilalians, left Upper Egypt for Libya and as far as Tunis, probably because grazing conditions had worsened as the Medieval Warm Period began.

Upper Egypt now forms seven governorates: Beni Suef, Minya, Asyut, Sohag, Qena, Luxor and Aswan. Its large cities include Asyut, Luxor, Edfu and Aswan. In twentieth-century Egypt the title Prince of the Sa'id, meaning Prince of Upper Egypt, was used by the heir apparent to the Egyptian throne.
upper-franconia: Upper Franconia is one of three regions of Bavaria that make up the historic region of Franconia, the others being Middle Franconia and Lower Franconia. It borders Thuringia to the north, Lower Franconia to the west, Middle Franconia to the south-west, the Upper Palatinate to the south-east, Saxony to the north-east and the Czech Republic to the east. It is subdivided into nine districts and four district-free cities, Bamberg, Bayreuth, Coburg and Hof, and its lowest level comprises 214 municipalities.

After the founding of the Kingdom of Bavaria the state was completely reorganised, and in 1808 it was divided into 15 administrative regions called Kreise. They were created in the fashion of the French departments, quite even in size and population, and named after their main rivers. Territorial changes, among them the loss of Tyrol and the addition of the Palatinate, reduced the number of Kreise to eight in the following years. One of these was the Mainkreis, or Main District. In 1837 King Ludwig I of Bavaria renamed the Kreise after historical territorial names and tribes of the area, which also involved some border changes and territorial swaps, and the Mainkreis became Upper Franconia.

Bayreuth is the capital. The main sights include the former episcopal residence of Bamberg, the former residence city of Coburg and the classicist centre of Hof, as well as Kulmbach, Kronach and Lichtenfels, Banz Abbey and the Basilica of the Fourteen Holy Helpers. The River Main and the Fichtel Mountains with the town of Wunsiedel, and the Franconian Forest, are scenic attractions, and there are numerous spa towns, among them Bad Staffelstein and Bad Steben. The region has more than 200 independent breweries, and a Franconian beer route runs through many of them.
upper-lusatia: Upper Lusatia, with Lower Lusatia to the north, makes up the region of Lusatia, named after the Slavic Lusici tribe. Most of it lies in the German state of Saxony, with an eastern part in Poland beyond the Neisse. Its historic capital is Bautzen, and its largest city is Görlitz, halved between Germany and Poland since 1945. The name Lusatia superior was first recorded in a deed of 1474; earlier the territory was called Milsko, after the West Slavic Milceni tribe. The south is shaped by the Lusatian Mountains, the westernmost range of the Sudetes, and the Spree rises in the Lusatian Highlands and flows through Bautzen.

Slavs settled the region from the 7th century, and the Milceni had a fortified centre where the Ortenburg in Bautzen now stands. They were forced to pay tribute in 932 and subdued by Otto I in 939. Bautzen was first mentioned in 1002, and the Peace of Bautzen of 30 January 1018 assigned the Milceni lands to Poland, though German rule returned by the Treaty of Merseburg in 1033. In the 12th century Upper Lusatia came to Bohemia under Přemyslid rule, and in the first century of that rule all its major towns and religious institutions apart from Bautzen were founded. German peasants settled alongside the Sorbs during the Ostsiedlung.

The Ascanian margraves of Brandenburg held it between 1253 and 1262, and in 1268 Margrave Otto IV divided it into the lands of Bautzen and Görlitz. King John of Bohemia incorporated Görlitz into the Bohemian Crown in 1329. In 1346 five royal cities and Zittau founded the Lusatian League, supported by King Charles IV, and the six towns gained political influence against the nobility.

After the death of Louis II of Bohemia at Mohács in 1526, Ferdinand I of Austria inherited the region. The Peace of Prague of 1635 transferred it to the Electorate of Saxony, and in 1815 the Congress of Vienna gave the north-eastern part to Prussia.

After the Second World War the border between East Germany and Poland was fixed at the Oder-Neisse line, which split the historic region between the two countries. The Sorbs, a West Slavic minority, still live in Upper Lusatia, and about 20,000 people between Kamenz, Bautzen and Hoyerswerda speak Sorbian. Muskau Park, at Bad Muskau and Łęknica, is a World Heritage Site, and the Sorbian Museum in Bautzen and the Lusatian Museum in Zgorzelec are dedicated to the region's history.
upper-mesopotamia: Upper Mesopotamia, also called the Jazira, is the uplands and outwash plain of north-western Iraq, north-eastern Syria and south-eastern Turkey. It extends south from the mountains of Anatolia, down the Tigris to Samarra and down the Euphrates to Hit, and includes the Sinjar plain. The Khabur runs for over 400 km across it from Turkey to the Euphrates. Mesopotamia is Greek for the land between the two rivers; after the Muslim conquests of the 7th century the region was called al-Jazira, Arabic for island, because the rivers almost enclose it.

The region is of great archaeological importance: at Hallan Çemi, Abu Hureyra and Mureybet people passed from hunting and gathering to growing wild wheat, barley and legumes from around 9000 BCE, and goats and sheep were domesticated soon after. At Göbekli Tepe the earliest ritual buildings date from before 9000 BCE, over five thousand years older than Stonehenge. In the Early Dynastic Period the royal archives at Ebla show Ebla, Mari and Nagar as the dominant states.

Upper Mesopotamia was the heartland of Assyria. It was part of the Akkadian Empire from the 23rd century BCE and an integral part of the Assyrian state from 2000 BCE until 608 BCE, when it fell to the Babylonians. It then passed to the Achaemenid Empire from 539 BCE, to the Seleucid Empire from 330 BCE, and to the Parthians, Romans and the Sasanian Empire. Syriac monasticism, which came in the late fourth century, flourished in the sixth and early seventh.

Under the Abbasids the Jazira was one of the highest tax-yielding provinces. The Hamdanids set up an autonomous state there in the 920s, and local dynasties, the Numayrids, Mirdasids and Uqaylids, held it until the Seljuq conquest. After the First Crusade the west became the County of Edessa; the region was later ruled by the Zengids and the Kurdish Ayyubids, then by the Artuqids, Kara Koyunlu, Akkoyunlu and Safavids, while the west passed from the Mamluk Sultanate to the Ottoman Empire in 1516–17.

After the First World War the region was divided among Iraq, Syria and Turkey. Its chief settlements are Mosul, Deir ez-Zor, Raqqa, al-Hasakah, Diyarbakır and Qamishli, and its Syrian part is described as Syria's breadbasket. It is regarded as the traditional Assyrian homeland, and Djezirah is one of the four dioceses of the Syriac Orthodox Church.
upper-silesia: Upper Silesia lies on the upper Oder River, north of the Eastern Sudetes and the Moravian Gate, which form its southern border with the historic region of Moravia. In the Silesian Beskids to the east the Vistula rises, and the Biała and Przemsza mark the border with Lesser Poland. To the north lies Greater Poland and to the west Lower Silesia. Most of the region is in Poland, covering most of the Opole Voivodeship and the western half of the Silesian Voivodeship, and a smaller part is in the Czech regions of Moravia-Silesia and Olomouc.
