Cieszyn Silesia and former Austrian Silesia are historical parts of it.

According to the Bavarian Geographer of the 9th century, the West Slavic Opolanie had settled on the upper Oder, centred on the stronghold of Opole. By 990 the Piast duke Mieszko I had conquered large parts of Silesia, and his son Bolesław I the Brave subdued the lands of the Opolanie. After the death of Bolesław III Wrymouth in 1138 Poland fragmented. In 1172 Mieszko IV Tanglefoot received the Duchy of Racibórz, and by 1202 he ruled all Upper Silesia as Duke of Opole and Racibórz. German settlers arrived in large numbers in the 13th century, and the region split further after 1281 into the duchies of Bytom, Opole, Racibórz and Cieszyn.

In 1327 the Upper Silesian dukes swore allegiance to King John of Bohemia, and by the Treaty of Trentschin in 1335 Silesia became a land of the Bohemian Crown. The Black Death halted the influx of German settlers, and a majority of the population still spoke Polish and Silesian. In 1469 King Matthias Corvinus of Hungary conquered the region, and after 1526 the Bohemian crown lands passed to the House of Habsburg. Prussia occupied most of Upper Silesia in 1742 and annexed it by the Treaty of Breslau, and it became an industrial area with plentiful coal and iron ore. Prussian Upper Silesia joined the German Empire in 1871.

After the First World War there were three Silesian Uprisings between 1919 and 1921. In the plebiscite of March 1921, 59.4 per cent voted against joining Poland and 40.6 per cent for it. The region was divided in 1922, with the eastern part ceded to Poland as the Silesian Voivodeship. After 1945 the area was placed under Polish administration, and most German speakers who had not fled were expelled. It became formally part of Poland by the border treaty of 14 November 1990.

The region is known for its heavy industry, mining and metallurgy. Its historical capital is Opole, but the largest towns, among them Katowice, lie in the Upper Silesian Industrial Region, with about 2,500,000 inhabitants. On the Czech side, Ostrava and Opava are among its larger cities.
uppland: Uppland lies on the eastern coast of Sweden just north of Stockholm and borders Södermanland, Västmanland and Gästrikland. It is bounded by Lake Mälaren and the Baltic Sea. The name means up land, a form that older English writing often renders Upland, and its Latinised form is Uplandia. The province was historically divided into chartered cities and districts: hundreds inland and, in the coastal archipelago of Roslagen, ship districts, called skeppslag. On the small uninhabited island of Märket in the Baltic, Uppland has a very short land border with Åland.

The earliest unambiguous mention of Uppland dates from 1296, when it was recorded as including the folklands of Fjärdhundraland, Attundaland, Tiundaland and Roslagen. Sigtuna, thought to have been founded around 980 and the oldest town in Sweden, lies in the province. Uppland ranked historically as a duchy, and its arms, granted in 1560, show a globus cruciger. Its dukes included Prince Waldemar from 1310 to 1318, with his wife Ingeborg Eriksdottir of Norway, Prince Gustav from 1827 to 1852 and Prince Sigvard from 1907 to 1934.

Uppsala is the seat of the only archbishop of the Lutheran Church of Sweden; before the Reformation the archdiocese belonged to the Roman Catholic Church. The province is known for having as many as 1,196 inscribed runestones, left by Vikings, many of whom came from Roslagen.

Today the traditional provinces of Sweden serve no administrative purpose. Most of Uppland lies in Uppsala County, though the larger part of its population lives in Stockholm County. The province holds Drottningholm Palace and the archaeological site of Birka, both World Heritage Sites, together with Skokloster Castle and the medieval Uppsala Cathedral, where many royals are buried. Among those connected with it are Gustav Vasa, St. Bridget of Sweden, Carl Linnaeus and Anders Celsius.
uppsala: Uppsala originally referred to a place a few kilometres north of the present city, now called Gamla Uppsala (Old Uppsala). The present city was called Aros, meaning river mouth, for its position at the mouth of the River Fyris on Ekoln, a bay of Lake Mälaren; the name became Östra Aros, East Aros, to distinguish it from Västra Aros, today's Västerås. According to the medieval writer Adam of Bremen, Old Uppsala was the main pagan centre of Sweden, and its temple contained idols of the Norse gods. Östra Aros was then a port town of Old Uppsala.

In 1160 King Eric Jedvardsson was attacked and killed outside the church of Östra Aros and later was venerated as a saint in the Catholic Church. In 1274 Östra Aros overtook Old Uppsala as the main regional centre. When the cathedral of Old Uppsala burned down, the archbishopric and the relics of Saint Eric moved to Östra Aros, where the present Uppsala Cathedral was built and inaugurated in 1435. A fire severely damaged the city in 1702. Uppsala Castle was begun in 1549 by King Gustav Vasa, and the cathedral was long the usual site of Swedish coronations.

The city lies on flat, fertile land about 71 km north of Stockholm, on the Fyris River. A glacial ridge, Uppsalaåsen, runs parallel to the river and carries the castle. The river divides the city into a historic quarter on the western bank, with a medieval street layout, and a modern commercial centre to the east. Clergy, royalty and academia historically lived in the Fjärdingen neighbourhood on the west side, and the ensemble of cathedral, castle and university buildings has remained largely undisturbed. Demolitions in the 1960s and 1970s destroyed some historical treasures.

Uppsala is the fourth-largest city in Sweden, with 177,074 inhabitants in 2019, and the capital of Uppsala County. Uppsala University, founded in 1477 under Bishop Jakob Ulvsson, is the oldest in Scandinavia. It was reorganised as a Lutheran institution in 1595 after the Uppsala Synod of 1593, and its student fraternities are called nations. The Gustavianum, built in 1625, holds a preserved 17th-century anatomical theatre built by Olof Rudbeck. Carl Linnaeus lived in the city for many years, and his house and garden can be visited. The Carolina Rediviva library, built in 1820 to 1841, holds over 5 million volumes. At Old Uppsala stand several large burial mounds of pre-Christian monarchs.
uppsala-university: Like most medieval universities, Uppsala grew out of an ecclesiastical centre. The archbishop of Uppsala had been one of the most important sees in Sweden since Christianity first spread to the region in the ninth century, and the town was long a hub of regional trade. The papal bull of Pope Sixtus IV granted the university its corporate rights and the same freedoms and privileges as the University of Bologna. It allowed the four traditional faculties of theology, law, medicine and philosophy, and the awarding of bachelor's, master's, licentiate and doctoral degrees. The archbishop of Uppsala was named chancellor. Lectures began on 7 October.

The Reformation of King Gustavus Vasa reduced the already small number of students, because Uppsala was seen as a centre of Catholicism and potential disloyalty to the Crown. Swedish students often travelled to Protestant universities in Germany, especially Wittenberg. At the end of the 16th century Uppsala became a bastion of Lutheranism, which Duke Charles, later Charles IX, used to consolidate his power against his nephew Sigismund III Vasa. The Uppsala Synod of 1593 established Lutheran orthodoxy, and Charles and the Council of state gave the university new privileges on 1 August of that year.

In the 17th century the expanding Swedish state needed many more civil servants and educators, and a large donation from King Gustavus Adolphus gave the university relative financial stability. In the 1630s Chancellor Axel Oxenstierna had it offer exercises such as riding, fencing, dance and modern languages to attract young noblemen. In the 18th century the emphasis moved towards the sciences: Anders Celsius became a professor in 1729 and Carl Linnaeus professor of medicine with botany in 1741. A chair in economics was established in 1741 with Anders Berch as its first holder.

The student nations, corporations of students grouped by province of origin, appear in Uppsala only about 1630 to 1640, probably under the influence of the German Landsmannschaften. In 1663 the consistory made membership legal and placed each nation under a professor. The Royal Academic Orchestra dates from 1627, and the Uppsala University Choir from 1830. The university library holds the Gothic Bible manuscript Codex Argenteus. Women's right to study was first raised in a motion in the last session of the estate parliament in 1865.
uqba-ibn-nafi: Uqba ibn Nafi belonged to the Banu Fihr, a clan connected to the Quraysh, and is often surnamed al-Fihri; his descendants were known as the Uqbids or Fihrids. He was the nephew of Amr ibn al-As and served the Rashidun Caliphate from the reign of Umar and later the Umayyad Caliphate under Mu'awiya I and Yazid I. His father, Nafi ibn Abd al-Qays, was one of the first Muslims to settle in Egypt and probably took part in the war against Nubia. Uqba entered the Maghreb with his uncle while still young. Arab historians described him as a pious man and called him Uqba al-mustajab, the one whose prayers were answered.

After Amr ibn al-As took Barqa, Uqba was sent to conquer the oasis of Fezzan and went on to Zawila, which he secured by a peace agreement. In 666 he advanced from Ghadames to Waddan, whose king he fined 360 slaves for breaking an earlier treaty, and then to Germa, the main city of Fezzan, whose king accepted Islam and agreed to a tribute of about 360 slaves. He also led an expedition into the southern desert as far as Kawar, near Kanem. He was appointed governor of Ifriqiya and was dismissed in 674. In Damascus he complained to Mu'awiya of his treatment, and the caliph promised to restore him.

Yazid I reinstated him in 681 for a second governorship. Uqba marched to Kairouan with ten thousand horsemen, removed Abu al-Muhajir Dinar and bound him in chains, and ordered people to return to Kairouan and develop it, so that the city flourished. He did not follow Abu al-Muhajir's policy, which had brought many Berbers of the Aures into Islam. He then left Zuhayr ibn Qays al-Balawi in charge of Kairouan and set out to complete the conquest of the Maghreb.

In 683 Uqba was ambushed by the Berber Christian king Kusaila and his Byzantine allies at the Battle of Vescera and killed beside his rival Abu al-Muhajir Dinar. His armies evacuated Kairouan and withdrew to Barqa, and Kairouan was recaptured in 688. He became remembered as a martyr, the first major Muslim figure martyred in North Africa, and groups such as the Fulani, the Kunta and the Iwellemmedan claim descent from him. A mausoleum mosque built in 686 gave rise to the village of Sidi Okba.

The chronicles of his conquests date from at least two centuries after the events. Ibn Idhari reports that at the Atlantic he said that, had the sea not prevented him, he would have galloped on for ever like Alexander the Great. Edward Gibbon called him the Conqueror of Africa.
ur: Ur lay near the mouth of the Euphrates on the Persian Gulf, although the coastline has since shifted and the site now stands well inland, on the south bank of the river. Its surroundings were probably marshy, so irrigation may have been unnecessary, and the canals visible in the ruins were likely used for transport. Fish, birds, tubers and reeds may have supported the city without an agricultural revolution of the kind sometimes thought a prerequisite for urban life.

The patron deity was the moon god Nanna, known as Sin in Akkadian, and the name of the city derives from UNUGKI, literally the abode of Nanna. The mound is roughly 1200 by 800 metres and rises about 20 metres above the plain. Occupation grew from about 15 hectares in the Jemdet Nasr period to 90 hectares in the Early Dynastic period, then 108 hectares in the Ur III period and 140 hectares in the Isin-Larsa period.

Early occupation dates to the Ubaid period, and the city is recorded in writing as a city-state from the 26th century BCE, its first recorded king being Mesannepada. The Royal Tombs of the Early Dynastic IIIa period held luxury goods of precious metals and semi-precious stones brought from Iran, Afghanistan, India, Asia Minor, the Levant and the Gulf. Later Ur came under Lagash, and when Sargon of Akkad conquered it he made his daughter Enheduanna high priestess of Nanna. She is regarded as possibly the first identifiable author in history, though Assyriologists are unsure whether she composed her hymns herself.

After Ur lost its political power, the Elamites severely damaged it, and it later fell to Hammurabi of the Old Babylonian Empire. In the reign of Samsu-iluna it was abandoned, and it afterwards belonged to the Sealand Dynasty and the Kassites. It passed under Assyrian rule, and in the 6th century BCE Nebuchadnezzar II built there and Nabonidus improved the ziggurat. After Babylonia fell to the Achaemenid Empire the city declined, and it was no longer inhabited by the early 5th century BCE, perhaps because of drought, shifting rivers and silting.

The site is Tell el-Muqayyar in Dhi Qar Governorate, Iraq, about 16 kilometres south-west of Nasiriyah. Pietro Della Valle visited it in 1625, and Henry Rawlinson's reading of inscribed bricks identified it as Ur. Leonard Woolley's excavations, which included the Royal Tombs and the Lyres of Ur, found 1850 burials, of which 17 were judged Royal Tombs. The Great Ziggurat, with its shrine of Nanna, is fully cleared and is the best-preserved landmark. Ur is possibly the Ur of the Chaldees of the Book of Genesis, though other sites have been proposed.
ur-nammu: According to the Sumerian King List, Ur-Nammu reigned for 18 years; year-names are known for 17 of them, though their order is uncertain. One records the devastation of Gutium, and two seem to commemorate his legal reforms, among them the year in which he made justice in the land. His military exploits included the conquest of Lagash and the defeat of his former masters at Uruk. He was recognised as a regional ruler of Ur, Eridu and Uruk at a coronation in Nippur, and he is believed to have built at Nippur, Larsa, Kish, Adab and Umma. He restored the roads and general order after the Gutian period.

His inscriptions report the defeat of a coalition of the Elamite ruler Kutik-Insusinak and cities including Tutub and Eshnunna. He ordered the construction of several ziggurats, including the Great Ziggurat of Ur. He held the titles King of Ur and King of Sumer and Akkad, and his personal goddess was Ninsuna. In royal hymns he and his son Shulgi call Lugalbanda and Ninsun their holy parents and describe themselves as brothers of Gilgamesh.

The Death of Ur-Nammu, a later Sumerian composition, describes his death, funeral and passage through the underworld. Its account of the death is damaged, vague and metaphoric, though some scholars have read it as saying that he died in battle at the hands of his own troops. His son Shulgi succeeded him.

Many scholars hold that Ur-Nammu was one of the few Mesopotamian kings of the third millennium BCE who was not deified after death, yet he was worshipped: the palace at Tummal included funerary chapels for him and his wife, and he may have been buried there. The Ur-Nammu Stela, found by Leonard Woolley in the temple precinct of Nanna at Ur in the 1920s, survives in 106 fragments and is held at the University Museum of the University of Pennsylvania.
ur-nanshe: Ur-Nanshe, also called Ur-Nina, was the first king of the First Dynasty of Lagash in the Sumerian Early Dynastic Period III. He was probably not of royal lineage, being the son of Gunidu, who is recorded without a royal title, and his inscriptions name Gurmu as his grandfather. He came to power after Lugalshaengur, the ensi, or high priest, of Lagash, who is known only from the macehead inscription of Mesilim. He was the father of Akurgal, who succeeded him, and the grandfather of Eannatum, who defeated Umma, as shown on the Stele of the Vultures, and continued his building work.

Ur-Nanshe is known through inscriptions to have commissioned many building projects, including canals and temples, and to have defended Lagash against its rival Umma, whose ensi Pabilgagaltuku he recorded capturing. The Perforated Relief of King Ur-Nanshe, now in the Louvre, attributes to him the temple of Ningirsu in Girsu, the temple of Nanshe in Nina and Apsubanda. A door socket in the Louvre adds the houses of Gatumdug and Ninmar, a harem, the Ibgal and the Kinir. The Ibgal of Inanna lies at al-Hiba, the ancient city of Lagash, where an oval wall surrounds the main mud-brick temple on the southwest edge of the city, an unusual position because Sumerian temples were usually central.

The Perforated Relief is a limestone slab with two registers. In the upper one Ur-Nanshe wears a kaunakes, a tufted wool skirt, and carries a basket of bricks on his head while his wife or daughter and four of his sons stand around him. In the lower one he sits at a banquet celebrating the building of the temple, with officials and three more sons, and he is drawn much larger than everyone else. An inscription in front of him reads that boats from the land of Dilmun carried wood to him, the oldest known written record of Dilmun and of imports into Mesopotamia. A hymn to Nanshe says that she seated Ur-Nanshe, the beloved lord of Lagash, on the throne.
ural-mountains: The Ural Mountains extend about 2,500 kilometres from the Kara Sea to the Kazakh Steppe. Vaygach Island and Novaya Zemlya continue the chain northward. Average altitudes are around 1,000 to 1,300 metres, and the highest point is Mount Narodnaya, at 1,895 metres. The Urals are among the oldest extant mountain ranges, with an age estimated at 250 to 300 million years, formed when the eastern edge of the supercontinent Laurasia collided with Kazakhstania. They hold about 48 species of economically valuable ores and minerals, among them iron, copper, gold and coal, and stones such as emerald, malachite and amethyst.

Merchants from the Middle East traded with the Bashkirs on the western slopes from the 10th century. The first Russian mention is in the Primary Chronicle, which describes a Novgorodian expedition to the upper Pechora in 1096. Ivan III captured Perm, Pechora and Yugra from Novgorod in 1472. Sigismund von Herberstein reported in 1549 that there were mountains behind the Pechora. In 1574 the Russians founded Ufa, and the Stroganovs, granted lands on the Kama and Chusovaya, provided the staging ground for Yermak's incursion into Siberia. Yermak crossed the Urals around 1581. Verkhoturye was founded in 1598, and its road became the only legal link between European Russia and Siberia for a long time.

Iron and copper were found in the 17th century and mining intensified under Peter I. Vasily Tatishchev planned the works that became Perm and Yekaterinburg, founded in 1723 by Georg Wilhelm de Gennin. Gold has been mined since 1747. The first railway across the Urals was built by 1878 and became part of the Trans-Siberian Railway in 1896. Magnitogorsk was founded in the 1930s, and in 1941 and 1942 factories were evacuated there from European Russia.

The Urals form part of the conventional boundary between Europe and Asia and separate European Russia from Siberia. They are one of the largest centres of metallurgy and heavy industry in Russia. The Virgin Komi Forests in the northern Urals are a World Heritage site. The plutonium plant Mayak, in operation from 1948, was the site of the Kyshtym disaster, and a storage tank explosion in 1957 contaminated over 23,000 square kilometres of land.
ural-river: The Ural, also called the Yaik, rises near Mount Kruglaya in the southern Ural Mountains and flows through Russia and Kazakhstan to the Caspian Sea. It is 2,428 kilometres long, which makes it the third-longest river in Europe after the Volga and the Danube. It runs south past Magnitogorsk and around the southern end of the Urals to Orsk, then west to Orenburg, passes into Kazakhstan and reaches the Caspian a few kilometres below Atyrau, where it forms a tree-like delta. Most authoritative sources count its whole length as part of the boundary between Europe and Asia.

Ptolemy, in the 2nd century CE, called the river Daïkos. Scholars disagree about the origin of the name: Gerard Clauson attributes it to a Sarmatian origin and disputes that it could be Turkic so early. A Russian chronicle of 1140 gives Yaik, and Catherine II renamed it the Ural in 1775.

From the 10th to the 16th centuries Saray-Jük, or Saraichik, meaning small Sarai, on the river was an important trade centre on the Silk Road. It became a stronghold of the Golden Horde in the 13th century and was destroyed in 1395 by the army of Timur. It was rebuilt and became the capital of the Nogai Horde in the 15th and 16th centuries, and the Ural Cossacks reduced it to a village in 1580.

After the Russian conquest of the Ural basin in the late 16th century, the Yaik Cossacks settled the shores. They fished for sturgeon in the river and the Caspian, and the best-known method was bagrenye, in which Cossacks gathered on the ice on the one day of the year when it was allowed, broke it with pike poles and speared the hibernating fish. Cossacks resented government rules and sometimes rebelled. The largest rebellion, Pugachev's Rebellion of 1773 to 1775, involved much of south-eastern Russia. After it, Catherine issued a decree of 15 January 1775 renaming most of the places involved, so that the Yaik River became the Ural River, Yaitsk became Uralsk and the Yaik Cossacks became the Ural Cossacks.

The river is navigated up to Uralsk, and its upper waters supply the Magnitogorsk Iron and Steel Works, built in the early 1930s. The lower reaches are used for irrigation. The delta wetlands are an important stopover for migrating birds along the Asian flyway.
uraniborg: Uraniborg, the Castle of Urania, was named for the Muse of astronomy. It served as an observatory and alchemy laboratory and was the first custom-built observatory in modern Europe, and the last built without a telescope as its main instrument. The cornerstone was laid on 8 August 1576, and the Flemish Renaissance building of brick framed in sandstone and limestone was built between 1576 and 1580 under the architect Hans van Emden and the sculptor Johan Gregor van der Schardt. The main building was square, about 15 metres on a side, with a semi-circular tower on its north and south sides. A planned wall was never built; an earth mound took its place and is the only remnant still in place.

The main floor held four rooms, one for Brahe's family and three for visiting astronomers. The northern tower housed the kitchens and the southern a library, where Brahe etched the motto Non haberi sed esse. The upper floor had a large room for royal visitors, among them James VI of Scotland, who came on 20 March 1590, and the primary instruments stood in the towers and on balconies. A loft held eight small rooms for students, and the basement had an alchemical laboratory and a small prison room. Gardens supplied herbs for his medicinal experiments, and the gatehouses held his printing workshop. Ponds and a paper mill lay beyond the walls.

Shortly after construction it became clear that wind moved the tower-mounted instruments, so Brahe built Stjärneborg nearby, with its instruments in pits at ground level. Among his instruments were a brass azimuthal quadrant of 1576, a Great Globe begun in 1580 that carried over 1,000 stars by 1595, a Triangular Sextant of 1582 and a Great Equatorial Armillary of 1585. Observations at their best were accurate to about a minute of arc, ten times better than earlier data.

Work at Uraniborg included the observation of the comet of 1577 and led to Brahe's geo-heliocentric Tychonic system of 1588. He described the instruments in his 1598 book Astronomiae instauratae mechanica. The building was one of the first observatories funded entirely by a government for research, and it is estimated to have cost about 1 percent of the state budget during construction.

Brahe left Ven in 1597 after losing the favour of Christian IV of Denmark, and the buildings were destroyed after his death in 1601. Johannes Kepler published his former master's star catalogue in 1627. The Round Tower in Copenhagen, inaugurated in 1642, replaced Uraniborg's astronomical role. Jean Picard visited the ruins in 1671 to record the site's position. Excavations in the 1950s revealed parts of Stjärneborg, the gardens have been replanted since 1985, and the site is now part of the Tycho Brahe Museum.
urasoe: Urasoe lies in the south of Okinawa Island, with Naha to the south, Ginowan to the north and Nishihara to the east. The city covers 19.09 square kilometres. The land is rugged and hilly to the east and slopes gently to the East China Sea in the west. It was once agricultural but is now heavily urbanised because of its closeness to Naha, the prefectural capital. The name combines two characters, 浦, meaning a coastal area, and 添, meaning ruling or uniting, and refers to ruling over many areas. An older form of the word is attested in Old Okinawan as uraosoi or uraosoe.

Urasoe was the original capital of the Okinawan kingdom of Chūzan for several centuries, until Shuri supplanted it in the late 14th or early 15th century. Shunten (1166 to 1237), the first known king of Chūzan, ruled from Urasoe, as did his son and grandson. For much of the 14th century Urasoe Castle was the largest on Okinawa, and it now contains the remains of several kings of the Ryukyu Kingdom.

Urasoe was completely razed in the Battle of Okinawa in 1945, in which 45 per cent of its population, 4,117 residents, died. The village office was re-established in 1946 to run basic administration, settle returning refugees and restore farmland. US military presence on the western coast grew in 1950 and eventually became Camp Kinser. The population grew rapidly from 1956 and Urasoe became a bedroom community of Naha. It was raised to city status on 1 July 1970.

Urasoe has seventy-two designated or registered cultural properties and monuments at national, prefectural or municipal level, including forty-four items of Ryūkyū lacquerware. The Urasoe Castle Site is a national historic site, and the Urasoe Shell Mound and Iso Castle Site are prefectural ones. The city is served by Naha Airport, the Okinawa Expressway and three stations of the Okinawa Urban Monorail. Orion Breweries has its headquarters there, and Camp Kinser, a United States Marine Corps base, lies on its coast.
urdu: Urdu is an Indo-Aryan language that originated in the upper Ganga-Yamuna doab, in and around the Delhi region, where Khari Boli was spoken. It shared a grammatical foundation with Khari Boli but was written in a revised Perso-Arabic script and borrowed vocabulary from Persian and Arabic. The contact of Hindu and Muslim cultures during the Muslim conquests of the twelfth to sixteenth centuries led to Hindustani, a product of what is called a composite Ganga-Jamuni tehzeeb.

Amir Khusrau, called the father of Urdu literature, founded an early literary tradition of Hindavi in the late thirteenth century. After the conquest of the Deccan, a form called Dakhini flourished as a vehicle of poetry, especially under the Bahmanids, with loanwords from Telugu and Marathi. The poet Ghulam Hamadani Mushafi used the name Urdu around 1780; ordu means army in Turkic languages.

Urdu is closely related to Hindi. They share a vocabulary base largely derived from Sanskrit and Prakrit, and the same phonology, syntax and grammar, so that many linguists count them as one language, Hindustani. Formal Urdu takes its literary and technical vocabulary from Persian and Arabic, formal Hindi from Sanskrit. Urdu is written right to left in an extension of the Persian alphabet, in the Nastaʿlīq style of calligraphy, and because Nastaʿlīq has thousands of ligatures, Urdu newspapers were handwritten by calligraphers until the late 1980s.

In 1837 Urdu became an official language of the British East India Company, replacing Persian across northern India; Persian had until then been the court language of the Indo-Islamic empires. In the early nineteenth century religious and social divisions led Urdu and Hindi to be set apart as distinct identities, associated with Muslims and Hindus respectively, each with its own script.

Urdu was chosen as a symbol of unity for the new Dominion of Pakistan in 1947, having already served as a lingua franca among Muslims in the north and northwest of British India. It is the national language of Pakistan, and in India it is among the languages of the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution.
urhi-teshub: Muršili III, known also as Urhi-Teshub, was the eldest surviving son of Muwatalli II and a grandson of Muršili II. He was a cousin of Tudhaliya IV and of Queen Maathorneferure. He took the throne at Tarhuntassa on his father's death, and his reign is dated about 1282 to 1275 BCE by the middle chronology or 1272 to 1265 BCE by the short chronology. A certain Hartapu calls himself a great king and son of the great king Muršili, normally identified with Muršili III, and he probably ruled Tarhuntassa in the second half of the 13th century BCE, so Muršili III seemingly had a son.

Muršili III moved the capital from Tarhuntassa, where it had been under Muwatalli, back to Hattusa. His legitimacy was severely weakened when the Assyrians captured Hanigalbat. In his seventh year he attacked and seized the strongholds of his uncle Hattusili at Hakpissa and Nerik to remove him as a threat to the throne. Hattusili wrote that he had submitted for seven years, and that when the king took Hakpissa and Nerik from him he submitted no more and made war, leaving the verdict to Ištar of Šamuha and the Storm God of Nerik.

In the revolt that followed Hattusili gathered a considerable force, including his local allies from Nerik and Hakpissa, many non-aligned Hittites who admired his record of service, and even some of the Kaska peoples, sworn enemies of the Hittites. His military success against Ramesses II of Egypt at the Battle of Kadesh was contrasted with the undistinguished occupant of the throne at Hattusa. Hattusili quickly defeated his nephew and seized the throne as Hattusili III, and he appointed Kurunta, Muršili's brother or brother-in-law, vassal king of Tarhuntassa to win his loyalty.

Hattusili III exiled his nephew to Syria. Muršili was at first given the fiefdom of Nuhašše and tried from there to keep his claim to the throne. After his plots failed he fled to Egypt, and Hattusili demanded that Ramesses II send him back.

Ramesses denied knowing where he was, and the two empires came dangerously close to war until they made peace in Year 21 of Ramesses II, with an extradition clause in the treaty. Muršili then disappears from history. A relief near Sirkeli Höyük, beside that of Muwatalli II, was deliberately destroyed in antiquity and is believed to have been his, a damnatio memoriae ordered by his uncle.
urho-kekkonen: Urho Kekkonen was born on 3 September 1900 at a small cabin in Pielavesi in Savo and spent his childhood in Kainuu. His family were farmers, and his father rose from farm-hand to forestry manager. During the Finnish Civil War he fought for the Kajaani chapter of the White Guard and later admitted to having killed a man in battle.

In his youth he was also a policeman and an athlete, and he trained as a lawyer. He chaired the nationalist organisation Suomalaisuuden Liitto from 1930 to 1932. In Germany between 1931 and 1933 he witnessed the rise of Adolf Hitler, and in 1934 he published a pamphlet, Demokratian itsepuolustus, warning of far-right radicalism. He joined the Agrarian League in 1933 and entered Parliament in 1936.

Kekkonen served as minister of justice, minister of the interior, speaker of Parliament and minister of foreign affairs, and was prime minister in 1950 to 1953 and 1954 to 1956. He was narrowly elected president in 1956 and was reelected in 1962 after the Note Crisis and the withdrawal of the main opposition candidate. He continued the active neutrality of his predecessor Juho Kusti Paasikivi, known as the Paasikivi–Kekkonen doctrine, under which Finland kept its independence and maintained trade with both NATO and Warsaw Pact states. Critics called this policy Finlandization.

He negotiated Finland's entry into EFTA, and historians credit his foreign and trade policies with keeping the market economy in step with Western Europe. In 1975 he hosted the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe in Helsinki. The balance of power tilted heavily towards the president. He favoured popular front cabinets of centrist and left-wing parties and often left out the National Coalition Party. In 1973 an emergency law extended his term by four years, passing Parliament by 170 votes to 28. Historians note that his perceived autocracy and the lack of genuine opposition weakened Finnish democracy.

Kekkonen was elected to a fourth term in 1978, but his health declined, and he resigned in late 1981 after years of memory lapses and failing eyesight. In April 1981 Prime Minister Mauno Koivisto stated that the cabinet was responsible to Parliament and not to the president, which is generally seen as the end of the Kekkonen era. Kekkonen died on 31 August 1986. Reforms of the Finnish Constitution between 1984 and 2003 increased the powers of Parliament and the prime minister at the expense of the president, and limited the president to two consecutive terms. Finland's second largest national park bears his name.
urmia: Urmia lies at an elevation of 1,330 metres (4,360 ft) above sea level along the Shahar River on the Urmia Plain, near the borders of Iran with Turkey and Iraq. Lake Urmia, one of the world's largest salt lakes, lies to the east of the city and the Turkish border to the west. The city is the trading centre of a fertile agricultural region where apples, grapes and tobacco are grown.

Several derivations of the name have been proposed. Richard Nelson Frye suggested an Urartian origin, while T. Burrow connected it with the Indo-Iranian words urmi, wave, and urmya, undulating. It may also come from the Assyrian Aramaic words ur, city, and mia, water, meaning city of water. In the Pahlavi era (1925 to 1979) the city was called Rezaiyeh, after Reza Shah.

According to Vladimir Minorsky there were villages on the Urmia Plain as early as 2000 BCE, under the influence of the Kingdom of Van. The city was an important town by the 9th century CE. After the Safavid shah Abbas the Great appointed Qasem Sultan Afshar governor of Mosul in 1622, an outbreak of plague forced him to leave, and he moved to western Azerbaijan, becoming the founder of the Afshar community of Urmia. The city became the capital of the Urmia Khanate in 1747, and the first Qajar monarch, Agha Mohammad Khan, was crowned there in 1795. In the Safavid period the neighbouring Ottoman Empire made several incursions and captured the city more than once, but the Safavids regained control each time.

In 1835 Urmia became the site of the first American Christian mission in Iran, led by Justin Perkins with Asahel Grant. During the nineteenth century the region saw a short-lived Assyrian renaissance, with many books and newspapers published in Syriac. Joseph Cochran and American medical colleagues built a medical college there in 1878. Around 1900 Christians made up more than 40 per cent of the city's population.

Urmia is the largest city of West Azerbaijan Province and the capital of the province and its county. Most residents are Azerbaijanis, with a large Kurdish minority and smaller Assyrian, Armenian and communities of speakers of Persian. Most are Muslims, but the city's churches, among them Assyrian, Armenian and Chaldean, preserve its Christian history, and it is the seat of a Chaldean Catholic archeparchy. Its population was 736,224 at the 2016 census. Urmia is known in Iran for volleyball and for Ashik music, which is registered in Iran's national heritage.
urnes-stave-church: An excavation in 1956 showed that two earlier churches had stood on the site. The first was built during the period of transition to Christianity in the palisade style, in which structural members were set into the ground. The second was built in the latter half of the 11th century. Both were small structures with a nave and chancel.

In the middle of the 12th century the second church was torn down, and a third, based on parts of the second but very different in design, was built. It was erected around 1130 or shortly after. Its design was immensely popular at the time and served as inspiration for later stave churches.

The church follows the basilica plan used by many Romanesque churches elsewhere in Europe, with cylindrical columns, cubic capitals and semicircular arches translated into timber. A raised central section of the nave, held by 16 large staves, defines the nave and aisles, and its roof stands 2 metres higher than the roofs of the aisles. The capitals are carved with human, animal and plant motifs, some of them traditional interlacing designs derived from the Viking tradition.

Strap-work elements salvaged from the 11th-century church were reused in the present building: several panels on the north wall, the north portal and a carved corner column. Their interlaced animals are among the last examples of Norse animal ornament and give the Urnes style its name. The struggle between a serpent and a great beast on the portal has been read as the onset of Ragnarok, and the animal as Níðhöggr eating the roots of Yggdrasil. Some scholars suggest that scenes from Norse mythology on the earlier church may be a reason for its early replacement.

In the 17th century the central nave was extended to the south, and furnishings were added, including a baptismal font in 1640, a wooden canopy over the altar in 1665, a pulpit in 1693 to 1695 and an altarpiece in 1699. Windows were added in the 18th century, and the richly decorated wall planks were covered during a restoration in the 20th century to stop further deterioration.

The Society for the Preservation of Norwegian Ancient Monuments has owned the church since 1881. The parish of Urnes was abolished in that year, and the church is now used only for special occasions such as baptisms and weddings. UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site in 1979.
urraca-of-leon-and-castile: Urraca was the only child of King Alfonso VI of León and Castile and his second wife, Constance of Burgundy. The place and date of her birth are unknown, but she was probably born in Sahagún or León around 1080. She married Raymond of Burgundy as part of Alfonso's diplomatic strategy of attracting alliances across the Pyrenees, after the Almoravids inflicted a heavy defeat on him at Sagrajas in 1086. Royal diplomas present the couple as rulers of Galicia from about 1090, although Alfonso VI kept control of its administration.

In 1093 the birth of an illegitimate brother, Sancho Alfónsez, threatened her position as sole heir. Alfonso regarded Sancho as his heir, and by March 1107 he was elected king. Raymond died in September 1107, and Urraca took responsibility for the administration of Galicia, where her infant son Alfonso Raimúndez was seen as Raymond's lawful successor. Sancho died fighting the Almoravids at Uclés on 29 May 1108, which made Urraca her father's sole heir.

Urraca succeeded her father, who died on 30 June or 1 July 1109, as the first queen regnant in European history. Alfonso I, King of Aragon and Navarre, married her at the castle of Monzón in October or November 1109. Two early chronicles say that Leonese aristocrats, convinced that a woman could not defend the kingdom against the Almoravids, forced the marriage on her. It proved unhappy: she accused Alfonso of physical abuse and separated from him. Galician nobles led by Pedro Fróilaz de Traba proclaimed Alfonso Raimúndez king, and the conflicts grew into continuous civil war.

Urraca's lover and chief supporter Gómez González was killed at the Battle of Candespina in 1111, and Pedro González de Lara replaced him. By the autumn of 1112 a truce was brokered and the marriage annulled on grounds of consanguinity. Urraca recovered Asturias, León and Galicia, but Alfonso occupied a significant part of Castile, and her half-sister Theresa and Count Henry of Portugal held Zamora and Extremadura. Theresa later agreed to be Urraca's vassal in exchange for a vast territory in León.

According to the twelfth-century Chronicon Compostellanum, Urraca died in childbirth on 8 March 1126 in the castle of Saldaña. The Historia Compostelana describes her as prudent, modest and sensible, but blames her failings on the weakness of women and calls her a Jezebel for her liaisons with magnates. Bernard F. Reilly notes that she remained in control of events and sees her solutions as pragmatic. Delaying the accession of her son Alfonso VII led to a turbulent transition, with the rebellion of Pedro González, an attempted invasion by the king of Aragon and renewed Galician revolts.
uruguay: Uruguay covers about 176,214 square kilometres of continental land and is the second-smallest sovereign nation in South America, after Suriname. The landscape is mostly rolling plains and low hill ranges called cuchillas, with a fertile coastal lowland and 660 kilometres of coastline. The highest point is Cerro Catedral, at 514 metres. The Río de la Plata lies to the south-west, and the Río Negro, dammed in 1945, formed the artificial Rincón del Bonete Lake. Montevideo is the southernmost national capital in the Americas, and Uruguay lies entirely south of the Tropic of Capricorn.

Hunter-gatherers lived in the region about 13,000 years ago. At the first contact with Europeans in the 16th century there were an estimated 9,000 Charrúa and 6,000 Chaná, with some Guaraní island settlements. Eastern Uruguay holds man-made tumuli called Cerritos de Indios, some about 5,000 years old. The Portuguese entered the region in 1512, and the Spanish in 1515. Fierce resistance and the lack of valuable resources limited settlement, the Spanish introduced cattle in 1603, and the first permanent Spanish settlement was Soriano in 1624. The Portuguese built a fort at Colonia del Sacramento in 1680, and the Spanish founded Montevideo in 1726 as a military stronghold.

British forces occupied Montevideo from February to September 1807. In 1811 José Gervasio Artigas, later Uruguay's national hero, led a revolt against Spanish authority and won the Battle of Las Piedras on 18 May. He became a champion of federalism and demanded autonomy for the Banda Oriental, while Buenos Aires pursued unitary centralism. Independence was secured between 1811 and 1828, after a struggle involving Portugal, Spain, the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata and the Empire of Brazil, and a constitution was enacted in 1830.

From the second half of the 19th century migration from Spain, Italy and France reshaped the population, and in the 20th century Uruguay became an advanced welfare state nicknamed the Switzerland of the Americas. Tensions during the Cold War, including the activities of the Tupamaros urban guerrilla movement, eroded democratic institutions, and a coup in 1973 began a dictatorship that lasted until 1985.

Uruguay is now a constitutional republic with a presidential system. Its 1967 constitution allows citizens to propose bills and call referendums, a feature drawn from Switzerland. Montevideo's metropolitan area holds about 1.9 million of its almost 3.5 million people, and 86.0 per cent identified as white in the 2023 census.
uruguayan-civil-war: The conflict grew out of rivalries among the leaders of Uruguayan independence. After the proclamation of independence in 1828, Juan Lavalleja, leader of the Thirty-Three Orientals, and the veteran commander Fructuoso Rivera contended for primacy. Rivera was chosen the first President of Uruguay on 6 November 1830 and defeated Lavalleja at Tupambaé on 18 September 1832. Lavalleja fled to the Brazilian province of Rio Grande do Sul, and an invasion he launched in March 1834 with the support of Juan Manuel de Rosas also failed.

Manuel Oribe, another of the Thirty-Three Orientals, was elected the second President on 1 March 1835. In January 1836 he removed Rivera from the army command, and on 16 July 1836 Rivera rebelled. Oribe's soldiers wore a white armband and Rivera's first wore blue, then red, since blue faded. From these marks came the conservative Blancos and the liberal Colorados.

Rivera was beaten at Carpintería on 19 September 1836 but, with help from the Riograndense Republic, defeated Oribe at Yucutujá in 1837 and at Palmar on 15 June 1838. France, then blockading Buenos Aires, backed Rivera, and Oribe resigned on 24 October 1838 and fled to Buenos Aires. Rosas refused to recognise Rivera and sought Oribe's return, and British and French intervention turned the struggle into an international war. On 6 December 1842 Oribe's Blancos crushed Rivera's army at Arroyo Grande and laid siege to Montevideo.

The siege lasted nine years. Montevideo had about thirty thousand inhabitants in 1843, only a third of them Uruguayan, and its defence rested largely on newly freed slaves, who numbered 5,000, and on foreign exiles. Uruguay had two governments: the Gobierno de la Defensa in Montevideo under Joaquín Suárez and the Gobierno del Cerrito under Oribe. British and French fleets protected the city from the sea, and French, Spanish and Italian legionnaires under Giuseppe Garibaldi fought for the Colorados. Britain and France withdrew in 1850 after a treaty favourable to Rosas.

A rising against Rosas by Justo José de Urquiza, governor of Entre Ríos, changed the situation in 1851. Brazil intervened in Uruguay in May 1851, and Rosas fell at Caseros in February 1852, after which Urquiza's forces lifted the siege. Montevideo then signed five treaties with Brazil, providing for perpetual alliance, joint navigation of the Río Uruguay, and the return of runaway slaves. Uruguay renounced its claims north of the Río Cuareim. Both sides had abolished slavery during the war, and the cattle industry was devastated.

Party feuding did not end. In 1870 the parties agreed spheres of influence, and the Revolution of the Lances followed in 1870 to 1872. The French author Alexandre Dumas described the siege in his novel The New Troy as a new Trojan war.
uruk: Uruk, the archaeological site known today as Warka, lies in Muthanna Governorate in Iraq, east of the present bed of the Euphrates, on an ancient channel of the river that is now dry. It is 93 kilometres northwest of ancient Ur and 108 kilometres southeast of Nippur.

The city formed when two smaller settlements of the Ubaid period, Unug and Kullaba, developed into cities and later merged. Their temple complexes became the Eanna District, dedicated to Inanna, and the Anu District. A canal system, described as Venice in the desert, ran through the city and joined it to the trade of the Euphrates and to the surrounding farmland.

The Uruk period, or Uruk expansion, saw a shift from small agricultural villages to a larger urban centre with a full-time bureaucracy, military and stratified society. Uruk was significantly larger and more complex than the other settlements of its time, which were generally about 10 hectares. Sumerian traders and colonists exported its culture, though Uruk could not keep long-distance control over colonies such as Tell Brak by military force.

According to the Sumerian King List the city was founded by the king Enmerkar, and Gilgamesh ruled it in the 27th century BCE. Proto-cuneiform tablets found there include the oldest known writing to feature a personal name, that of Kushim, who as an accountant recorded transactions in barley. After the Early Dynastic period the Akkadian Empire annexed Uruk and it declined, but it revived under the sovereignty of Ur, when the Eanna District was restored.

Following the collapse of Ur it declined steeply until about 850 BCE, when the Neo-Assyrian Empire annexed it as a provincial capital. It flourished under the Neo-Babylonians and Seleucids, and the Bīt Reš temple was one of the two main centres of Neo-Babylonian astronomy. A shift in the Euphrates and salinization from irrigation may have contributed to its decline. By 300 CE it was mostly abandoned, and by about 700 CE completely so. The last dated cuneiform tablet from Uruk, an astronomical almanac, dates to 79 or 80 CE.

The site covers about 5.5 square kilometres and has three major tells, those of the Eanna district, Bit Resh and Irigal. William Kennett Loftus visited it in 1849 and led the first excavations from 1850 to 1854. Julius Jordan's team from the German Oriental Society found the temple of Ishtar in 1912 and 1913, along with part of a brick city wall about 9 kilometres long, which is estimated to date from around 3000 BCE.

German archaeologists worked there for 39 seasons. Among the finds is the Mask of Warka, a carved marble female face of about 3100 BCE, probably a depiction of Inanna. Linguists have also proposed that the name Iraq derives from Uruk.
uruk-period: The Uruk period is named after the city of Uruk in southern Mesopotamia and follows the Ubaid period and precedes the Jemdet Nasr period, which is often treated as its final stage. In the broadest sense it covers the whole fourth millennium BCE.

The term was coined at a conference in Baghdad in 1930, together with the Ubaid and Jemdet Nasr periods, using data from Ur, Ubayd, Kish, Girsu, Jemdet Nasr and Susa and the first discoveries made by German archaeologists at Uruk in 1929. The Uruk culture is marked by what is sometimes called an urban revolution: the appearance of cities and the state, with a greater specialisation of activities and functions.

Southern Mesopotamia was the most productive farmland in the Near East, with irrigation based on barley, date palms and sheep kept for wool, and the marshes supplied fish, birds and reeds. Innovations included irrigated agriculture with the ard, a wooden plough, the potter's wheel, standardised ceramics and bricks produced in large quantities, and large-scale wool production in textile workshops.

Instruments for supervising workers and resources developed with state institutions, and the first writing, proto-cuneiform, appears around 3400 to 3300 BCE, essentially for administrative purposes. Uruk itself was the largest settlement by far: it may have covered 230 to 250 hectares in the Late Uruk period, with a population of between 25,000 and 50,000.

These innovations were once thought to have begun in Uruk, but neighbouring regions, including Susiana, north Mesopotamia, western Syria and south-eastern Anatolia, took part in the process. The Uruk expansion saw the setting up of outposts and colonies from southern Mesopotamia on trade routes, at sites such as Godin Tepe, Nineveh and Hacinebi, and along the Euphrates at Habuba Kabira and Jebel Aruda. Beveled-rim bowls typical of the culture are found from the Caucasus to Pakistan. The Late Uruk phase, about 3500 to 3300 or 3200 BCE, marked the peak, and after about 3300 or 3200 the Near East became culturally more fragmented.
urumqi: Ürümqi lies west of the Tian Shan mountain ranges, in the pass between the Bogda Shan to the east and the Tian Shan to the west that connects the Dzungar Basin to the north with the Turpan Depression to the south. Although it is surrounded by deserts, the Gurbantünggüt in the north and the Taklamakan in the south, small rivers flowing from the snow-capped mountains water the area. The name comes, according to Herold J Wiens, from the Oirat words ürü and mchi, together meaning beautiful pasture. The city has an average elevation of 800 metres.

In prehistory the site was occupied by a nomadic people known in Chinese accounts as the Jushi. A town called Urabo stood about 10 kilometres from the present southern suburbs, and the Tang government founded a city called Luntai in 648 CE as part of the Protectorate General to Pacify the West, collecting taxes from caravans on the northern Silk Road. Little is known of the area between the Tang and the Qing, and researchers generally believe there were no permanent settlements for most of that period. The Mongols called the wider area Bishbalik, meaning five cities. Turpan, 200 kilometres to the southeast, remained more important.

The Qing took Ürümqi in 1755 during their conquest of the Dzungar Khanate, and the Dzungars of the region were eliminated in what is called the Dzungar genocide. The Qing built a fort and established garrisons of Manchu and Mongol bannermen and Han Chinese troops. They began a walled city in 1763, completed in 1767, which the Qianlong Emperor named Dihua, meaning to enlighten and civilize. A second city, Gongning Cheng, was built in 1771 for the bannermen and became the seat of government, while Dihua grew into Xinjiang's commercial and financial centre. Han Chinese and Hui Muslims from Gansu and Shaanxi settled there. In 1884 the Guangxu Emperor made Xinjiang a province with Dihua as its capital.

Warlords ruled Xinjiang from the city after the Qing fell, among them Yang Zengxin, Jin Shuren and Sheng Shicai. The name Ürümqi was restored on 1 February 1954 because the Chinese Communist Party considered Dihua belittling and ethnically chauvinist. In 1962, after 60,000 people left Yining and Tacheng for the Soviet Union, the government moved its administrative buildings and industrial focus to Ürümqi and began a railway to the east.

Ürümqi is the capital and largest city of the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region and has an estimated population of over 4.5 million, predominantly Han Chinese with one of the largest Uyghur populations in China. It has been a multiethnic city since the Qing conquest. Xinjiang University and Xinjiang Normal University are based there.
usama-ibn-munqidh: Usama was born on 4 July 1095, the son of Murshid and the nephew of Nasr, emir of Shaizar. His father gave up the emirate to Usama's uncle Sultan, being more interested in religion and hunting than in politics. Shaizar was attacked many times by the Banu Kilab of Aleppo, the Hashshashin, the Byzantines and the crusaders, but its natural fortifications meant that it never fell. Usama learned the Quran, hunted and trained for battle as a faris. By his own account he first fought in 1119, in a raid on the crusaders at Apamea. After Sultan had a son of his own, Usama's position at Shaizar became untenable, and he could not return for good after his father's death in 1137.

Captured in a battle near Homs, Usama entered the service of Zengi, the atabeg of Mosul and Aleppo. After the Byzantine emperor John II Comnenus besieged Shaizar in April 1138, he moved to Damascus and the service of Mu'in ad-Din Unur. He travelled several times to the Kingdom of Jerusalem on diplomatic missions and became friendly with members of the Knights Templar. Suspected of plotting against Unur, he fled to Fatimid Cairo in November 1144.

In Cairo he became a wealthy courtier and adviser to the vizier Ibn as-Sallar, and was again caught up in plots. Ibn al-Athir says Usama instigated the vizier's assassination in 1153. He reached Damascus in June 1154 and lost his library to raiders when bringing his family there in 1156. In 1157 an earthquake destroyed Shaizar and killed most of his relatives. He later served Nur ad-Din, the Artuqid Kara Arslan at Hisn Kayfa and, from 1174, Saladin. He died in Damascus on 17 November 1188.

Usama was known to his contemporaries as a poet and adib, a man of letters, and compiled anthologies such as the Kitab al-'Asa, the Book of the Staff. His best-known work, the Kitab al-I'tibar, written around 1183 as a gift for Saladin, is a book of examples from which to draw lessons and describes the crusaders he knew, some of them friends. It survived in a single manuscript in the Escorial, discovered by Hartwig Derenbourg in 1880. It is an anthology of humorous and moralising tales, not a chronological memoir, and some anecdotes about the crusaders are obvious jokes. Carole Hillenbrand wrote that it would be dangerously misleading to take its evidence at face value.
usambara-mountains: The Usambara Mountains are the easternmost ranges of the Eastern Arc Mountains, in the Lushoto District of the Tanga Region. They are about 90 kilometres long and 30 to 50 kilometres wide, and they formed nearly two million years ago by faulting and uplifting, from Precambrian metamorphic rocks. Two sub-ranges are distinguished: the West Usambaras, which are higher, and the East Usambaras, which lie nearer the coast, receive more rainfall and are significantly smaller.

The highest point is Chambolo peak at 2,289 metres. Because there were no glaciations and the climate stayed fairly consistent, the rainforest has evolved over a long period and holds a high number of endemic species, among them the Usambara eagle-owl, the Usambara akalat, the Usambara weaver and the African violet.

The mountains were inhabited by Bantu, Shambaa and Maasai people, a mix of farmers and herders. A Shambaa kingdom based at Vugha was founded by Mbegha in the first half of the 18th century. His grandson Kinyashi Muanga Ike gave it a stronger political and military structure, and under Kinyashi's son Kimweri ye Nyumbai it grew to cover both the West and East Usambaras and to reach the coast and the Pangani River valley. After Kimweri died in 1862 the kingdom fell apart in a succession struggle.

In the late 19th century German colonists in the Usambara District of German East Africa brought cash crops such as coffee, tea and quinine, and designated forests as reserves for water conservation or timber. In 1882 the district's governor, Walter von Saint Paul-Illaire, sent seeds of a small herb to his father, and Hermann Wendland described the plant as Saintpaulia ionantha, the African violet.

After the First World War the area became part of the British mandate territory of Tanganyika, whose administration continued to reserve and exploit the forests. Foreign-controlled logging companies carried out large-scale deforestation from the 1950s, and by 2000 nearly 70 percent of the original forest cover of the East Usambaras had been lost, and over 85 percent in the West.

The range can be reached from the town of Lushoto in the west and from Amani in the east. Much of the area is farmed by subsistence farmers who depend on the forests for timber, medicinal plants and fuelwood. Its watersheds supply water to much of the population of north-eastern Tanzania. Protected zones have been created in the range and expanded with help from the Tanzanian government, non-governmental organisations, research teams and donor countries such as Norway. The Mazumbai Forest Reserve is regarded as the last pristine tropical forest in the East Usambaras.
usedom: Usedom, in Polish Uznam, is the second largest Pomeranian island after Rügen and the most populous island in the Baltic Sea. It lies north of the Szczecin Lagoon estuary of the Oder. Its total area is 445 square kilometres, of which 373 are in the German part and 72 in the Polish part. About 80 per cent of the island belongs to the German district of Vorpommern-Greifswald in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, and the eastern part, with the largest town, Świnoujście, lies in the Polish West Pomeranian Voivodeship. The Strait of Świna separates it from the island of Wolin, and the Peenestrom divides it from the mainland. The island is mostly flat and partly covered by marshes.

The area has been settled since the Stone Age and was probably inhabited by Germanic Rugians before Polabian Slavs moved in during the fifth to seventh centuries. Trade centres such as Vineta or Jomsborg and Menzlin were established around the island. In the 1110s the Danes destroyed the town of Uznam. In the 1120s the island and Western Pomerania came under Polish suzerainty under Bolesław III Wrymouth as the vassal Duchy of Pomerania, and Otto of Bamberg was entrusted with converting its people; in 1128 the Pomeranian Duke Wartislaw I was converted. The Premonstratensians founded a monastery at Grobe in 1155, moved in 1309 to Pudagla.

On 26 June 1630 Gustavus Adolphus landed with a Swedish army at Peenemünde during the Thirty Years' War. When the last duke of Pomerania, Bogislaw XIV, died in 1637 the duchy ceased to exist. Sweden annexed Usedom after the war and held it until 1720, when it was sold to the Prussian king Frederick William I for 2 million thalers. Frederick the Great developed a seaport at Swinemünde in 1740, and with Prussia the island became part of the German Empire in 1871.

In the Second World War the Luftwaffe tested missiles and rockets, including the V-1 and V-2, near Peenemünde, using thousands of slave labourers, and a subcamp of Sachsenhausen stood in the town of Usedom. In 1945 the eastern part, with Swinemünde, was assigned to Poland at Potsdam, and the surviving German inhabitants were expelled. Since the 19th century the seaside resorts of Ahlbeck, Heringsdorf and Bansin, the three imperial spas, have drawn visitors, and the island is one of Germany's major holiday areas.
usingen: Usingen lies on the Usa River in the Usinger Becken at the north-eastern edge of the Taunus, about 30 km north of Frankfurt am Main, 27 km south of Wetzlar and 38 km north-east of Wiesbaden. The town core stands about 300 metres above sea level. Until 1972 this residential and school town was the seat of the former district of Usingen, which was then merged with the Obertaunus district to form the Hochtaunuskreis.

Usingen, in Latin Osinga, probably existed in Frankish times as a fortified stopping place at an old crossroads. It is first mentioned in the Codex Eberhardi, a manuscript from the Fulda monastery, in references generally dated between 754 and 802. In 1207 it passed to the Counts of Diez. The Counts of Nassau acquired the Usinger Land by pledge in 1326 and for good by 1405. A Nassau castle and a wall with five towers protected the small weaving town in the Middle Ages, and it probably received town rights in the 14th century.

When the Nassau-Saarbrücken lands were divided on 31 March 1659, Count Walrad received the Usinger Land. He governed for 43 years and served as field marshal of the Dutch States Army under William III of Orange. After the Thirty Years' War and three town fires in the 17th century, which reduced the population, he settled Huguenots in the town and had the New Town built. A great fire in 1692 destroyed the Upper Town, which he ordered rebuilt in symmetrical rows of houses. He had a new stately home built on the castle's site in 1660–1663. The Princes of Nassau-Usingen lived there from 1688 to 1744.

Usingen has been a school town since the Reformation, with a Latin school until 1817, a teachers' college from 1851 to 1926 and the Christian-Wirth-Schule since 1926. Fire destroyed the palace in 1873, and it was rebuilt and now houses that school. The Huguenot church of 1700, built by Benedikt Burtscher, stands at the old marketplace and is now the town library. The violinist August Wilhelmj was born in Usingen on 21 September 1845. In 1972 Usingen merged with Eschbach, Kransberg, Merzhausen, Michelbach, Wernborn and Wilhelmsdorf.
usman-dan-fodio: Usman was born in Gobir on 15 December 1754 into the Toronkawa, a Fulani scholarly clan whose ancestors had migrated from Futa Tooro in the 1300s and settled in Hausaland. His family moved to Degel, where he studied the Quran with his father before moving to other teachers. At the age of 20 he set up his own school at Degel. From 1774 he travelled as an itinerant preacher, for twelve years in Gobir and Kebbi and then five years in Zamfara. His students included his younger brother Abdullahi and the Hausa ruler Yunfa.

In his writings he condemned the ruling elite for enslavement, idol worship, overtaxation, arbitrary rule and greed, and he insisted on the Maliki school of law. Peasants and other poorer people followed him in large numbers, as did Fulani and Tuareg pastoralists whose cattle officials had seized.

In 1802 Yunfa, once his student, turned against him, revoked the autonomy of Degel and tried to have him killed at Alkalawa. Usman wrote the Masa'il muhimma on the obligation to emigrate from persecution, and his community fled to Gudu, a journey of four or five days. There his followers elected him Commander of the Believers, with Abdullahi dan Fodio and Muhammed Bello the first to pledge allegiance. He was about fifty, took no part in the fighting and left the military command to others.

The Muslims defeated a Gobir force at Tabkin Kwotto and, after the harvest of October 1804, began an aggressive campaign in the hinterland of Alkalawa. After the defeat of Gobir, many Hausa kings attacked the Muslim communities in their lands, and Usman appointed fourteen leaders and sent them back to their territories to lead jihad. He passed the actual leadership of the Sokoto state to his son Muhammed Bello and moved to Sokoto in 1815.

Usman died at Sokoto on 20 April 1817, aged 62. Muhammed Bello succeeded him as second caliph, and his brother Abdullahi became emir of Gwandu. By 1830 the jihad had engulfed most of what is now northern Nigeria and northern Cameroon, and until the British conquest at the beginning of the 20th century there were twelve caliphs. He had promoted education for women as well as men, and his daughter Nana Asma'u translated some of his works into local languages. Muslims view him as a mujaddid, a renewer of the faith. His example inspired later jihads, including those of Seku Amadu and Omar Saidou Tall.
ustase: The word ustaša comes from the Croatian verb ustati, to rise up, and was also a military rank in the Imperial Croatian Home Guard. A major influence on the movement was the 19th-century activist Ante Starčević, who advocated Croatian unity and independence and was anti-Habsburg and anti-Serbian. During the 1920s the lawyer Ante Pavelić, a follower of Josip Frank's Pure Party of Rights, became the leading advocate of Croatian independence, and in 1927 he secretly contacted Benito Mussolini.

The organisation was active as one body from 1929, took the name Ustaša – Croatian Revolutionary Movement in 1933, and in 1932 its newspaper, signed by Pavelić, proclaimed violence and terror as its main means. In 1933 it issued the Seventeen Principles, its official ideology, which declared that people not Croat by blood would be excluded from political life.

Before the Second World War the organisation engaged in terrorism against the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, and with IMRO it assassinated King Alexander I in 1934. The Axis powers invaded Yugoslavia on 6 April 1941. Vladko Maček, leader of the Croatian Peasant Party, refused German offers to lead a government, and on 10 April Slavko Kvaternik proclaimed the Independent State of Croatia, an Italo-German quasi-protectorate headed by Pavelić as Poglavnik.

In May 1941 Ustaše ministers declared the aim of an ethnically pure Croatia, and the stated policy was to kill one third of the Serbs, expel one third and convert one third to Catholicism. The regime cooperated with Nazi Germany in the Holocaust and carried out genocide against Serbs, Jews and Roma. The first mass killing of Serbs was on 30 April 1941, when 196 villagers were killed at Gudovac. A first group of camps opened in spring 1941, and the Jasenovac complex was built between August 1941 and February 1942. Bosniaks were regarded as Muslim Croats and not persecuted on racial grounds. In spring 1942 Ustaše and Chetniks signed collaboration agreements against the partisans.

The movement collapsed in 1945. Many members fled to countries including Canada, Australia, Germany and Argentina, and the survivors split into rival groups, among them Pavelić's Croatian Liberation Movement. Pavelić was shot near Buenos Aires on 9 April 1957 and later died of his injuries. The greeting Za dom, spremni, meaning For home, ready, is today associated with Ustaše sympathisers.
usumacinta-river: The Usumacinta River, named after the howler monkey, runs through south-eastern Mexico and north-western Guatemala. It is formed by the junction of the Pasión River, which rises in the Sierra de Santa Cruz in Guatemala, and the Salinas River, also called the Chixoy or Negro, which descends from the Sierra Madre de Guatemala. It defines part of the border between Guatemala and the Mexican state of Chiapas, forms canyons in the Cañón del Usumacinta reserve, and then crosses the plain of Tabasco to the Gulf of Mexico. With the Salinas, Chixoy and Negro in Guatemala, its length is about 1,000 kilometres.

The Palizada and the San Pedro y San Pablo branch from the main stem and empty into the Laguna de Términos. In Tabasco the Grijalva River joins the Usumacinta at Tres Brazos, and the two form the wetlands of the Pantanos de Centla, a biosphere reserve of 302,702 hectares.

The river and its tributaries were important trade routes for the ancient Maya. Yaxchilan and Piedras Negras, two of the most powerful cities of the Classic period, lie on its banks, and artistic similarities between Yaxchilan and Chinkultic suggest communication between this region and the western Maya sites. Before roads such as the Border Highway, built by the Mexican government in the early 1990s, reached the jungle, the river was the only means of travel, and hardwood trunks were floated downstream to Tabasco.

In the 1980s many Guatemalan refugees fled across the river into Mexico, and others formed communities in the jungle on the Guatemalan shore, hiding from the government until the peace accords of the 1990s. A hydroelectric project proposed in the 1980s at Boca del Cerro, near Tenosique, would have flooded Piedras Negras and Yaxchilan. It failed for reasons that included siltation, geology and seismic activity, helped by protests from conservationists, archaeologists and writers. A smaller project proposed in 1990 was also defeated. Frans and Trudi Blom had proposed in the 1950s that a part of the Selva Lacandona be reserved for the Lacandon Maya, linking the preservation of culture to that of habitat.

The Usumacinta marks the only visible natural boundary between the Yucatán Peninsula and the rest of Mexico. Its Guatemalan and Mexican banks hold some of the best-known Maya sites, among them Yaxchilan and Piedras Negras.
utagawa-hiroshige: Hiroshige was born Andō Tokutarō in the Yayosu Quay section of the Yaesu area of Edo, into a samurai family. His father, Gen'emon, was fire warden for the Yayosu Quay area. His mother died in early 1809 and his father later that year, after handing his fire warden duties to his twelve-year-old son, a post that left him much leisure. He studied Kanō-style painting under Okajima Rinsai, and, after Toyokuni had no room for him, joined the Utagawa school under Toyohiro. By 1812 he was permitted to sign his works under the art name Hiroshige. His early work included book illustrations and prints of beauties and kabuki actors.

Not until 1829 to 1830 did Hiroshige begin the landscapes he is known for, such as the Eight Views of Ōmi. In 1832 he joined an official procession to Kyoto, which let him sketch the Tōkaidō route, and on his return he produced The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō, which made his success. The designs drew on his travels along the whole 490 kilometres and included details of date, location and anecdotes of his fellow travellers. The series was reissued in three versions, one made jointly with Kunisada. He also produced forty-six of the seventy prints of The Sixty-nine Stations of the Kisokaidō, jointly with Keisai Eisen.

His subjects were atypical of ukiyo-e, whose usual focus was beautiful women, popular actors and the pleasure districts. Hokusai's Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji influenced his choice of subject, though his approach was more poetic and ambient. He pioneered the vertical format in landscape printing, and in his Edo series he often places large objects, people or animals in the foreground, a device derived from Western art. Hiroshige produced over 8,000 works.

In 1856 Hiroshige retired from the world and became a Buddhist monk, the year he began his Edo series, which a wealthy Buddhist priest paid for in advance. He never lived in financial comfort. He died in the great Edo cholera epidemic of 1858, at the age of 62, and was buried in a Zen temple in Asakusa. For scholars and collectors his death marked the start of a rapid decline in ukiyo-e, especially under the westernisation after the Meiji Restoration of 1868. His work influenced European painting in the trend of Japonism: Monet and Manet collected and studied his compositions, and Van Gogh copied two of the Edo views.
utah: Utah is a landlocked state in the Mountain West and one of the Four Corners states, sharing a border with Arizona, Colorado and New Mexico, and also bordering Wyoming, Idaho and Nevada. It lies at the convergence of three geological regions: the Rocky Mountains, the Great Basin and the Colorado Plateau. Most of the western half lies in the Great Basin. The Wasatch Range runs down the middle of the northern third, and the Uinta Mountains in the northeast hold Kings Peak, the highest point. At the western base of the Wasatch Range lies the Wasatch Front, a series of valleys and basins stretching from Brigham City to Nephi, where about 75 per cent of the population lives.

The Ancestral Puebloans and the Fremont people lived in Utah for thousands of years before Europeans arrived; the Fremont built houses of straw and disappeared from the region around the 15th century. The Navajo settled in the region around the 18th century, and in the mid-18th century the Goshute, Paiute, Shoshone and Ute also settled there. The name Utah comes from the Spanish Yuta, recorded from the 17th century and borrowed from the name of the Ute, a people whose name for themselves is Núuchi-u. It is commonly said to mean people of the mountains.

Francisco Vázquez de Coronado explored southern Utah in 1540 while looking for Cíbola. A group led by two Catholic priests, the Domínguez-Escalante expedition, left Santa Fe in 1776 hoping to find a route to California and travelled as far north as Utah Lake. In 1821, the year Mexico became independent, the region became part of its territory of Alta California.

Many early settlers, even under Mexico, came from the United States, among them Mormons fleeing persecution. In 1848, after the Mexican-American War, the region was annexed by the United States and became Utah Territory. Disputes between the Mormon community and Congress delayed statehood until 1896, when, after Utah agreed to outlaw polygamy, it was admitted as the 45th state.

The capital is Salt Lake City, on the Wasatch Front. The 2020 census counted 3,271,616 people. Slightly over half of Utahns are Mormons, mostly members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, which has its world headquarters in Salt Lake City, and Utah is the only state where a majority belongs to a single church.
utah-territory: The Territory of Utah was an organised incorporated territory of the United States from 9 September 1850 until 4 January 1896, when it was admitted as the 45th state. At its creation it included all of present-day Utah, most of Nevada apart from a part of the south including the Las Vegas area, much of western Colorado and the extreme southwest corner of Wyoming. The area had been inhabited by indigenous people for over 12,000 years, including the Puebloan builders of stone masonry and the Fremont culture, who left after a long drought in the 1200s. The Navajo, Paiute and Shoshone settled later, and Juan Antonio de Rivera of New Spain is the first known European to enter, in 1765.

Mormon pioneers began settling the Salt Lake Valley in 1847 and relied on institutions of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints in place of secular civil government. They drafted a constitution for a State of Deseret in 1849, with proposed borders covering the Great Basin and the Colorado River watershed, and petitioned Congress under Brigham Young to admit it. Congress instead organised the territory as part of the Compromise of 1850, which sought to preserve the balance between slave and free states, without mentioning slavery. President Millard Fillmore signed the act on the day California was admitted.

Young was inaugurated as first governor. The capital was at Fillmore from 1850 to 1856, then moved to Salt Lake City. Mormon governance was controversial in the rest of the country, partly because of newspaper depictions of the polygamous marriages practised by the settlers.

Non-Mormon settlers were drawn to the west by the 1858 silver discovery at the Comstock Lode, and the Nevada Territory was created from the western part in 1861 as the federal government sought more control over silver mining. Gold at Breckenridge in 1859 brought miners from the east, and in 1861 Congress transferred a large part of the eastern territory to the new Colorado Territory.

In 1869 the territorial legislature approved women’s suffrage, and on 12 February 1870 the right to vote was extended to free white women who were US citizens aged 21 or older. Seraph Young Ford, a schoolteacher, cast her ballot in the Salt Lake City municipal election on 14 February 1870, the first woman to vote under an equal suffrage law in the United States.

Utah stayed a territory 46 years, much longer than Nevada, admitted in 1864, and Colorado, admitted in 1876. The beehive, chosen as the emblem of the provisional State of Deseret in 1848, stands for industry, and the sego lilies beside it for peace; both appear on the state coat of arms.
uthman-ibn-affan: Uthman was born in Mecca around 576 into the Banu Abd Shams clan of the Quraysh and its leading family, the Banu Umayya, then the most powerful family of the Quraysh. According to the account of the 9th-century scholar Ibn Sa'd, he became the fourth convert to Islam, and Ibn Ishaq holds that Abu Bakr brought him to Muhammad.

Under pressure from the Quraysh he migrated to Abyssinia with his wife Ruqayya, a daughter of Muhammad, in April 615, and in 622 the couple were among the third group of Muslims to migrate to Medina. His marriages to two of Muhammad's daughters, Ruqayya and Umm Kulthum, earned him the title Dhu al-Nurayn, the Possessor of Two Lights.

Before dying, the caliph Umar appointed a council of six early companions, among them Uthman and Ali ibn Abi Talib, to choose his successor, and Uthman, then aged 68, was elected. His rule saw expansion into Persia, as far as Khorasan and Transoxiana, and westward to Ifriqiya, and he delegated military authority to kinsmen such as Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan. In 649 Mu'awiya was allowed to set up a navy, which defeated the Byzantine fleet at the Battle of the Masts in 655.

Around 650, noticing differences in how the Qur'an was recited as Islam spread, he ordered a committee headed by Zayd ibn Thabit to prepare a standard text from the copy kept by Hafsa bint Umar. Copies were sent to the main cities and other versions were ordered burnt. Shi'a Muslims use the same Qur'an but do not believe it was first compiled by Uthman.

Discontent grew over his fiscal policies and his appointment of relatives to office. Around 654 he called his twelve provincial governors to Medina, and rebel contingents of about 1,000 each came from Egypt, Kufa and Basra.
